Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 1–3:

[Page 122]
[Surat al-Waqi'ah]
It has ninety-six verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿When the Event occurs,﴾ ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence,﴾ ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others].﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the Event occurs,﴾ ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence,﴾ ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others].﴾

As for the connection of this surah with what precedes it, it is in several respects.

The first: that the previous surah includes an enumeration of the blessings bestowed upon man, and a demand that he be thankful, and a prohibition against denying them, as has passed. This surah includes mention of the recompense of good for those who give thanks and of evil for those who deny and disbelieve.

The second: that the previous surah contains admonitions by mentioning the favours toward the servants, and this surah likewise mentions the recompense concerning them on the Day of Mutual Disillusion (al-Tanad).

The third: that the previous surah is a surah manifesting mercy, and this surah is a surah manifesting awe, in contrast with that surah along with what precedes it. As for the connection of the first with the last: at the end of that surah there is an allusion to the attributes by way of negation and affirmation, and at the beginning of this surah there is an allusion to the Resurrection and what it contains of rewards and punishments; and each of them indicates the exaltedness of His name, the greatness of His station, the perfection of His power and the might of His dominion. Then, in the verse there are issues:

First issue: In its interpretation there are several opinions. The first: the meaning is, when the Resurrection—the Event—or the Earthquake—the Event—occurs, which everyone acknowledges, and no one can deny it, and the obstinacy of the obstinate will be nullified; so it will abase the disbelievers into the depths of the Fire and exalt the believers into the ranks of Paradise: these in the Blazing Fire and those in bliss. The second: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ the people will be shaken, so it abases the high and exalts the low. On this view, it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We turned its uppermost part to its lowest﴾ [al-Hijr: 74] in indicating the severity of the Event, because the punishment that made the high low by demolition, and the low high, until the low land became like firm mountains, and firm mountains like low land, is more intense and more emphatic; so the lofty towers became level with the earth. The Event that occurs lifts up the low, making parts of the earth high and parts of the heaven low. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾; for it is an indication that the earth moves with a disturbing motion and the mountains are pulverized, so the low earth becomes like firm mountains, and the towering mountains become like the low earth, as the blowing of the wind does to sandy land. The third: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾

Page 123

its occurrence becomes manifest to everyone, and the manner of its occurrence; so there is no denying it and no interpretation that appears. So His saying: ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾ is coordinated with ﴿denying﴾ in sequence, so that it is like the speaker's saying: "I have no doubt or error in the matter," i.e., no one has the power to raise the low or abase the high.

Second issue: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ may be that "the Event" is an attribute of a omitted noun, which is the Resurrection or the Earthquake as we have explained; and it may be that the omitted noun is something unspecified, and the feminine ta' indicates the severity of the matter that occurs and its awesomeness, as one says: "The occurring one occurred," meaning the matter occurred whatever it was; and our saying "the matter is occurring" only indicates the occurrence of a matter, even if it is slight in comparison to his saying "the occurring one occurred," since in "the occurring one" there is an added attribute beyond the mere fact of being something. Let us explain this by showing that the ha' serves intensification in their saying: "So-and-so is a transmitter (rawiyah) and a genealogist (nassabah)." When they wished to intensify his being a transmitter, they could have used an attribute after the predicate and said: "So-and-so is a good, or fine, or excellent transmitter," but they turned from lengthiness to brevity with added benefit, and said: they bring a letter in place of a word, just as we bring the ha' of feminization when we say "zalimah" (oppressive, feminine) instead of the speaker's saying "zalim unthā" (a female oppressor). For this reason they were obliged to state the female when the ha' cannot express it, as in their saying "shah unthā" (a female sheep); and like writing in the plural, where we say "qālū" instead of the speaker's saying "qāla," and "qālā" instead of his saying "qāla" and "qāla"; so likewise in intensification, they wished to bring a letter that replaces a word, and the letter indicating the addition should be at the end, because addition comes after the origin of a thing; so they placed the ha' when it is not for feminization and singularity in the singular word, not in the plural, for intensification. Having established this, we say of "the occurring one occurred" and "the Event occurred": this has the meaning but not the wording. As for meaning, because by their saying "the occurring one occurred" they intended that the occurring is an addition beyond the basic sense of what occurs. As for wording, because if the ha' were for intensification, it would not be permissible to attach a feminine pronoun to the verb; rather they should have said "kāna al-kā'in" and "waqa'a al-wāqi'," and this is not possible. We say: what is meant by it is intensification.

Third issue: What does ﴿idhā﴾ govern? We say: there are three views. The first: a preceding verb that makes idhā an object, not an adverb, namely "udhkur" (remember), as if He said: "Remember the Resurrection." The second: its governing element is "laysa li-waq'atihā kādhibah" (there is no denying its occurrence), as you say: "On Friday I have no business." The third: "some will be abased and some exalted," which is indicated by ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾. It was also said that its governing element is His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?﴾, i.e., on the Day of the occurrence of the Event.

Fourth issue: ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾ indicates that it occurs at once, so "waqʿah" is for a single occurrence. His saying ﴿kādhibah﴾ may bear several meanings:

The first: "kādhibah" is an attribute of an omitted noun which is replaced by it; its estimate: "there will be no soul that denies."

The second: the ha' is for intensification, as you say of "al-wāqi'ah," and its explanation has already passed.

The third: it is a verbal noun like "al-'āqibah." If we take the first view, then the lam may bear two meanings:

One of them: that it is for causation, i.e., no soul will lie on that day because of the severity of its occurrence, as one says: "There is no liar before the king because of his control of affairs," so it is a general negation in the sense that everyone affirms him in what he says; and he said: and before it there were souls that lied in many matters, but there is no liar, so he says: there is no Resurrection because of the severity of its occurrence and the manifestness of the matter; and as one says: the matter does not admit denial because of its manifestness to everyone; so it is a specific negation in the sense that no one denies, so he says: there is no Resurrection, and before it there were souls asserting it, lying about it.

The second: that it is for transitivity, as one says: "There is no striker for Zayd," and then its estimate: when the Event occurs, there is no matter for its occurrence that has a liar if it reports about it; so it is abasing and exalting, abasing some and exalting others.

On this view, it is not a governing element in "idhā," and it has the sense of "there is no liar for it." It says: it is an easy matter that can be borne, as is said to one who undertakes a great matter thinking he can bear it: "Ask yourself," i.e., you made the matter easy for yourself, and it is not easy.

Page 124

If we take the second view, namely intensification, then there are two meanings:

One of them: there is no great liar for it, in the sense that whoever lies and undertakes a great lie cannot lie because of the terror of that day.

The second: that if anyone lied and said on that day "there is no Resurrection and no Event," he would be a great liar, and there is no liar of such greatness on that day. The first is more indicative of the terror of the day. On the third view, what we have mentioned returns to the meaning that there is no liar on that day, but rather everyone affirms it.

Fifth issue: ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾ its estimate is "it is abasing and exalting," and this has been mentioned in the general exegesis, and there are other views on it:

The first: "abasing and exalting" are two attributes of the lying soul, i.e., there will be no one for its occurrence who denies it or who alters the speech, so that it abases one matter and exalts another, and so it is abasing; or it may be an addition to explain the truthfulness of creation on that day and the impossibility of their lying; and the liar alters speech, then when he wishes to deny lying about himself he says: "I did not recognize a single word of what happened," and perhaps he says: "I did not recognize a single letter," and this is because the liar may lie about the essence of the matter, and perhaps he lies about an attribute of its attributes; and an attribute may be noticed, and may not be noticed in a considered way, and may not be noticed at all.

(Example of the first): one says: "Zayd did not come," while he has come.

(Example of the second): "He did not come on Friday."

(Example of the third): "He did not come at the early morning of Friday," while he came at the early morning of Friday, and "he did not come at the very beginning of the early morning of Friday."

The second is less than the first, and the fourth less than all. So when one says: "I do not know a single lying word," he denies lying in the report and in its attribute; and one who says: "I did not recognize a single letter" denies something beyond that; and one who says: "I did not recognize a single trace" is above that. So His saying: ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence, abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾ means: whoever alters, altering even if it is slight.

Fifth issue: ﴿abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾ its estimate is "it is abasing and exalting," and this has been mentioned in the general exegesis, and there are other views on it:

The first: "abasing and exalting" are two attributes of the lying soul, i.e., there will be no one for its occurrence who denies it or who alters the speech, so that it abases one matter and exalts another, and so it is abasing; or it may be an addition to explain the truthfulness of creation on that day and the impossibility of their lying; and the liar alters speech, then when he wishes to deny lying about himself he says: "I did not recognize a single word of what happened," and perhaps he says: "I did not recognize a single letter," and this is because the liar may lie about the essence of the matter, and perhaps he lies about an attribute of its attributes; and an attribute may be noticed, and may not be noticed in a considered way, and may not be noticed at all.

(Example of the first): one says: "Zayd did not come," while he has come.

(Example of the second): "He did not come on Friday."

(Example of the third): "He did not come at the early morning of Friday," while he came at the early morning of Friday, and "he did not come at the very beginning of the early morning of Friday."

The second is less than the first, and the fourth less than all. So when one says: "I do not know a single lying word," he denies lying in the report and in its attribute; and one who says: "I did not recognize a single letter" denies something beyond that; and one who says: "I did not recognize a single trace" is above that. So His saying: ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence, abasing [some] and exalting [others]﴾ means: whoever alters, altering even if it is slight.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾ ﴿and become scattered dust﴾. That is, the earth became a high heap of sand and the mountains became flattened, spread-out sand. God's words ﴿and become scattered dust﴾ are like His words describing the mountains: ﴿like wool carded out﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. The benefit of mentioning the verbal noun (masdar) has already been explained, and it is that it indicates the action was a considered matter and was not something of no account to be paid attention to. It is said of such a thing, "It is nothing," so when a speaker says, "I struck him a considered blow," no speaker would say of it, "It is not a blow," belittling it, as one says, "This is nothing."

As for the governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿When it is shaken﴾, it allows several possibilities:

The first: that ﴿When it is shaken﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿When it occurs﴾, so the governing element for it is what we mentioned before.

The second: that the governing element of ﴿When it occurs﴾ is His words ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾, and the governing element of ﴿When it is shaken﴾ is His words ﴿bringing low, lifting high﴾. The meaning is: the Event is brought low and lifted high at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled. The fa' (then) denotes temporal sequence, because the earth, unless it is moved, and the mountains, unless they are broken up, do not become scattered dust. Bass means overturning (taqlib). Haba' is the air mixed with earthly particles that appear in the sunlight's motes when its ray falls through a window opening. Some have said, those who hold that there is a correspondence between letters and meanings: when air is mixed with heavy earthly particles, a letter becomes heavy in its pronunciation, so the light waw was replaced by the ba', which is not pronounced except by closing the two lips with some force; or there is a certain heaviness in the ba'.

Then He, exalted is He, said:

﴿And you will be in three classes﴾ ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ That is: on that Day you will be three categories of people. He explained it afterwards with His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: The fa' (the "so" particle, fa') indicates explanation and elaboration of what came in the division. It is as if He said: "Three classes: the companions of the right hand, the companions of the left hand, etc.," then He clarified the state of each group, saying: ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ So He omitted the division first and was satisfied with what indicates it, for He mentioned the three divisions together with their conditions. His saying ﴿And you will be in three classes﴾ preceded and makes unnecessary the enumeration of the divisions. Then He repeated each one to explain its condition.

The second issue: ﴿The companions of the right hand﴾ are the people of Paradise. Their being called "companions of the right hand" is either because they are among those whose books are given to them in their right hands, or because their right hands are illuminated by a light from Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Their light running before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. Or it is because the right side (yamin) is meant to indicate the sign of good, and the Arabs took omens from the sanih (the bird or animal that passes from left to right of the one observing it, which they considered auspicious) — the one that passes on the right side of the birds and beasts when one is taking omens (zajr). The original basis of this is a legal (hukmi) matter: when Allah, exalted is He, created the creation, He had in everything a sign of His power and choice, even in the human self there are signs that cannot be counted or enumerated. The signs of choice are the establishment of two different things in two similar places, or the establishment of two similar things in two different places, since the state of a human being is among the most similar of things, for he is created from a similar (drop). Then He, exalted is He, placed in the right side of the human a strength that is not in the left side. If the people of knowledge gathered to mention for it a preponderating cause other than the power and will of Allah, they would not be able to do so. For if some of them claims shrewdness and intelligence and says: "The liver is on the right side, and it has the strength of nutrition, and the spleen is on the left side, and it has no strength of evident benefit, so the right side became strong because the liver is on the right," we say: this is evidence of choice, for the right is like the left, and Allah's specifying the right by placing the liver there is evidence of choice. If it is established that a human's right side is stronger than his left, then they preferred the right over the left, and they made the right side for the nobles, and it was said of one who has high status that he is "of the companions of the right." They gave him a word on the pattern of 'azīz (noble). So the matter should be as in the pattern of "sami' and basir" (hearing and seeing), and of that which does not change, like "tawil and qasir" (tall and short). It was said of him: "al-yamin," which indicates strength. And they placed its opposite as "al-yasar," on the pattern (fa'al) which is specific to a dispraised name when calling by such a name, for when cursing and calling by a dispraised name, the pattern is used with a kasra ending, so one says: "ya fajjar, ya fassaq, ya khabath" (O wicked one, O sinner, O corrupt one). It was also said: "al-yamin" is "al-yasar," and afterwards the word was used for the right. As for "al-maymanah," it is a noun of place (maf'alah), as if it were the place in which the right is, and every place that is on the right side of a person in a direction is the place of the right, so it is "maymanah," like our saying "malʿabah" (playground).

The third issue: Allah's making the creation into three categories is an indication of the predominance of mercy. This is because the sides of a human are four: his right and left, and behind him and in front of him. The right is opposite the left, and behind is opposite the front. Then He, exalted is He, by the companions of the right hand indicated the saved ones who are given their books in their right hands, and they are of the most noble and honored side. By the companions of the left hand He indicated those whose state is contrary to the companions of the right, and they are those who are given their books in their left hands, humiliated. And He mentioned the foremost ones, who have no reckoning, and who precede the creation without reckoning, neither by right nor left. [This shows] that those who are in the highest station are on the right side, and they are those brought near before Allah; they speak on behalf of others, intercede for others, and fulfill people's needs. These are higher in rank than the companions of the right hand. Then He, exalted is He, did not say that opposite them are a people who would be lagging behind and delayed from the companions of the left hand, not regarded because of the intensity of anger against them. The division was customarily fourfold, but because of excellence it became threefold. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32], and He did not say: "Among them is one who lags behind all of them."

The fourth issue: What is the wisdom in beginning with the companions of the right hand, then moving to the companions of the left hand, and then to the foremost ones, whereas in the explanation He clarified the state of the foremost ones, then the companions of the left hand, in order? (The answer): We say: Mentioning the event and what occurs at its happening of terrifying matters is only for one who does not have, in the love of Allah, exalted is He, what would restrain him from disobedience. As for those whose inner self is occupied with their Lord, they do not grieve over punishment. So when He, exalted is He, mentioned ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾, and there was in it of frightening what is not hidden, and frightening through those who desire and fear through reward and punishment is more fitting, He mentioned what He mentioned to cut off excuses, not to benefit the news. As for the foremost ones, they do not need encouragement or warning. So He, glorified is He, first mentioned the companions of the right hand, who listen and desire, then He mentioned the foremost ones, so that the companions of the right hand would strive and draw near to their rank, even though no one attains it except by a pulling from Allah. For the one who is foremost attains what he attains by a pull. To this refers His saying: "A pull from the pulls of the Most Merciful is better than seventy years of worship."

The fifth issue: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾? We say: It is a type of eloquence (balaghah). Its explanation is that the speaker begins to explain a matter, then falls silent from speech, indicating that the listener cannot bear to hear it, as one says to another: "I will tell you what happened to me," then says there, answering himself: "I do not fear that it would sadden you." And as one says: "Who knows so-and-so?" which is more eloquent than describing him, because when the listener hears his description, he says: "This is the extent of what he is," but when he says: "Who knows so-and-so?" by supposing that the listener has something of himself, and then says: "So-and-so, at this news, is greater than what I have supposed, and more striking than what I know of him."

The sixth issue: What is its i'rab (grammatical analysis), and from it its meaning is known? We say: ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), for which the speaker intended to mention its predicate (khabar) but turned back from mentioning and abandoned it. And His saying ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ is an interrogative clause in the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), as you say to one who claims knowledge, questioning and testing him, claiming that he does not know the answer: "What is the meaning of such-and-such?" — to the extent that you wish and desire that he would not answer your question, and if he answered you would dislike it, because your speech is understood as if you were saying: "You do not know the answer." Having understood this, it is as if the speaker, at the beginning of the matter, was giving information, then did not give any information, because in giving information there is lengthiness, and then he did not fall silent, and he said that while testing, claiming that you do not know its reality. This is because whoever begins a speech and mentions the subject, then falls silent about the predicate, may be silent because he knows that the addressee already knows the predicate without its mention, just as a speaker, when he wants to inform another that Zayd has arrived, and says: "Zayd..." then before saying "has come," his eye falls on Zayd and he sees him sitting beside him, so he falls silent and does not say "has come," because the speech has departed from its benefit. And he may fall silent about mentioning the predicate from the outset, because he knows that the subject alone suffices for one who asks "Who has come?" If he says "Zayd," it is an answer. We often say "Zayd" and do not say "has come." And silence about the predicate may be an indication of the length of the story, as in the saying of one who says: "The angry one (al-ghadban) concerning Zayd," and falls silent, then says: "What shall I say about him?" Having understood this, we say: When He said ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾, it was as if He wanted to bring the predicate, but He fell silent about it, then said to Himself: "Silence may give the impression that the matter of the predicate is obvious, as one is silent about Zayd in answer to 'Who has come?'" So He said: ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾, testing and claiming that they do not understand, so that

[Page 127]

this would be evidence that His silence about the subject was not because the matter was obvious, but because it was hidden and strange. This is an eloquent aspect. There is also an apparent aspect, which is to say: its meaning is that it is a single interrogative clause, as if He said: "And the companions of the right hand, what are they?" in the form of a question, except that He put the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, and said: ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾. Bringing the explicit noun is an indication of glorifying their matter, since He mentioned them explicitly twice. The same applies to His saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ And likewise in His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality!﴾ and in His saying: ﴿The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity!﴾.

The seventh issue: What is the wisdom in choosing the word ﴿al-mash'amah﴾ (the left side) in contrast to ﴿al-maymanah﴾ (the right side), whereas in explaining their conditions He said: ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾? We say: The "right" (al-yamin) was set for the side that is known first. Then they took omen by it and derived from it words in various contexts, and they said: "This is blessed (maymun)," and they said: "He is blessed by it (ayman bihi)." They set for the side opposite to it the "left" (al-yasar), from "a little thing" (al-shay' al-yasir), indicating its weakness. So it came to be opposite the right in whatever way it turns: one says "al-yusra" opposite "al-yumna," "al-aysar" opposite "al-ayman," and "al-maysarah" opposite "al-maymanah." The word "al-shimal" is not used as "al-yamin" is used, so one does not say "al-ashmal" or "al-mashmalah." And "al-mash'amah" is used as "al-maymanah" is used. So one does not say, opposite "al-yamin," a word from the root of ill omen (shu'm). As for "al-sha'am" (Syria), it is not opposite the right, but opposite Yemen (yaman). Having understood this, we say: After they had spoken of the "right," they did not abandon it, and they limited themselves to using the word "right" for the known side of the human, and the word "left" (al-shimal) as its opposite. And two other words arose for it. One of them is "al-shimal," because they looked at the stars in the sky and made their passage the face of a human, and made the sky two sides, and made one of them stronger, as they saw in the human. So they called the stronger "al-janub" (the south), because of the strength of the side, as one says "ghadub" and "ra'uf" (intensive forms). Then they saw opposite the janub another side, which included the settlement of the world, so they called it "al-shimal" (the north). The other word is "al-mash'amah" and "al-ash'am," opposite "al-maymanah" and "al-ayman." This is because when they took from the "yamin" the blessing (yumn) and other things for optimism (tafa'ul), they placed ill omen (shu'm) opposite it, not in their own limbs and sides, out of aversion to making one of the sides of their own selves an ill omen. And when they had set this and the matter continued upon it, they moved the "right" from its side to something else. So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the disbelievers with two different words, and He said: ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾ and ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾... and He left out the word "al-maysarah" and "al-yasar" which indicate ease of matters, and here He said: ﴿And the companions of the mash'amah﴾ with the more terrible of the two names. For this reason they said of the armies: "al-maymanah" and "al-maysarah," avoiding the word of ill omen (shu'm).

And he may fall silent about mentioning the predicate from the outset, because he knows that the subject alone suffices for one who asks "Who has come?" If he says "Zayd," it is an answer. We often say "Zayd" and do not say "has come." Having understood this, we say: When He said ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾, it was as if He wanted to bring the predicate, but He fell silent about it, then said to Himself: "Silence may give the impression that the matter of the predicate is obvious, as one is silent about Zayd in answer to 'Who has come?'" So He said: ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾, testing and claiming that they do not understand, so that

[Page 127]

this would be evidence that His silence about the subject was not because the matter was obvious, but because it was hidden and strange. This is an eloquent aspect. There is also an apparent aspect, which is to say: its meaning is that it is a single interrogative clause, as if He said: "And the companions of the right hand, what are they?" in the form of a question, except that He put the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, and said: ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾. Bringing the explicit noun is an indication of glorifying their matter, since He mentioned them explicitly twice. What is the Inevitable Reality!﴾ and in His saying: ﴿The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity!﴾.

The seventh issue: What is the wisdom in choosing the word ﴿al-mash'amah﴾ (the left side) in contrast to ﴿al-maymanah﴾ (the right side), whereas in explaining their conditions He said: ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾? We say: The "right" (al-yamin) was set for the side that is known first. Then they took omen by it and derived from it words in various contexts, and they said: "This is blessed (maymun)," and they said: "He is blessed by it (ayman bihi)." They set for the side opposite to it the "left" (al-yasar), from "a little thing" (al-shay' al-yasir), indicating its weakness. So it came to be opposite the right in whatever way it turns: one says "al-yusra" opposite "al-yumna," "al-aysar" opposite "al-ayman," and "al-maysarah" opposite "al-maymanah." The word "al-shimal" is not used as "al-yamin" is used, so one does not say "al-ashmal" or "al-mashmalah." And "al-mash'amah" is used as "al-maymanah" is used. So one does not say, opposite "al-yamin," a word from the root of ill omen (shu'm). As for "al-sha'am" (Syria), it is not opposite the right, but opposite Yemen (yaman). Having understood this, we say: After they had spoken of the "right," they did not abandon it, and they limited themselves to using the word "right" for the known side of the human, and the word "left" (al-shimal) as its opposite. And two other words arose for it. One of them is "al-shimal," because they looked at the stars in the sky and made their passage the face of a human, and made the sky two sides, and made one of them stronger, as they saw in the human. So they called the stronger "al-janub" (the south), because of the strength of the side, as one says "ghadub" and "ra'uf" (intensive forms). Then they saw opposite the janub another side, which included the settlement of the world, so they called it "al-shimal" (the north). The other word is "al-mash'amah" and "al-ash'am," opposite "al-maymanah" and "al-ayman." This is because when they took from the "yamin" the blessing (yumn) and other things for optimism (tafa'ul), they placed ill omen (shu'm) opposite it, not in their own limbs and sides, out of aversion to making one of the sides of their own selves an ill omen. And when they had set this and the matter continued upon it, they moved the "right" from its side to something else. So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the disbelievers with two different words, and He said: ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾ and ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾... and He left out the word "al-maysarah" and "al-yasar" which indicate ease of matters, and here He said: ﴿And the companions of the mash'amah﴾ with the more terrible of the two names. For this reason they said of the armies: "al-maymanah" and "al-maysarah," avoiding the word of ill omen (shu'm).

[Page 125]

Then He, exalted is He, said:

﴿And you will be in three classes﴾ ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ That is: on that Day you will be three categories of people. He explained it afterwards with His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: The fa' (the "so" particle, fa') indicates explanation and elaboration of what came in the division. It is as if He said: "Three classes: the companions of the right hand, the companions of the left hand, etc.," then He clarified the state of each group, saying: ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ So He omitted the division first and was satisfied with what indicates it, for He mentioned the three divisions together with their conditions. His saying ﴿And you will be in three classes﴾ preceded and makes unnecessary the enumeration of the divisions. Then He repeated each one to explain its condition.

The second issue: ﴿The companions of the right hand﴾ are the people of Paradise. Their being called "companions of the right hand" is either because they are among those whose books are given to them in their right hands, or because their right hands are illuminated by a light from Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Their light running before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. Or it is because the right side (yamin) is meant to indicate the sign of good, and the Arabs took omens from the sanih (the bird or animal that passes from left to right of the one observing it, which they considered auspicious) — the one that passes on the right side of the birds and beasts when one is taking omens (zajr). The original basis of this is a legal (hukmi) matter: when Allah, exalted is He, created the creation, He had in everything a sign of His power and choice, even in the human self there are signs that cannot be counted or enumerated. The signs of choice are the establishment of two different things in two similar places, or the establishment of two similar things in two different places, since the state of a human being is among the most similar of things, for he is created from a similar (drop). Then He, exalted is He, placed in the right side of the human a strength that is not in the left side. If the people of knowledge gathered to mention for it a preponderating cause other than the power and will of Allah, they would not be able to do so. For if some of them claims shrewdness and intelligence and says: "The liver is on the right side, and it has the strength of nutrition, and the spleen is on the left side, and it has no strength of evident benefit, so the right side became strong because the liver is on the right," we say: this is evidence of choice, for the right is like the left, and Allah's specifying the right by placing the liver there is evidence of choice. If it is established that a human's right side is stronger than his left, then they preferred the right over the left, and they made the right side for the nobles, and it was said of one who has high status that he is "of the companions of the right." They gave him a word on the pattern of 'azīz (noble). So the matter should be as in the pattern of "sami' and basir" (hearing and seeing), and of that which does not change, like "tawil and qasir" (tall and short). It was said of him: "al-yamin," which indicates strength. And they placed its opposite as "al-yasar," on the pattern (fa'al) which is specific to a dispraised name when calling by such a name, for when cursing and calling by a dispraised name, the pattern is used with a kasra ending, so one says: "ya fajjar, ya fassaq, ya khabath" (O wicked one, O sinner, O corrupt one). It was also said: "al-yamin" is "al-yasar," and afterwards the word was used for the right. As for "al-maymanah," it is a noun of place (maf'alah), as if it were the place in which the right is, and every place that is on the right side of a person in a direction is the place of the right, so it is "maymanah," like our saying "malʿabah" (playground).

The third issue: Allah's making the creation into three categories is an indication of the predominance of mercy. This is because the sides of a human are four: his right and left, and behind him and in front of him. The right is opposite the left, and behind is opposite the front. Then He, exalted is He, by the companions of the right hand indicated the saved ones who are given their books in their right hands, and they are of the most noble and honored side. By the companions of the left hand He indicated those whose state is contrary to the companions of the right, and they are those who are given their books in their left hands, humiliated. And He mentioned the foremost ones, who have no reckoning, and who precede the creation without reckoning, neither by right nor left. [This shows] that those who are in the highest station are on the right side, and they are those brought near before Allah; they speak on behalf of others, intercede for others, and fulfill people's needs. These are higher in rank than the companions of the right hand. Then He, exalted is He, did not say that opposite them are a people who would be lagging behind and delayed from the companions of the left hand, not regarded because of the intensity of anger against them. The division was customarily fourfold, but because of excellence it became threefold. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32], and He did not say: "Among them is one who lags behind all of them."

The fourth issue: What is the wisdom in beginning with the companions of the right hand, then moving to the companions of the left hand, and then to the foremost ones, whereas in the explanation He clarified the state of the foremost ones, then the companions of the left hand, in order? (The answer): We say: Mentioning the event and what occurs at its happening of terrifying matters is only for one who does not have, in the love of Allah, exalted is He, what would restrain him from disobedience. As for those whose inner self is occupied with their Lord, they do not grieve over punishment. So when He, exalted is He, mentioned ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾, and there was in it of frightening what is not hidden, and frightening through those who desire and fear through reward and punishment is more fitting, He mentioned what He mentioned to cut off excuses, not to benefit the news. As for the foremost ones, they do not need encouragement or warning. So He, glorified is He, first mentioned the companions of the right hand, who listen and desire, then He mentioned the foremost ones, so that the companions of the right hand would strive and draw near to their rank, even though no one attains it except by a pulling from Allah. For the one who is foremost attains what he attains by a pull. To this refers His saying: "A pull from the pulls of the Most Merciful is better than seventy years of worship."

The fifth issue: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿what are the companions of the right hand!﴾? We say: It is a type of eloquence (balaghah). Its explanation is that the speaker begins to explain a matter, then falls silent from speech, indicating that the listener cannot bear to hear it, as one says to another: "I will tell you what happened to me," then says there, answering himself: "I do not fear that it would sadden you." And as one says: "Who knows so-and-so?" which is more eloquent than describing him, because when the listener hears his description, he says: "This is the extent of what he is," but when he says: "Who knows so-and-so?" by supposing that the listener has something of himself, and then says: "So-and-so, at this news, is greater than what I have supposed, and more striking than what I know of him."

The sixth issue: What is its i'rab (grammatical analysis), and from it its meaning is known? We say: ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), for which the speaker intended to mention its predicate (khabar) but turned back from mentioning and abandoned it. [Page 128]

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding its i'rab (grammatical analysis, the parsing of its case endings and structure), there are three possibilities. The first: ﴿And the foremost﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the companions of the right" (أصْحابِ المَيْمَنَةِ), and the sentence is complete at that point. Then His saying ﴿the foremost﴾ ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ forms a single sentence. The second: His saying ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ is a single sentence, like the speaker who says "You are you" (أنْتَ أنْتَ). As the poet said:

*"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."*

In this there are two aspects. One is that the repetition is due to the fame of the subject by what it is, so there is no need for a predicate about it. This is what the poet meant, and it is the well-known view among the grammarians (nuhat). The other is to indicate that the subject contains something that knowledge cannot encompass, that cannot be described, and that is known only as the subject itself. This is like the one who says to another, "Tell me about the state of the king," and he replies, "I know of the king only that he is a king." So His saying ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ means that they cannot be described except by themselves, for their condition and what they are upon is beyond what human knowledge can encompass.

*(Here is a subtle point):* In the case of the companions of the right, He said ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾ in the interrogative form. Although it was for emphasis on their greatness (al-iʿjaz), He made them the object of the question. Here, He did not say "And the foremost, what are the foremost?" because the interrogative used for emphasis (al-istifham alladhi li-l-iʿjaz) is directed at one who claims knowledge, so it is said to him: "If you know, then explain the matter." But when one admits ignorance, one is not told, "You lied," nor "How is such-and-such, and what is the answer to that?" Likewise, in ﴿And the foremost﴾ He did not place them in a position where they make claims, so that the question would be put to them and their inability revealed. Rather, He based the matter on the fact that they admit inability at the outset. On this view, His saying ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ is like the words of a scholar to one who asks about an intricate question, while the scholar knows that the asker will not understand it, even though he has explained it in the utmost clarity, namely that the matter is as it is, and he does not occupy himself with further explanation.

The third: "the foremost" (as-sabiqun) in the second occurrence is an emphatic repetition (taʾkid) of His saying ﴿And the foremost﴾. The middle view is the most just and the most correct. On the middle view there is another opinion: that what is meant is that those who were foremost to the good things in this world are the ones foremost to Paradise in the Hereafter.

**The second issue:** ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ implies restriction (al-hasr), so it should follow that no one other than them is brought near. Yet He said of the angels that they are "brought near" (muqarrabun). We say: ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ among the three groups (al-azwaj al-thalathah). If it is objected that ﴿the companions of the right﴾ are not among the brought near, we say: nearness has degrees, and ﴿the foremost﴾ are at the utmost nearness, and there is no limit to that. There is also another possibility, which is to say: what is meant is that the foremost are brought near to the gardens while the companions of the right are headed toward the path of Paradise. For, in the measure that the believer is reckoned with an easy reckoning and his book is given to him in his right hand, the foremost have already drawn near to the abode, or He has brought them near to Himself in Paradise, while the companions of the right are still on their way toward what the brought near have reached. Moreover, the journey and the ascent do not cease, for the journey toward God has no end and the ascent has no limit. Thus, whenever the companions of the right draw near to the rank of the foremost, the foremost will have moved on to a place higher than it. So those are the ones brought near, in the Gardens of Bliss, in the highest ʿIlliyyin, at the time when the companions of the right arrive at the dark-eyed maidens (al-Hur al-ʿIn).

**The third issue:** After explaining the categories of the three groups (al-azwaj), He did not return to describing their states in the order in which they were mentioned. Rather, He described the state of the foremost although He had placed them last, and He postponed the mention of the companions of the left although He had mentioned them first before the foremost. We say: We have already explained that when mentioning the Event (al-waqiʿah), He mentioned first the one for whom the mention of terrors is beneficial, and postponed the one whose state does not change with fear and hope. But when it comes to explanation, He mentioned the foremost first, because of their excellence and the excellence of their condition.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In Gardens of Delight﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: Here He defined "delight" (al-na'im) with the definite article, while at the end of the surah He said: ﴿Then rest and sweet basil and a Garden of Delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89] without the article. What is mentioned at the end of the surah concerns one of the foremost (al-sabiqun), so he has a garden from these gardens, and this is definite by virtue of its being an idafa (construct) to a definite noun, whereas that one is indefinite. So what is the difference between them? We say: the difference is both verbal and semantic. The verbal difference is that "the foremost" (al-sabiqun) is defined by the article of comprehensive inclusion (al-lam al-mustaghriqah) for their whole category, so he placed the position of the two definites as definite. As for there, it is indefinite, because His saying "if he is among those brought near" means "if he is one of them," so He made its position indefinite, although it is permissible for the person to be definite while its position is indefinite, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 15] and ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and a river﴾ [al-Qamar: 54], and also the reverse.

As for the semantic difference: we say that when mentioning the plural, He made the gardens plural in all other places, so the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens﴾, and the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾, ﴿in gardens of﴾. But the foremost are a type of the God-fearing, and among the God-fearing there are also those other than the foremost. Then the foremost have ranks above which there are no ranks, so these [ranks] became known because they are at the utmost height, or because no one is above them. As for the rest of the God-fearing, each one has a rank, and above it is a rank, so they are in gardens proportionate in station, not gathered in one place due to the difference of their stations. The gardens of the foremost are of one measure at the highest of the 'Illiyyun, which everyone knows; but as for the individual among them, his station is among the stations, and not everyone knows that it belongs to such-and-such foremost person, so he is not known. As for their stations, everyone knows them, and knows that they are for the foremost, but one does not know which belongs to the God-fearing in a particular manner.

Second issue: The idafa of the Garden to delight (al-na'im) is of what kind? We say: it is the idafa of a place to what occurs in the place, as one says: "the house of hospitality" (dar al-diyafah), "the house of the call" (dar al-da'wah), "the house of justice" (dar al-'adl). Likewise "the Garden of Delight." Its benefit is that a garden in this world may be for delight, and it may be for occupation and making a living from the price of its fruits, unlike the Garden in the Hereafter, which is for delight only.

Third issue: ﴿In gardens of delight﴾ may be a predicate following a predicate, and it may be a single predicate. The first: its estimate is "Those brought near are existing in gardens," like His saying: ﴿The Lord of the Throne, the Glorious, ﴾ ﴿Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj: 15-16]. The second: its estimate is "They are the ones brought near in the gardens from Allah," as one says: "He is the chosen one of the king in this town." On the first aspect, its benefit is explaining the bliss of their bodies and the honour of their souls: they are brought near to Allah, so they are in utmost pleasure and in gardens; their bodies are in utmost bliss. Unlike those brought near to kings, who enjoy closeness but whose bodies have no comfort; rather they are in toil from standing and attending to affairs. For this reason He said ﴿In gardens of delight﴾ and did not restrict it to "gardens." On the second aspect, its benefit is distinguishing them from the angels, for the ones brought near in our present day in the heavens are the angels, while the foremost who are brought near are in the Garden, so the ones brought near elsewhere are the angels. And there is a subtle point in this: the nearness of the angels is the nearness of the elite before the king, who are occupied with tasks; they are not in delight, though they are in great pleasure, and they never cease being fearful and standing at the door of Allah, orders coming to them and obligation not lifted from them. But the foremost have nearness to Allah as the companions of kings have, so no task is in their hands and no order comes to them; they take pleasure in nearness and enjoy comfort.

Then He said, may He be exalted: ﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾ ﴿and a few from the later generations﴾. This is one report after another. It contains several issues:

The first issue: I have already mentioned that His saying ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ is a sentence. The predicate normally is the same as the subject, due to the obviousness of their condition or the obscurity of their matter to others. So how does a predicate come after it? We say: that intended meaning has conveyed the mention of another predicate for another intended meaning, just as someone says, "Zayd, his condition is not hidden from you," indicating that he is one of the well-known people, and then he proceeds to describe a condition that is hidden from the listener, even though he said, "is not hidden." That was to clarify that he is not one of the strangers. Likewise here, He said, ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ to clarify their greatness, then He mentioned the condition of their number.

The second issue: Who are the ﴿earlier generations﴾? We say: the well-known view is that they are those who lived before our Prophet (ﷺ). He said ﴿multitude﴾, and a multitude (thullah) is a great group, because those before our Prophet, among the messengers and prophets, had great companions, who, when gathered together, would be far more numerous than the foremost of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). On this basis, it has been said that when this verse was revealed, the Companions (al-Sahaba) found their fewness difficult to bear, so there was revealed after it: ﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later generations﴾. This is extremely weak for several reasons:

The first: the number of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), even if it is at that time and until the end of time, compared to those who passed away, is extremely small. Then what benefit is there in God's blessing on a great multitude of the earlier generations? This is nothing but an unacceptable contradiction.

The second: this is like abrogation (naskh) in reports, and that is extremely far-fetched.

The third: what comes after it does not remove this, because the multitude from the earlier generations here refers to the foremost of the earlier generations, and this is evident, because the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) is numerous, and God, may He be exalted, showed them mercy, pardoning them for matters for which others were not pardoned, and He gave the Prophet (ﷺ) intercession, so the number of those saved, who are the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), increased. As for those in the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) who did not sin and did not commit a major sin, they are extremely few, and they are the foremost.

The fourth: this is a misconception. They should have rejoiced at this verse, because when He, may He be exalted, said ﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾, the first of the messengers and prophets entered into it, and there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ). So when He made a few of his Ummah alongside the messengers, prophets and saints (awliya') who were in one rank, that is a blessing for them. Perhaps it is an indication of His, peace be upon him, saying: "The scholars of my Ummah are like the prophets of the Children of Israel."

The second point: what is meant is His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the emigrants and the helpers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100]. Most of them have the highest rank, due to His saying: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the victory﴾ [al-Hadid: 10], and so on. ﴿And a few from the later generations﴾ are those who did not catch up with them from among those who came after them. On this basis, His saying ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7] is an address to those present at the time of the revelation, and it does not explain the earlier generations who were before our Prophet, peace be upon him. This is evident, because address relates only to those present in terms of the wording, and others enter into it by evidence.

The third point: ﴿A multitude from the earlier generations﴾ are those who believed and did righteous deeds by themselves, and ﴿a few from the later generations﴾ are those about whom God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and their descendants followed them in faith﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. So the believers and their descendants, if they are among the companions of the right, are equal in number, because every child who dies while one of his parents is a believer is among the companions of the right. As for if they are among the foremost believers, their children rarely attain the rank of the foremost, and often the child of a believer is in a better condition than the father, due to the father's shortcoming and a disobedience that was not found in the young child. On this basis, His saying ﴿the later generations﴾ means the later followers from among the young children.

Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Upon couches woven [with gold]﴾, ﴿reclining upon them, facing one another﴾.

Al-Mawdunah (al-mawḍūnah) is that which is woven, strong in its weft and warp. From it comes the expression for a woven coat of mail: mawdūnah. The wad̲in (al-waḍīn) is a broad rope from which a girdle is made, because of the strength of its warp and weft. The couches of kings have legs of some solid material, and their seats are made with silk and other materials, because it is softer than wood and similar things in hardness. These couches have legs of precious gems, and their base is of stretched gold. God's words ﴿reclining upon them﴾ are for emphasis (ta'kīd), and the meaning is that they are upon couches, reclining upon them, facing one another. The benefit of the emphasis is that one should not suppose they are upon couches while reclining on something else, as is the case of one who sits on a small chair that cannot accommodate reclining, so something else is placed beneath him to lean on. When He said "upon couches, reclining upon them", this indicates that their settling and their reclining are all upon couches. God's words ﴿facing one another﴾ have two interpretations:

The first: that none of them turns his back on another.

The second: that none of the foremost (al-sābiqīn) sees anyone other than himself above him. This is closer, because His words ﴿facing one another﴾ on the first interpretation require saying that "facing one another" means that each one faces another at one time, and this is understood only where there is no difference of directions. On this view, the meaning of the speech is that they are spirits who have no backs or sides, so that by "the foremost" is meant those whose bodies are luminous spirits, all of whose directions are a face, like light that faces everything and turns its back on no one. The first interpretation is closer to the attributes of physical things.
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾.

Wildān (al-wilḍān) is the plural of walīd, which originally is a form (fa'īl) in the sense of maf'ūl, meaning one who is born (mawlūd), but it became dominant for children, regardless of their being born. The proof is that they called a small girl walīdah, and if they had considered the original sense they would have stripped it of the ta' marbūṭah, as with qatīl. Having established this, we say: regarding wildān there are two interpretations:

The first: that it is in the original sense, and they are the young children of believers. This is weak, because God has informed us that He will join the children of believers to their fathers, and among believers there are righteous ones who have no children, so it is not permissible for the child of a believer to serve another believer. This necessitates either that they have special attachment to some of the righteous, and that whoever has no child has no young boys circulating upon him, or that the child of one serves someone other than his father, which involves a defect regarding the father. On this interpretation it was said they are the young children of unbelievers, and this is closer than the first, since it does not involve the corruption we mentioned.

The second: that it is in the usage in which the original sense is not considered, namely that the intended meaning is young children regardless of their being born. In that case it is like God's words ﴿And there will circulate among them boys belonging to them﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 24]. Regarding God's words ﴿made eternal (mukhalladūn)﴾ there are two interpretations.

The first: that it derives from khulūd, eternity and permanence. On this interpretation two further meanings appear:

One: that they are made eternal, with no death and no extinction.

Two: that they do not change from their state, and they remain children permanently, not growing older and not having beards.

The second interpretation: that it derives from al-khaladah, which is an earring, meaning they have rings in their ears. The first is more apparent and more fitting.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿with cups, and jugs, and a cup from a flowing spring﴾.

The vessels of wine are found at gatherings. As for the *kub* (cup), there are two views:

First: it is of the kind of the *aqdah* (drinking bowls), and it is a large bowl.

Second: it is of the kind of the *kiyzan* (pitchers), having no handle and no spout. The *ibriq* (ewer) has a handle and a spout.

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the difference between *al-akwab* (cups), *al-abariq* (ewers), and *al-ka's* (the cup), where He mentioned the *akwab* and *abariq* in the plural, and the *ka's* in the singular, and did not say *wa-ku'us* (and cups)? We say: this follows the custom of the Arabs in drinking. They have many vessels containing wine, prepared and set out before them. As for the *ka's*, it is the bowl from which wine is drunk when it contains wine, and no one drinks at one time except from one cup. The vessels full of wine at one time, however, are found in abundance. If it is said: circulating the *ka's* is the custom of the people of this world, whereas circulating the *akwab* and *abariq* is not customary, so what is the benefit in it? We say: they are not circulated in this world in order to remove hardship from the one who circulates them, because of their weight. Otherwise they are needed, as shown by the fact that when one finishes, he returns it to the place where it was. As for the Hereafter, the vessels will move by themselves, and the young servant with them, out of honour, not for carrying.

There is another view from the standpoint of language: the *ka's* is a vessel that contains a drink, so the drink is included in its meaning. The *ibriq* is a vessel for which it is not required, in applying the name *ibriq* to it, that it contain a drink. Once this is established, we say: a full vessel is considered for what is in it, not for the vessel itself. If that is so, then the *ka's* is considered by what is in it, but in it is a drink of a single kind, and this is what is considered. A noun is not made plural except when its kinds are diverse. Thus one does not say of loaves of a single kind *akhbaz* (breads); one says *akhbaz* only when some are black and some white. Likewise meats: one says *luhum* (meats) when the animals from which the meats come are diverse, and one does not say of two pieces of meat *lahmani* (two meats). As for things that are of distinct categories, they are made plural. The bowls, even if they are large, when they are filled with wine of a single kind, it is not permissible to say of them *khumur* (wines). So He did not say *kus'* (cups), for otherwise that would have given preference to the containers. For the *ka's*, insofar as it is a drink of a single kind, is not made plural, so the plural is left aside in preference to the side of the contained. This differs from the *ibriq*, for in it only the vessel is considered. On this basis the eloquence of the Qur'an becomes clear, since the word *kus'* (cups) does not occur in it, as what is in them is one kind of wine. This is a noble inquiry in the language.

The second issue: placing the *ka's* last is a good ordering. Likewise in mentioning the *akwab* first, since the drink is poured from the cup into the ewer and from the ewer into the *ka's*.

The third issue: ﴿from a flowing spring﴾ is either an explanation of what is in the *ka's*, or an explanation of what is in the *akwab* and *abariq*. We say: it is possible that all of them are from a flowing spring, and the first is more apparent by the wording, while the second is not so. When He said ﴿and a cup﴾, it is as if He said "and a drink," and the listener would need to know what the drink is. As for the ewer, its indication of the drink is not by the wording. As for the meaning, the fact that all of them are full is the truth, and because circulating an empty vessel is not becoming. So the apparent sense is to explain what is in all of them. Something that supports the first view is that when He mentioned the vessels, He mentioned their kind, not the type of what is in them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups﴾ [al-Insan: 15], and when He mentioned the *ka's*, He explained what was in it, saying: ﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾. It is possible that the circulating of the ewers, even if they are empty, is for adornment and beautification, and in the Hereafter they will be for honour and luxury and nothing else.

The fourth issue: what is the meaning of *ma'in*? We have mentioned in the surah of al-Saffat that it is either *fa'il* or *maf'ul*, and there has been a difference of opinion about it. If we say it is *fa'il*, it is from the *ma'in* of water, when it flows. If we say it is *maf'ul*, it is from *ana'ahu*, when one singles it out by its eye and distinguishes it. The first is more correct and more apparent, because the *ma'iyn* (the one affected by the evil eye) gives the impression that it is defective, since the saying of someone, "So-and-so affected me by the eye," means "he harmed me when his eye struck me." Also, describing it as *maf'ul* has no benefit. As for flowing in the drink, if it is in water, it is a praiseworthy attribute; and if it is in something else, it is a wondrous matter not found in this world, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and rivers of wine﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿They will not be affected by headache from it, nor will they be intoxicated﴾. And on this there are several issues:

The first issue: regarding ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ (lā yuṣaddaʿūn), there are two interpretations:

The first: no headache will befall them from it. It is said: "So-and-so gave me a headache" (ṣaddaʿanī fulān), meaning he caused me to have a headache.

The second: ﴿nor will they be intoxicated (lā yunzifūn) from it﴾, meaning they will not exhaust it. The apparent view is that the root of the word ṣudāʿ (headache) derives from this, because the pain in the head, in most cases, arises from humours and wind in the membranes of the brain, which cause pain, so one who has a headache feels as if it is splitting through the membrane of his brain.

The second issue: if the meaning is the negation of headache, how is it appropriate to use "from it" (ʿan-hā), when the word used for cause is "min" (from), as one says: "he fell ill from such-and-such" (marida min kadhā), whereas for separation one says "ʿan" (from/away from), as in "he recovered from the illness" (bari'a ʿan al-maraḍ)? We say: the answer is that the cause which establishes a matter in a thing is as if something separates from it and establishes its action in its place. Thus there are two matters and two perspectives: when you look at the locus and see something in it, you say: "where is this from?" meaning, from what did the beginning of its existence come? So your gaze falls on the cause, and you say: "this is from that," meaning its origin is from it. When you look at the side of the effect, you see the matter that proceeded from it as if it has departed from it and clung to the locus; therefore that cannot be found again, while the cause was as if in it and moved away from it in most cases. Here, then, the two matters are among bodies and things which have nearness and distance. Once this is known, we say: the purpose here is to explain the wine of the Hereafter in itself and what is upon it, so the gaze falls upon it, not upon the drinkers. Had the intended meaning been that they are not affected by headache from it due to some attribute in them, it would not be a praise of it. But when he says: "it does not cause headache due to a quality in it," that is praise of it. So when the gaze fell upon it, he said: "from it" (ʿan-hā). As for when you describe a man by his heavy drinking and his strength to endure it, you say of him: "he is not affected by headache from such-and-such wine." But when you describe the wine itself, you say: "no one is affected by headache from this."

The third issue: God's saying ﴿nor will they be intoxicated (lā yunzifūn)﴾ has already been explained in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt. What is fitting to mention here is that we say: if the meaning of ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾ is "they will not become drunk," then we say the meaning of ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ is either that headache will not befall them, or that they will not run out. If we take the first view, the sequence is most excellent, since it follows a progression: God's saying ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ means headache will not befall them, but this does not negate intoxication, so He said after it ﴿nor will it cause intoxication﴾, like one who says: "there is no great harm in it," then says: "nor is there little," completing the explanation. Had you reversed the order, it would not be good. If we say ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾ means they will not run out, the sequence is likewise: our saying ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ means they will not run out of it, and despite its abundance and their continual drinking, they will not become drunk. The fact that they do not become drunk because the drink runs out is not surprising; but that they do not become drunk while continually drinking is astonishing. And if we say ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾ means their drink will not be exhausted, as we explained there, then we say also: if ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ means headache will not befall them, the sequence is most excellent, because his saying ﴿they will not be affected by headache﴾ would not be an explanation of a wondrous matter if their drink were scant; so He said ﴿they will not be affected by headache from it﴾, while they do not run out of the drink nor are they drained of the drink. And if it means ﴿nor will they be drained from it﴾, the sequence is good, because its meaning is that they will not be drained from it, that is, they will not be removed from what they are in, nor will what they have been given of the drink be taken from them; then, when they have finished it with drinking, they are given more.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fruit of what they choose﴾ ﴿and the flesh of fowl of what they desire﴾. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: What is the reason for the genitive case (al-jarr), when fruit is not carried around by the youths (al-wildan), and the conjunction requires that (i.e., that it be governed by the same preposition)? We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first of them: that fruit and meat in this world are sought in two states: the state of drinking (al-shurb) and the state of not drinking. Fruit is taken from the branches of trees, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Its clusters hang low﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23] and He said: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and so on. As for the state of drinking, it is permissible that the youths carry it around, so they hand them the strange fruits and the wondrous meats, not for eating but for honor, just as the host places varieties of fruit by his guest with his own hand, even though each of them shares with the other in proximity to them.

The second aspect: that it is a conjunction in meaning with "gardens of bliss", i.e., they are the ones brought near, in gardens and fruit, and meat and houris, meaning they revolve among these blessings. It is well known that it is a conjunction in wording due to proximity (li'l-mujawarah), not in meaning. And why would this not be permissible, when it is permissible to say "he girded a sword and a spear" (taqallada sayfan wa rumhan)?

The second issue: Is there eloquence in specifying choosing (al-takhyir) with fruit and desiring (al-ishtiha') with meat? I say: how could there not be, when in every letter of the Qur'an there is eloquence and excellence, even though my dull intellect cannot encompass it, and my meager knowledge cannot reach it? What appears to me in this is that when meat and fruit are present before one who is hungry, his soul inclines to the meat, and when they are present before one who is satiated, he inclines to the fruit. The hungry one is desirous (mushtahin), and the satiated one is not desirous; rather he is choosing: if he wishes to eat he eats, and if he does not wish, he does not eat. And one does not say of the hungry one "if he wishes to eat," because "in" (in) enters only upon the uncertain. When this is known, it is established that in this world meat is chosen by the one who desires it, and fruit is chosen by the one who does not desire it. The depiction of Paradise is according to what is understood in this world, so meat is specified with desire and fruit with choice. The verification of this from the standpoint of the wording is that choice is taking the good from two matters, and the two matters between which choice occurs outwardly do not have for the chooser at first an inclination toward one of them; then he reflects and deliberates, and takes what his view prefers over the other. Thus tafakkuh (enjoying fruit) is what occurs when there is no need. As for when someone desires a specific fruit, so he summons it and eats it, he is not one who enjoys fruit; rather he is one who removes a need. As for the fruits of Paradise, they are first present before the people of Paradise without any prior inclination on their part toward them, and then they enjoy them according to their choice. As for meat, their souls incline toward it with the least inclination, so it is present before them. And the inclination of the soul toward what is eaten is desire (shahwah). This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its clusters hang low﴾, and His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fruit abundant﴾ ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾; this is evidence that they are constantly present. The conclusion is that fruit is present before them, so the believer chooses after its presence; and meat, the believer seeks it, and his soul inclines to it with the least inclination. That is because fruit delights the eyes by its presence, whereas meat does not delight the eyes by its presence. Furthermore, there is a subtle point in the wording: He, exalted is He, said ﴿of what they choose﴾ and did not say "of what they opt for" (mimma yakhtarunа), despite the closeness of the two in meaning. It is that choosing (al-takhayyur) is of the category of effort (al-takalluf), as if they take what is in the utmost perfection, and this is not found except in one who has no need and no compulsion.

The third issue: What is the wisdom in placing fruit before meat? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first of them: the custom in this world is to present fruits at the meal, and Paradise was described according to what is known of it in this world and in accordance with what is known there, especially the custom of drinking people (ahl al-shurb). It seems that the intended purpose is to explain the condition of drinking among the people of Paradise.

The second: the wisdom in this world requires eating fruit first, because it is lighter, passes down more quickly, and needs less lengthy stay in the stomach for digestion; and because fruit stirs up appetite for eating, whereas meat repels it.

The third: from what we have mentioned emerges an answer free of the wording of choice and desire: namely, that when He, exalted is He, explained that fruit is constantly present and available, while meat is desired and is present at the time of desire, this indicates the absence of hunger, because the hungry one's need for meat is greater than his choosing of meat. So He said ﴿and fruit﴾ because the state in Paradise resembles the state of the satiated in this world, so he inclines more to fruit, and therefore He placed it first. And this aspect is more sound, because among fruits there are some that are not eaten except after the meal, so the first answer does not hold as a reply for all of them.
