Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 22–23:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And maidens with lovely, wide eyes﴾ ﴿like pearls well-guarded﴾.

There are readings (qira'at, the recognized variant recitations of the Qur'an) of this. The first is the nominative (raf'), which is the well-known reading, and it is in coordination ('atf) with "wildan" (youths). If it is said: He said before it, ﴿Fair maidens, cloistered in pavilions﴾ [al-Rahman: 72], indicating that they are secluded and veiled, then how is your statement that it is coordinated with "wildan" correct? We say: the answer to this is from two aspects.

The first, which is the well-known one, is that we say: it is coordinated with them in wording but not in meaning, or it is coordinated in meaning by way of implicit supposition and understanding, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿youths will circulate among them﴾ means: for them there are youths, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there will circulate among them youths of their own﴾. So ﴿and maidens with lovely eyes﴾ means: and for them there are maidens with lovely eyes.

The second is that it may be said: the maidens are not restricted to one category. Rather, for the people of Paradise there are ﴿maidens cloistered﴾ in tents, honored, and for them are companions and servants, and there are maidens who circulate with the youthful attendants who serve drink, so it is as if He said: youths and women will circulate among them.

The second reading is the genitive (jarr) by coordination with "akwab" (cups) and "abariq" (pitchers). If it is asked: how can they be circulated with among them? We say: the answer has already been given at His saying ﴿and the flesh of fowl﴾. Or it is in coordination with ﴿gardens﴾, meaning: ﴿those brought near﴾ ﴿in gardens of bliss﴾ ﴿and maidens﴾. It is also read ﴿ḥūran ʿīnan﴾ (maidens with lovely eyes) in the accusative (naṣb). Perhaps what results from this reading, which is not coordination, is the same meaning as coordination. But this reader must supply a governing verb, so he says: they are given maidens. Thus the meaning does not depart from agreement with the coordinating particle, the same as the one who reads it nominatively, who says: and for them there are maidens with lovely eyes. So there is no departure from agreement with the coordinating particle.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿like pearls well-guarded﴾, involves several discussions.

The first: the kaf (ka-) is for comparison, and "mithl" (likeness) is literally for comparison. So if He had said "amthal al-lu'lu' al-maknun" (likenesses of well-guarded pearls), there would be no need for the kaf. So what is the reason for combining the two words of comparison? We say: the well-known answer is that the two words of comparison convey emphasis and intensification of the comparison. If it is said: that is not so; rather, they do not convey what either one of them conveys, because if you say, for example, "he is like a pearl" to the one compared, not in the respect for which the comparison is made... We say: the verification in this is that when a thing has a likeness, it is its like. So when you say "he is like the moon," it is not in intensity like your saying "he is a moon." Similarly our saying "he is like a lion" and "he is a lion." So when you say "like the likeness of pearls," it is as if you said "like the pearls." Your saying "he is pearl" is more eloquent than your saying "he is like pearl." This discussion is useful to us here, but it is not useful to us in His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], because negation stands opposite affirmation, and the meaning of negation is not understood from speech unless the affirmation opposed to it is understood. So we say: His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ is in opposition to the statement of one who says: "there is like unto Him something." It denies what he affirmed. But the meaning of "like unto Him something," if we do not take the kaf as additional, is that "a likeness of His likeness is something." This is a statement that indicates that He has a likeness, and that His likeness has a likeness. So when we say "it is not so," it is a refutation of him, and refuting him is correct. What remains is to say: one who refutes someone who affirms certain things does not thereby negate everything he affirmed. So if one says: "Zayd is a good scholar," then one replies to him: "Zayd is not a good scholar," it does not follow from this that the reply negates his being a scholar. So whoever says ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ in the sense of "there is no likeness of His likeness" does not necessarily negate His likeness; rather it may negate the likeness of the likeness. So the one who refutes is not thereby a monotheist, which would take the statement out of conveying tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). So we say: it does convey tawhid. For if we say "there is no likeness of His likeness," it follows that He has no likeness, because if He had a likeness, He would be the likeness of His likeness, and He is a thing, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. For the reality of "thing" is that which exists, so the likeness of His likeness is a thing, and that is negated by our saying "there is no likeness of His likeness." So it is known that the statement does not depart from conveying tawhid. Thus it is known that taking the words in their literal sense conveys intensification in the statement regarding His saying ﴿like﴾. As for not taking it literally in His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾, that is more concise, so the kaf is made additional, lest it lead to ta'til (the denial of God's attributes), which is the denial of God. We say: there is benefit in this, namely that it is a negation together with an indication of the proof for the negation. That is because He, exalted is He, is wajib al-wujud (necessarily existent). The one who affirmed a partner agrees with us, and none opposes us except the mu'attil (one who denies divine attributes), and the affirmation of Him is evident. And if He is necessarily existent, then if He had a likeness, He would be outside His being necessarily existent, because He and His likeness would be equal in reality; otherwise that would not be His likeness. And they would be multiple, so there must be a distinguishing attribute joined to Him by which He is distinguished from His likeness. So if He were composite, He would not be necessary, because every composite is contingent. So if He had a likeness, He would not be He, and so affirming a likeness for Him entails negating Him. So His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾, if we take it to mean "there is no likeness of His likeness," and the statement of the unbeliever stands opposite it: "a likeness of His likeness is something," then it affirms that He is a likeness of His likeness, and His likeness departs from the reality of its own essence, and thus does not remain necessarily existent. So mentioning the two likenesses verbally conveys tawhid together with an indication of the proof for the invalidity of the polytheist's claim. And if we say "there is nothing like Him," it would be a negation without an indication of proof. The verification in this is that we say, in negating a likeness in refutation of the polytheist: "God has no likeness," then we argue for it and say: if He had a likeness, He would be a likeness of that likeness, so He would be contingent and needy, and therefore not a god. And if He had a likeness, Allah would not be a god who is necessarily existent, because on the supposition of a likeness to Him, He shares with it in something and is distinct from it in something, so it would be necessary to abandon Him. So if He had a likeness, He would depart from the reality of being God. So affirming a partner leads to negating the Deity. So His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ is tawhid through proof, and "there is no likeness of Him, nothing" is tawhid without proof. Some of this I found in the words of the Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, after I had finished writing this, of what agreed with my thought with his thought. Yet I acknowledge that I have derived from him benefits I cannot count.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿well-guarded pearls﴾, it indicates the extreme of their purity, that is, pearls whose color the sun and the air have not changed.

What remains is to say: one who refutes someone who affirms certain things does not thereby negate everything he affirmed. So if one says: "Zayd is a good scholar," then one replies to him: "Zayd is not a good scholar," it does not follow from this that the reply negates his being a scholar. So whoever says ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ in the sense of "there is no likeness of His likeness" does not necessarily negate His likeness; rather it may negate the likeness of the likeness. So the one who refutes is not thereby a monotheist, which would take the statement out of conveying tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). So we say: it does convey tawhid. For if we say "there is no likeness of His likeness," it follows that He has no likeness, because if He had a likeness, He would be the likeness of His likeness, and He is a thing, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. For the reality of "thing" is that which exists, so the likeness of His likeness is a thing, and that is negated by our saying "there is no likeness of His likeness." So it is known that the statement does not depart from conveying tawhid. Thus it is known that taking the words in their literal sense conveys intensification in the statement regarding His saying ﴿like﴾. As for not taking it literally in His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾, that is more concise, so the kaf is made additional, lest it lead to ta'til (the denial of God's attributes), which is the denial of God. We say: there is benefit in this, namely that it is a negation together with an indication of the proof for the negation. That is because He, exalted is He, is wajib al-wujud (necessarily existent). The one who affirmed a partner agrees with us, and none opposes us except the mu'attil (one who denies divine attributes), and the affirmation of Him is evident. And if He is necessarily existent, then if He had a likeness, He would be outside His being necessarily existent, because He and His likeness would be equal in reality; otherwise that would not be His likeness. And they would be multiple, so there must be a distinguishing attribute joined to Him by which He is distinguished from His likeness. So if He were composite, He would not be necessary, because every composite is contingent. So if He had a likeness, He would not be He, and so affirming a likeness for Him entails negating Him. So His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾, if we take it to mean "there is no likeness of His likeness," and the statement of the unbeliever stands opposite it: "a likeness of His likeness is something," then it affirms that He is a likeness of His likeness, and His likeness departs from the reality of its own essence, and thus does not remain necessarily existent. So mentioning the two likenesses verbally conveys tawhid together with an indication of the proof for the invalidity of the polytheist's claim. And if we say "there is nothing like Him," it would be a negation without an indication of proof. The verification in this is that we say, in negating a likeness in refutation of the polytheist: "God has no likeness," then we argue for it and say: if He had a likeness, He would be a likeness of that likeness, so He would be contingent and needy, and therefore not a god. And if He had a likeness, Allah would not be a god who is necessarily existent, because on the supposition of a likeness to Him, He shares with it in something and is distinct from it in something, so it would be necessary to abandon Him. So if He had a likeness, He would depart from the reality of being God. So affirming a partner leads to negating the Deity. So His saying ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾ is tawhid through proof, and "there is no likeness of Him, nothing" is tawhid without proof. Some of this I found in the words of the Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, after I had finished writing this, of what agreed with my thought with his thought. Yet I acknowledge that I have derived from him benefits I cannot count.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿well-guarded pearls﴾, it indicates the extreme of their purity, that is, pearls whose color the sun and the air have not changed.

[Page 136]

[Page 137 is omitted from the translation.]

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾.

Regarding its grammatical case (naṣb), there are two possibilities:

The first: it is a maf'ūl lahu (object of purpose, i.e., an accusative of reason), which is the apparent reading. Its implied sense is: "He did this to them so that it would be a reward, and so that they would be recompensed for their deeds." On this reading there is a subtle point, which is that we say: the meaning is that all of this is the reward for your deeds, but as for the increase (al-ziyādah), none of you can comprehend it.

The second: it is a maṣdar (verbal noun, absolute object), because the evidence that everything Allah does is a reward means that it is as if He had said: "You are being recompensed with a recompense." As for His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾, we have already mentioned its benefit in the sūrah of al-Ṭūr, which is that He, exalted is He, said concerning the believers: ﴿so He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, and concerning the disbelievers: ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 7]. This indicates that the punishment is exactly the recompense for what they did, so there is no addition to it for them. As for the reward, ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, Allah does not give them the very same thing as their deeds; rather, He gives them, because of their deeds, what He gives them. The disbeliever, however, is given exactly what he did. Thus there is in this the meaning of His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'ām: 160].

There are several issues here:

The first issue: it is a principle of uṣūl (foundational theory) which Imam Fakhr al-Dīn, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in many places, and we will mention some of it.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: this indicates that reward is obligatory upon Allah, because recompense is not something one can demand. Imam Fakhr al-Dīn, may Allah have mercy on him, answered this with many answers, and I think that he did not mention what I would say about it, which is what they mentioned. Even if it were correct, there would be no benefit in the promise of these things. That is because, when reason judges that withholding recompense is ugly, and reason knows that what is ugly does not occur from Allah, it is known that Allah gives these things because they are recompenses, and delivering recompense is obligatory. But if we hold our own doctrine (that reward is a bounty), the verses become informative and glad-tidings, because glad-tidings are only of good concerning an unknown matter. It cannot be said: "The recompense was obligatory upon Allah, but the report of these things would not be mentioned as glad-tidings." For we say: if the recompense itself is obligatory, then what Allah, exalted is He, has given us of blessings in this world is a recompense, and the reward of the Hereafter would only be an act of grace from Him. The most that can be said is that He, exalted is He, perfected the blessing by His saying: "This is your recompense," meaning: "I have made it a recompense for you," and it was not specified or obligatory. Just as a generous man who gives a great deal to one who brings him something small, so that the one thinks he is depositing it with him, or ordering him to carry it to a place, and he says to him: "This is for you," and he rejoices. Then he says: "This is a great favour that obliges me to much service," so he says to him: "This is the recompense for what you brought, and I do not ask of you any service in return for it. If you bring any service, it will have a new reward." This would be the utmost of grace. At this point we say: all of this applies when the one who comes is not a slave. But when a slave does what his master has obligated upon him, he does not deserve any wage for it, especially if he does what he was commanded with some defect. So what do you think of our state with Allah, mighty and majestic? Moreover, a master does not own from his slave anything except his frame, whereas Allah, exalted is He, owns from us our selves and our bodies. Then, if you reflect on the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority), you will find that they realized the meaning of servanthood to the utmost degree of realization, and acknowledged that they are slaves who own nothing, and that a slave has no debt owed to him by his master. The Mu'tazilah did not realize servanthood, and they made between themselves and Allah a transaction which necessitates demand. We hope that Allah, exalted is He, will realize with us ownership (al-mālikiyyah) to the utmost degree of realization, and will meet our basic needs and purify our deeds, just as a master meets the need of his slave by feeding and clothing him, and purifies his fast by the zakāt al-fiṭr. And if the slave commits a crime, he does not let the injured party take him; rather he chooses to ransom him and frees his neck from the crime. Likewise, Allah meets our needs in the Hereafter, and the most important of needs is that He show mercy to us and pardon us, and cover us with forgiveness and good pleasure, since He has prevented others from taking possession of our necks by choosing to ransom us. I hope that He does not do with our brothers, the Mu'tazilah, what two parties in a reckoning do with each other, insisting on the smallest and the largest, and demanding whatever surplus falls to one of them, be it little or much.

The second issue: They said: if there were a vision (ru'yah) in the Hereafter, it would be a recompense, and Allah has restricted recompense to what He mentioned. The answer to this is: we say, why have you said that it would be a recompense? Rather, it would be a bounty from Him beyond the recompense. Grant that it would be a recompense, but why have you said that mentioning the recompense is a restriction, and that it is not so? For whoever says to another, "I gave you such-and-such as a recompense for a deed," does not contradict his saying, "And I gave you something else above it as a recompense for it as well." Grant that it is a restriction, but why have you said that nearness (qurbah) does not indicate vision? If it is said: He said concerning the angels, ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ [al-Nisā': 172], and nearness did not necessarily entail vision. We reply: we have answered that their nearness is like the nearness of one who is with the king for the performance of tasks, who is under obligation and stands before him at the door, from which his orders come out to him, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 6]. The nearness of the believer is the nearness of one granted favour by the king, which is only for conversation and companionship in this world. But the one who is brought near under obligation does not enter upon the king every time he goes to the door, whereas the one who is granted favour does not go to him without entering upon him. Thus the difference is clear.

What indicates that His saying ﴿those brought near﴾ contains an indication of vision is that Allah, exalted is He, in the sūrah of al-Muṭaffifīn mentioned the righteous and the wicked. Then He, exalted is He, said concerning the wicked: ﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 15], and He said concerning the righteous: ﴿from which drink those brought near﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 28]. He did not mention, in contrast to "veiled," anything indicating a difference between the state of the righteous and the state of the wicked in veiling and nearness. For His saying ﴿indeed, in ʿIlliyyūn﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 18], although it is evidence of nearness and elevation of rank, is in contrast to His saying ﴿indeed, in Sijjīn﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7]. So His saying concerning them, ﴿from which drink those brought near﴾, together with His saying, ﴿and their Lord gave them a pure drink﴾ [al-Insān: 21], indicates that what is meant by it is the nearness that belongs to the king's companions in the presence of the king. And His saying concerning the angels in that sūrah, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 21], indicates that what is meant by it is the nearness that belongs to the Book and the reckoning in the presence of the king, because in this world one of them envies the other. For the scribe, if his nearness to the king is due to service, does not choose the nearness of the Book and the reckoning, but rather the nearness of the boon-companion. Then between that type of nearness and the nearness due to writing there is something that leads him to prefer the other. In the sūrah of al-Muṭaffifīn, His saying ﴿they will be veiled﴾ indicates that those brought near are not veiled from looking upon Allah, exalted is He. And our saying "companions of the king" should not be understood, in the apparent sense that suggests direction in the view of the common people, nor the nearness that the layman understands as place, except in the view of the learned, the reliable, the wise and the good.

The third issue: They said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ indicates that the deed is theirs and occurs by their act. We say: there is no dispute that in the linguistic reality the word "ʿamal" (deed) was coined for action, and "majnūn" (mad) for one who has no intellect, and "ʿāqil" (sane) for one who has attained perfection in it. That is nothing other than the linguistic usage for what is perceived by the senses. Everyone sees motion in bodies and says: "It moved and it stopped," in the literal sense, just as he says: "The millstone turns," and "the stone rises." What is in question is the power by which the act occurs in the visible locus, and that lies outside the linguistic usage.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Exalted said: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor any sinful speech﴾ ﴿except the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: What is the wisdom in mentioning it (the hearing of peace) separately from the recompense, even though it is among the great blessings? We say: In this there are subtle points.

The first: This is among the most complete of blessings, so He made it part of the increase (ziyadah), which for some includes the vision (of Allah), and it has no counterpart in deeds. We only said that it is among the most complete blessings because it is the blessing of hearing the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as we will explain, that what is meant by His saying ﴿peace﴾ is what He mentioned in Surat Ya-Sin: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. So He did not mention it among what He made a recompense. This, according to our view on ﴿those who are brought near﴾, does not indicate the vision.

The second: He, the Exalted, began with the most complete blessing, which is the blessing of seeing, namely seeing by looking, as has passed, and He closed with its like, which is the blessing of being addressed.

The third: When He, the Exalted, mentioned the blessings of action and set them against their deeds, saying ﴿as a recompense for what they used to do﴾, He mentioned the blessings of speech in return for their good remembrances (adhkar). They did not mention the intellectual pleasures, which correspond to the deeds of their hearts, of their sincerity and their belief, because the deed of the heart is not seen and not heard. So what Allah the Exalted gives them of blessing will be a blessing that no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and to this is the allusion in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." And his saying (peace be upon him): "and no human heart has conceived" is an allusion to the increase. What indicates the blessing of speech in return for their good speech is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings"﴾ [Fussilat: 30], up to His saying:
[p. 139]
﴿as a hospitable gift from the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [Fussilat: 32].

The second issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor any sinful speech﴾ is a negation of what is disliked, because idle talk is speech that is not regarded, since among men of standing it is disliked. And negating what is disliked is not counted among the great blessings that have been mentioned, especially since you have stated that the delay of this blessing is because it is more complete. If someone says, "So-and-so in such-and-such a town is respected and honored, he is not beaten and not insulted," then he is not honored and he is blameworthy. The one who intrudes (al-waghil) is blameworthy, and he is the one who enters upon a people who are drinking and eating, so he eats and drinks with them without being invited or given permission. So, in relation to them, he is in the position of speech that is not regarded, and this is idle talk (laghw). Likewise, what is derived from it, such as al-wulugh (lapping), is not used except when the one lapping is a dog or something resembling it of beasts of prey. As for sinful speech (ta'thim), it is the attribution of sin, and its meaning is that one mentions nothing but falsehood and no one attributes anything except to falsehood. As for the order of mention, it is because idle talk is more general than sinful speech, i.e., it makes the speaker sinful, as when you say, "he is a wicked person (fasiq) or a thief," and the like. In sum, the speaker is divided into one who engages in idle talk and one who does not. The one who does not engage in idle talk intends enjoining good and forbidding evil, so he takes people to task by their words, and nothing is taken against him. So He, the Exalted, said: No one engages in idle talk, nothing idle proceeds from him, and nothing resembling idle talk. It is as though one were to say to him: "The truthful one does not engage in idle talk and does not sin." And there is no doubt that falsehood is the worst of what resembles it, so He said: no one sins.

The third issue: The Exalted said in Surat al-Naba': ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor lying (kidhdhab)﴾ [al-Naba': 35]. Is there a difference between the two? We say: Yes. Kidhdhab is one who frequently denies (takdhib), and its meaning there is that they do not hear lying, nor does anyone say to another, "You lied." Its benefit is that they do not recognize a lie from a specific person among people, nor from any unspecified individual among them, because of the difference between their state and the state of this world. For we know that some people are liars by name, and if we did not know this, we would be certain that among people there is a liar, because one of them says to his companion, "You lied." If he is truthful, then his companion is a liar, and if he is not truthful, then he is a liar. So he knows that in this world there is a liar, specific or unspecified. But this is not the case in the Hereafter, so there is no lying therein. And here He said: ﴿nor any sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25], and this is more eloquent than denial (takdhib). For whoever says about someone he does not know, "he is an adulterer" or "a drinker of wine," for example, he commits sin, and he may be truthful. So whatever is not based on knowledge is sinful, and no one says to another, "You spoke of what you have no knowledge of." Thus the expression here is more eloquent, because He confined the surah to explaining the states of the categories, since those mentioned here are the foremost (al-sabiqun), and in Surat al-Naba' they are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). And we have explained that the foremost are above the God-fearing.

The fourth issue: ﴿except the saying﴾ is an exception that is either contiguous (istithna' muttasil) or disjunctive (istithna' munqati', i.e., not of the same genus). We say: In this there are two views:

One of them, and it is the more apparent, is that it is disjunctive, because peace is not of the same genus as idle talk. Its meaning is: "but they hear a saying: peace, peace."

The second: that it is contiguous. Its basis is that we say: figurative usage (majaz) may occur in meaning, and among its instances is that you say, "I have no sin except that I love you, so you harm me." You make an exception of his love from the sin, and you do not intend a disjunctive exception, because by this statement you do not intend to show that you love him; rather you intend to clear yourself of sins. Its basis is that between them lies the utmost opposition, and between them are intermediate matters. An example is hot and cold, and between them is the lukewarm, which is closer to hot than to cold and closer to cold than to hot. The intermediate is called "cold" when compared to hot, so one says, "this is cold," and it is described in relation to cold as "hot." Having established this, we say: The statement of the speaker, "I have no sin except that I love you," means: you find nothing that approaches sin except love, for I have matters above it, which, when you attribute them to sin, you find between them the utmost opposition. So this is like his saying: "The degrees of love for me are your obedience, and above them is that the best side is the least of your affairs on the side of guarding my soul," as an allusion to exaggeration, just as one says, "this is nothing," belittling it in relation to what is above it. So His saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾ means: they hear therein speech that is surpassing, of great benefit and complete delight. The least of it and the closest to idle talk is the saying of some of them to others, "Peace be upon you." So they hear nothing that approaches idle talk except peace. So what do you think of that which is far from it, as cold water is far from what is lukewarm and true, and water whose coldness the sun has broken, when hot water is requested from it, and one says, "I have no hot water except this," meaning: I have nothing that is far from truly cold water and near to hot except this. In it is extreme exaggeration and exquisite eloquence. In this case, idle talk is figurative and the exception is contiguous. If it is said: If there is no alternative to figurative usage, and idle talk is interpreted as what is near to it in relation to it, then let the exception be interpreted as "but" (lakin), since both affirm the opposite of what preceded. We say: Figurative usage in nouns is preferable to figurative usage in particles, because nouns accept change in signification and change in circumstances, whereas particles do not, since particles do not become figurative except by being combined with a noun, while a noun becomes figurative without being combined with a particle. For you say, "I saw a lion shooting," and it is figurative without being combined with a particle. Likewise when you say to a man, "This is a lion," and you mean by lion one of complete courage. Also, the speaker's purpose in his saying, "I have no sin except that I love you," is not achieved by the figurative usage you mentioned, and also, departing from the original usage has no benefit except in exaggeration and eloquence.

The fifth issue: Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿qila﴾ (saying), there are two views:

One of them: that it is a verbal noun (masdar) like qawl (saying), so qila is a verbal noun, just as qawl is a verbal noun, but this form does not appear for it in the pattern fa'ala yaf'ulu except with a letter [of the root being weak].

The second: that it is a noun (ism), and qawl is the verbal noun. It is like al-sidl and al-sitr: with a kasra on the sin it is a noun, and with a fatha it is a verbal noun. This second view is the more apparent. On this basis we say: The apparent view is that it is a noun derived from the verb qala and qila, for what has no stated agent. As for what is said, that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade "qil and qal," its meaning is that he forbade disputation and narrating matters that occurred among peoples, which have no benefit in mentioning them and contain nothing but mere narration without admonition or wisdom, based on his saying (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on a servant who speaks good and profits, or keeps silent and is safe." On this basis, qil is a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown, and qal is a noun for speech derived from qila, meaning what has no stated agent. You say, "So-and-so said such-and-such, then it was said to him such-and-such, so he said such-and-such," and the essence of his speech is "qil and qal." On this basis, qil is a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown, and qal is derived from qila, which is qala. One might object: This is invalid because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 88], for the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: Allah knows the saying of Muhammad: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾, just as Noah (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants﴾ [Nuh: 27]. On this basis, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So overlook them and say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89] is a guidance to him, lest he invoke against his people in his despair of them, as Noah invoked against them. And if the saying is attributed to Muhammad (ﷺ), then qil would not be a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown? We say: The answer to this is in two respects.

One of them: that our statement that it is a noun derived from qila, which is established for a saying whose speaker is unknown in origin, does not preclude its being used for the saying of one who is known, which is other than its original meaning.

The second, and it is the subtle answer: We say that the ha' in ﴿wa-qilihi﴾ is a pronoun, as in rabbihi, and like the unspecified pronoun according to the Kufans, which is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n). According to the Basrans, it is as in His saying: ﴿for indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46], where the ha' does not refer to any previously mentioned thing. However, the Kufans made it for an unknown referent, while the Basrans made it the pronoun of the narrative. The more apparent view in this matter is the view of the Kufans. On this basis, the meaning of their expression is: the saying of the speaker among them reached the utmost of Allah the Exalted's knowledge: "O my Lord, indeed these are..." — an indication that the specific attribute of that saying applies to everyone, namely that they will not believe, because He knows that they are speaking this and that they are aware of it. And the people of heaven knew that with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, He knows it, and so He knows the saying of one who says: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾ without
[p. 141]

...the specification of one saying, since all share in it. This is supported by the fact that if the pronoun referred to a known referent, then either it refers to something mentioned before it, but nothing before it is such that the pronoun can refer to it; or it refers to a known referent that is not mentioned, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). But the address in His words ﴿so turn away﴾ would require Him to say, "and his saying, O Lord," because Muhammad (ﷺ) is the first addressee of God's speech. He had said before it, ﴿And if you asked them﴾ [Luqman: 25], and He had said earlier, ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], and he was the first addressee. Once this is established, we say: if you reflect on the usage of the word qawl (saying) in the Qur'an, you will find that what we have mentioned is observed and taken into account. So He said here, ﴿except a saying: Peace, peace﴾, because this saying is not restricted to one speaker rather than another. Thus it is heard constantly from the angels and from people, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, ﴿Peace﴾﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], where the one who gives the greeting is alone, namely God, as if He said: "Peace, a saying from Us." He also said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God and does righteousness﴾ [Fussilat: 33], and: ﴿it is firmer in treading and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6]; because the caller is specific, namely the messengers and those of the community who follow them, and everyone who stands in prayer at night, his speech is upright and his path is straight. And He said, ﴿and his saying, O Lord﴾, because everyone says, "They do not believe." As for them, it is due to their acknowledgment and affirmation; and as for others, it is due to their disbelief, their excess and their persistence. What we have mentioned is supported by His saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk or sinning﴾. The connected exception (istithna' muttasil) brings the meaning closer in relation to others, and it is a saying whose speaker is not known, so He said, ﴿except a saying﴾, which is "Peace upon you." As for the saying of one who is known, namely God, it is the farthest from idle talk to the utmost degree, and between them is the furthest extent of difference. So He said, ﴿Peace, a saying﴾.

The sixth issue: "Salaman" (Peace). There are three aspects to it:
The first: it is an adjective, which God has described ﴿qawl (saying)﴾ with, as a thing is described by a verbal noun, as one says: "a just man" (rajul 'adl) and "a fasting people" (qawm sawm). Its meaning is: "except a saying that is free from defects."
The second: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whose implied construction is: "except that they say peace."
The third: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿qawl (saying)﴾, its implied construction being: "except peace."

The seventh issue: Is there any benefit in the repetition of "peace"? We say: it contains an indication of the completion of blessing. This is because the effect of greeting in this world is not complete except through the greeting and the returning of the greeting. Just as one of two people meeting in this world says to the other, "Peace be upon you," and the other replies, "And upon you be peace," so in the Hereafter they say, ﴿Peace, peace﴾. Then, when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Peace, a saying from a Lord Most Merciful﴾, there was no response to it, because God's greeting upon His servant grants him security. As for God, He is exalted above anyone granting Him security. Rather, the response, if there is one, is the saying of the one who is granted security: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God."

The eighth issue: What is the difference between His words, ﴿Peace, peace﴾ with both in the accusative, and His words, ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]? We say: We have mentioned there that His words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [Maryam: 47] are more complete and more eloquent than their saying, "Peace upon you" in the accusative. Abraham (peace be upon him) intended to show them favour by greeting them and to answer them with the best of what they had offered. Here, however, none of the people of Paradise shows favour to another in the way of that situation, since they are of one kind, namely believers, and no one attributes shortcoming to another.

The ninth issue: If the saying of the speaker, ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, is more complete and more eloquent, then what about the well-known recitation (al-qira'ah al-mashhurah) being in the accusative? And the one who reads ﴿salamun﴾ (in the nominative) is not in the same position as the one who reads it in the accusative. We say that this is in terms of both wording and meaning. As for the wording, the exception is from what is heard, which is an object in the accusative; so the accusative is governed by His words, ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾. As for the meaning, we have explained that the exception is connected, and their saying ﴿salam﴾ (in the nominative) is further from idle talk than their saying ﴿salaman﴾ (in the accusative). So He said, ﴿except a saying, "Peace,"﴾ so that it would be closer to idle talk than otherwise, even though in itself it is far from it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Exalted said: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor any sinful speech﴾ ﴿except the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: What is the wisdom in mentioning it (the hearing of peace) separately from the recompense, even though it is among the great blessings? We say: In this there are subtle points.

The first: This is among the most complete of blessings, so He made it part of the increase (ziyadah), which for some includes the vision (of Allah), and it has no counterpart in deeds. We only said that it is among the most complete blessings because it is the blessing of hearing the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as we will explain, that what is meant by His saying ﴿peace﴾ is what He mentioned in Surat Ya-Sin: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. So He did not mention it among what He made a recompense. This, according to our view on ﴿those who are brought near﴾, does not indicate the vision.

The second: He, the Exalted, began with the most complete blessing, which is the blessing of seeing, namely seeing by looking, as has passed, and He closed with its like, which is the blessing of being addressed.

The third: When He, the Exalted, mentioned the blessings of action and set them against their deeds, saying ﴿as a recompense for what they used to do﴾, He mentioned the blessings of speech in return for their good remembrances (adhkar). They did not mention the intellectual pleasures, which correspond to the deeds of their hearts, of their sincerity and their belief, because the deed of the heart is not seen and not heard. So what Allah the Exalted gives them of blessing will be a blessing that no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and to this is the allusion in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." And his saying (peace be upon him): "and no human heart has conceived" is an allusion to the increase. What indicates the blessing of speech in return for their good speech is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings"﴾ [Fussilat: 30], up to His saying:
[p. 139]
﴿as a hospitable gift from the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [Fussilat: 32].

The second issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor any sinful speech﴾ is a negation of what is disliked, because idle talk is speech that is not regarded, since among men of standing it is disliked. And negating what is disliked is not counted among the great blessings that have been mentioned, especially since you have stated that the delay of this blessing is because it is more complete. If someone says, "So-and-so in such-and-such a town is respected and honored, he is not beaten and not insulted," then he is not honored and he is blameworthy. The one who intrudes (al-waghil) is blameworthy, and he is the one who enters upon a people who are drinking and eating, so he eats and drinks with them without being invited or given permission. So, in relation to them, he is in the position of speech that is not regarded, and this is idle talk (laghw). Likewise, what is derived from it, such as al-wulugh (lapping), is not used except when the one lapping is a dog or something resembling it of beasts of prey. As for sinful speech (ta'thim), it is the attribution of sin, and its meaning is that one mentions nothing but falsehood and no one attributes anything except to falsehood. As for the order of mention, it is because idle talk is more general than sinful speech, i.e., it makes the speaker sinful, as when you say, "he is a wicked person (fasiq) or a thief," and the like. In sum, the speaker is divided into one who engages in idle talk and one who does not. The one who does not engage in idle talk intends enjoining good and forbidding evil, so he takes people to task by their words, and nothing is taken against him. So He, the Exalted, said: No one engages in idle talk, nothing idle proceeds from him, and nothing resembling idle talk. It is as though one were to say to him: "The truthful one does not engage in idle talk and does not sin." And there is no doubt that falsehood is the worst of what resembles it, so He said: no one sins.

The third issue: The Exalted said in Surat al-Naba': ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor lying (kidhdhab)﴾ [al-Naba': 35]. Is there a difference between the two? We say: Yes. Kidhdhab is one who frequently denies (takdhib), and its meaning there is that they do not hear lying, nor does anyone say to another, "You lied." Its benefit is that they do not recognize a lie from a specific person among people, nor from any unspecified individual among them, because of the difference between their state and the state of this world. For we know that some people are liars by name, and if we did not know this, we would be certain that among people there is a liar, because one of them says to his companion, "You lied." If he is truthful, then his companion is a liar, and if he is not truthful, then he is a liar. So he knows that in this world there is a liar, specific or unspecified. But this is not the case in the Hereafter, so there is no lying therein. And here He said: ﴿nor any sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25], and this is more eloquent than denial (takdhib). For whoever says about someone he does not know, "he is an adulterer" or "a drinker of wine," for example, he commits sin, and he may be truthful. So whatever is not based on knowledge is sinful, and no one says to another, "You spoke of what you have no knowledge of." Thus the expression here is more eloquent, because He confined the surah to explaining the states of the categories, since those mentioned here are the foremost (al-sabiqun), and in Surat al-Naba' they are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). And we have explained that the foremost are above the God-fearing.

The fourth issue: ﴿except the saying﴾ is an exception that is either contiguous (istithna' muttasil) or disjunctive (istithna' munqati', i.e., not of the same genus). We say: In this there are two views:

One of them, and it is the more apparent, is that it is disjunctive, because peace is not of the same genus as idle talk. Its meaning is: "but they hear a saying: peace, peace."

The second: that it is contiguous. Its basis is that we say: figurative usage (majaz) may occur in meaning, and among its instances is that you say, "I have no sin except that I love you, so you harm me." You make an exception of his love from the sin, and you do not intend a disjunctive exception, because by this statement you do not intend to show that you love him; rather you intend to clear yourself of sins. Its basis is that between them lies the utmost opposition, and between them are intermediate matters. An example is hot and cold, and between them is the lukewarm, which is closer to hot than to cold and closer to cold than to hot. The intermediate is called "cold" when compared to hot, so one says, "this is cold," and it is described in relation to cold as "hot." Having established this, we say: The statement of the speaker, "I have no sin except that I love you," means: you find nothing that approaches sin except love, for I have matters above it, which, when you attribute them to sin, you find between them the utmost opposition. So this is like his saying: "The degrees of love for me are your obedience, and above them is that the best side is the least of your affairs on the side of guarding my soul," as an allusion to exaggeration, just as one says, "this is nothing," belittling it in relation to what is above it. So His saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾ means: they hear therein speech that is surpassing, of great benefit and complete delight. The least of it and the closest to idle talk is the saying of some of them to others, "Peace be upon you." So they hear nothing that approaches idle talk except peace. So what do you think of that which is far from it, as cold water is far from what is lukewarm and true, and water whose coldness the sun has broken, when hot water is requested from it, and one says, "I have no hot water except this," meaning: I have nothing that is far from truly cold water and near to hot except this. In it is extreme exaggeration and exquisite eloquence. In this case, idle talk is figurative and the exception is contiguous. If it is said: If there is no alternative to figurative usage, and idle talk is interpreted as what is near to it in relation to it, then let the exception be interpreted as "but" (lakin), since both affirm the opposite of what preceded. We say: Figurative usage in nouns is preferable to figurative usage in particles, because nouns accept change in signification and change in circumstances, whereas particles do not, since particles do not become figurative except by being combined with a noun, while a noun becomes figurative without being combined with a particle. For you say, "I saw a lion shooting," and it is figurative without being combined with a particle. Likewise when you say to a man, "This is a lion," and you mean by lion one of complete courage. Also, the speaker's purpose in his saying, "I have no sin except that I love you," is not achieved by the figurative usage you mentioned, and also, departing from the original usage has no benefit except in exaggeration and eloquence.

The fifth issue: Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿qila﴾ (saying), there are two views:

One of them: that it is a verbal noun (masdar) like qawl (saying), so qila is a verbal noun, just as qawl is a verbal noun, but this form does not appear for it in the pattern fa'ala yaf'ulu except with a letter [of the root being weak].

The second: that it is a noun (ism), and qawl is the verbal noun. It is like al-sidl and al-sitr: with a kasra on the sin it is a noun, and with a fatha it is a verbal noun. This second view is the more apparent. On this basis we say: The apparent view is that it is a noun derived from the verb qala and qila, for what has no stated agent. As for what is said, that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade "qil and qal," its meaning is that he forbade disputation and narrating matters that occurred among peoples, which have no benefit in mentioning them and contain nothing but mere narration without admonition or wisdom, based on his saying (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on a servant who speaks good and profits, or keeps silent and is safe." On this basis, qil is a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown, and qal is a noun for speech derived from qila, meaning what has no stated agent. You say, "So-and-so said such-and-such, then it was said to him such-and-such, so he said such-and-such," and the essence of his speech is "qil and qal." On this basis, qil is a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown, and qal is derived from qila, which is qala. One might object: This is invalid because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 88], for the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: Allah knows the saying of Muhammad: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾, just as Noah (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants﴾ [Nuh: 27]. On this basis, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So overlook them and say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89] is a guidance to him, lest he invoke against his people in his despair of them, as Noah invoked against them. And if the saying is attributed to Muhammad (ﷺ), then qil would not be a noun for a saying whose speaker is unknown? We say: The answer to this is in two respects.

One of them: that our statement that it is a noun derived from qila, which is established for a saying whose speaker is unknown in origin, does not preclude its being used for the saying of one who is known, which is other than its original meaning.

The second, and it is the subtle answer: We say that the ha' in ﴿wa-qilihi﴾ is a pronoun, as in rabbihi, and like the unspecified pronoun according to the Kufans, which is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n). According to the Basrans, it is as in His saying: ﴿for indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46], where the ha' does not refer to any previously mentioned thing. However, the Kufans made it for an unknown referent, while the Basrans made it the pronoun of the narrative. The more apparent view in this matter is the view of the Kufans. On this basis, the meaning of their expression is: the saying of the speaker among them reached the utmost of Allah the Exalted's knowledge: "O my Lord, indeed these are..." — an indication that the specific attribute of that saying applies to everyone, namely that they will not believe, because He knows that they are speaking this and that they are aware of it. And the people of heaven knew that with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, He knows it, and so He knows the saying of one who says: ﴿and his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe"﴾ without
[p. 141]

...the specification of one saying, since all share in it. This is supported by the fact that if the pronoun referred to a known referent, then either it refers to something mentioned before it, but nothing before it is such that the pronoun can refer to it; or it refers to a known referent that is not mentioned, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). But the address in His words ﴿so turn away﴾ would require Him to say, "and his saying, O Lord," because Muhammad (ﷺ) is the first addressee of God's speech. He had said before it, ﴿And if you asked them﴾ [Luqman: 25], and He had said earlier, ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], and he was the first addressee. Once this is established, we say: if you reflect on the usage of the word qawl (saying) in the Qur'an, you will find that what we have mentioned is observed and taken into account. So He said here, ﴿except a saying: Peace, peace﴾, because this saying is not restricted to one speaker rather than another. Thus it is heard constantly from the angels and from people, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, ﴿Peace﴾﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], where the one who gives the greeting is alone, namely God, as if He said: "Peace, a saying from Us." He also said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God and does righteousness﴾ [Fussilat: 33], and: ﴿it is firmer in treading and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6]; because the caller is specific, namely the messengers and those of the community who follow them, and everyone who stands in prayer at night, his speech is upright and his path is straight. And He said, ﴿and his saying, O Lord﴾, because everyone says, "They do not believe." As for them, it is due to their acknowledgment and affirmation; and as for others, it is due to their disbelief, their excess and their persistence. What we have mentioned is supported by His saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk or sinning﴾. The connected exception (istithna' muttasil) brings the meaning closer in relation to others, and it is a saying whose speaker is not known, so He said, ﴿except a saying﴾, which is "Peace upon you." As for the saying of one who is known, namely God, it is the farthest from idle talk to the utmost degree, and between them is the furthest extent of difference. So He said, ﴿Peace, a saying﴾.

The sixth issue: "Salaman" (Peace). There are three aspects to it:
The first: it is an adjective, which God has described ﴿qawl (saying)﴾ with, as a thing is described by a verbal noun, as one says: "a just man" (rajul 'adl) and "a fasting people" (qawm sawm). Its meaning is: "except a saying that is free from defects."
The second: it is a verbal noun (masdar), whose implied construction is: "except that they say peace."
The third: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿qawl (saying)﴾, its implied construction being: "except peace."

The seventh issue: Is there any benefit in the repetition of "peace"? We say: it contains an indication of the completion of blessing. This is because the effect of greeting in this world is not complete except through the greeting and the returning of the greeting. Just as one of two people meeting in this world says to the other, "Peace be upon you," and the other replies, "And upon you be peace," so in the Hereafter they say, ﴿Peace, peace﴾. Then, when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Peace, a saying from a Lord Most Merciful﴾, there was no response to it, because God's greeting upon His servant grants him security. As for God, He is exalted above anyone granting Him security. Rather, the response, if there is one, is the saying of the one who is granted security: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God."

The eighth issue: What is the difference between His words, ﴿Peace, peace﴾ with both in the accusative, and His words, ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]? We say: We have mentioned there that His words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [Maryam: 47] are more complete and more eloquent than their saying, "Peace upon you" in the accusative. Abraham (peace be upon him) intended to show them favour by greeting them and to answer them with the best of what they had offered. Here, however, none of the people of Paradise shows favour to another in the way of that situation, since they are of one kind, namely believers, and no one attributes shortcoming to another.

The ninth issue: If the saying of the speaker, ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, is more complete and more eloquent, then what about the well-known recitation (al-qira'ah al-mashhurah) being in the accusative? And the one who reads ﴿salamun﴾ (in the nominative) is not in the same position as the one who reads it in the accusative. We say that this is in terms of both wording and meaning. As for the wording, the exception is from what is heard, which is an object in the accusative; so the accusative is governed by His words, ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾. As for the meaning, we have explained that the exception is connected, and their saying ﴿salam﴾ (in the nominative) is further from idle talk than their saying ﴿salaman﴾ (in the accusative). So He said, ﴿except a saying, "Peace,"﴾ so that it would be closer to idle talk than otherwise, even though in itself it is far from it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ ﴿And acacias layered with fruit﴾.

When He had described the foremost, he began to speak of the companions of the right side (al-maymanah) among the three categories of spouses. On this there are several questions.

The first question: What is the benefit of mentioning them with the expression ﴿companions of the right side (al-maymanah)﴾ when speaking of the divisions, and with the expression ﴿companions of the right hand (al-yamin)﴾ when speaking of the blessings? We say: al-maymanah is a noun of place (maf'alah), either meaning the place of the right hand, like al-mahkamah meaning the place of judgment, i.e., the place in which the right hand is; or meaning the place of blessing (al-yumn), like al-manarah meaning the place of fire and al-majmarah meaning the place of embers. Whichever it is, the form (al-maymanah) indicates a place. But the three categories are, at the outset, distinguished from one another and separated, as in His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be divided [into groups]﴾ [al-Rum: 14], and He said: ﴿they will be separated﴾; so they are separated by place. Therefore, at the beginning He pointed to them with an expression that indicates place. Then, when it comes to the reward, their division occurs by an unspecified matter in which they do not share, like place; so He said: ﴿and the companions of the right hand﴾. And there are several explanations of this:

One of them: the companions of the right hand are those who take their books in their right hands.

The second: the companions of strength.

The third: the companions of light, and its explanation has already preceded.

The second question: What is the wisdom in His saying ﴿among lote-trees﴾, and what blessing is there in their being among lote-trees, when the lote-tree is one of the trees of the desert, neither bitter, nor sweet, nor fragrant? We say: There is in it a profound wisdom which both the earlier and the later scholars overlooked. They limited themselves, in answer and approximation, to the point that Paradise is depicted by what is precious and praiseworthy among the Arabs. That is correct, but it is not outstanding. The outstanding and refined answer, which befits the interpretation of the speech of Allah, is that we say: We have explained many times that the eloquent speaker mentions two extremes, and the mention of both includes an indication of everything between them, as one says: "So-and-so is king of the East and the West," and it is understood from this that he is king of both and of what lies between them; and one says: "So-and-so pleased the young and the old," and it is understood from this that he pleased everyone, and so on. So we say: There is no doubt that the adornment of places in which one takes pleasure with trees, and those trees are sometimes sought for their very leaves, for gazing at them and seeking shade under them; sometimes their fruits are intended; and sometimes both are combined. But the leaves of trees are of many kinds, and they fall into two types: small leaves and large leaves. The lote-tree is extremely small in leaf, and the talh, which is the banana tree, is extremely large in leaf. So His saying ﴿among lote-trees without thorns and acacias layered with fruit﴾ is an indication of what has the smallest leaves among trees and what has the largest leaves among them. Thus the indication to the two extremes came comprehensive of all trees with regard to their leaves. The leaf is one of the purposes of the tree, and its counterpart in mention is the mention of the palm and the pomegranate when intending to mention fruits, because between them is the utmost difference, as we have explained in its place. So the indication to these two came comprehensive of all trees with regard to their fruits. Similarly we said regarding the date palm and the grapevine: the date palm is among the greatest fruit-bearing trees, and the vine is among the smallest fruit-bearing trees, and between them are trees; so the indication to these two came comprehensive of all the other trees. This is an outstanding answer, which Allah, exalted is He, has granted us success in.

The third question: What is the meaning of al-makhdud (without thorns)? We say there are two views on it:

One of them: it means having its thorns removed, for the thorns of the lote-tree break its leaves; were it not for this, it would be the most pleasant place for the Arabs, because it provides shade on account of the abundance of its leaves and the overlapping of some of them with others.

The second: makhdud means bent downward, for the tops of the branches of the lote-tree in this world tend upward, unlike fruit trees whose tops hang down. In that case its meaning is that it differs from the lote-tree of this world, which has abundant fruit.

صفحة ١٤٣
The fourth question: What is the talh? We say: The apparent view is that it is the banana tree, and with this the benefit we mentioned is completed. It is narrated that Ali, peace be upon him, heard someone reciting ﴿wa-talhin mandud﴾, and said: "What is the matter with the talh? It is only (wa-talin), [the spathe/flower-cluster]," and he cited the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿for it are spathes stacked one upon another﴾ [Qaf: 10]. They said: "It is so in the codices (al-masahif)." He said: "The codices should not be altered." We say: This is evidence of the miraculous nature of the Qur'an and of the abundance of Ali's knowledge, may Allah be pleased with him. As for the miracle: Ali was among the eloquent Arabs, and when he heard this he understood it as talʿ and persisted in it, and the letter had not been fixed merely because his mind rushed to a meaning; then he said to himself that this speech is of the utmost beauty, because He, exalted is He, mentioned the tree from which the leaf is sought for shade, and the tree from which the fruit is sought for benefit, so He mentioned both types. Then, when he came to know the reality of the word, he knew that talh in this place is better, and it is more eloquent than the speech he had thought to be of the utmost eloquence, so he said: "The codex has shown me that it is better than what I had imagined," and the codex is not to be altered. What supports this is that if it were (talʿ), the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and abundant fruit﴾ would be a repetition of letters without benefit; whereas with talh, the benefit of His saying ﴿and fruit﴾ becomes clear, and we shall explain it, God willing, exalted is He.

The fifth question: What is al-mandud? We say: it is either the leaves or the fruit, and the apparent view is that what is meant is the leaves, because the banana tree, from its base to its top, is leaf upon leaf; it grows like wheat, leaf after leaf, and its stalk thickens and its leaves rise, and some of them remain without others, as in the case of reeds. The bananas of this world, when they are fixed, have a gap between them and the reed, and there is no leaf upon them; but the bananas of the Hereafter have their leaves connected to one another, so it has more leaves. It is also said that al-mandud means fruit-bearing. If it is asked: if the talh is a tree, it cannot be mandud, rather it has a mandud fruit; how then is it described as such? We say: This is of the type "beautiful of face," where a thing is described on account of the quality of what is connected to it. One says "Zayd is beautiful of face," and sometimes the face is omitted and one says "Zayd is beautiful," meaning beautiful of face; but it is not omitted if it would cause confusion. So it is correct to say "Zayd is struck by the boy" (mudrub al-ghulam), and it is not permissible to omit "the boy," because that would give rise to the false impression; but in "beautiful of face" it is permissible to omit "the face."

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ ﴿And acacias layered with fruit﴾.

When He had described the foremost, he began to speak of the companions of the right side (al-maymanah) among the three categories of spouses. On this there are several questions.

The first question: What is the benefit of mentioning them with the expression ﴿companions of the right side (al-maymanah)﴾ when speaking of the divisions, and with the expression ﴿companions of the right hand (al-yamin)﴾ when speaking of the blessings? We say: al-maymanah is a noun of place (maf'alah), either meaning the place of the right hand, like al-mahkamah meaning the place of judgment, i.e., the place in which the right hand is; or meaning the place of blessing (al-yumn), like al-manarah meaning the place of fire and al-majmarah meaning the place of embers. Whichever it is, the form (al-maymanah) indicates a place. But the three categories are, at the outset, distinguished from one another and separated, as in His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be divided [into groups]﴾ [al-Rum: 14], and He said: ﴿they will be separated﴾; so they are separated by place. Therefore, at the beginning He pointed to them with an expression that indicates place. Then, when it comes to the reward, their division occurs by an unspecified matter in which they do not share, like place; so He said: ﴿and the companions of the right hand﴾. And there are several explanations of this:

One of them: the companions of the right hand are those who take their books in their right hands.

The second: the companions of strength.

The third: the companions of light, and its explanation has already preceded.

The third question: What is the meaning of al-makhdud (without thorns)? We say there are two views on it:

The second: makhdud means bent downward, for the tops of the branches of the lote-tree in this world tend upward, unlike fruit trees whose tops hang down. In that case its meaning is that it differs from the lote-tree of this world, which has abundant fruit.

صفحة ١٤٣
The fourth question: What is the talh? We say: The apparent view is that it is the banana tree, and with this the benefit we mentioned is completed. It is narrated that Ali, peace be upon him, heard someone reciting ﴿wa-talhin mandud﴾, and said: "What is the matter with the talh? They said: "It is so in the codices (al-masahif)." He said: "The codices should not be altered." We say: This is evidence of the miraculous nature of the Qur'an and of the abundance of Ali's knowledge, may Allah be pleased with him. As for the miracle: Ali was among the eloquent Arabs, and when he heard this he understood it as talʿ and persisted in it, and the letter had not been fixed merely because his mind rushed to a meaning; then he said to himself that this speech is of the utmost beauty, because He, exalted is He, mentioned the tree from which the leaf is sought for shade, and the tree from which the fruit is sought for benefit, so He mentioned both types. The bananas of this world, when they are fixed, have a gap between them and the reed, and there is no leaf upon them; but the bananas of the Hereafter have their leaves connected to one another, so it has more leaves. We say: This is of the type "beautiful of face," where a thing is described on account of the quality of what is connected to it. One says "Zayd is beautiful of face," and sometimes the face is omitted and one says "Zayd is beautiful," meaning beautiful of face; but it is not omitted if it would cause confusion. So it is correct to say "Zayd is struck by the boy" (mudrub al-ghulam), and it is not permissible to omit "the boy," because that would give rise to the false impression; but in "beautiful of face" it is permissible to omit "the face."

Whichever it is, the form (al-maymanah) indicates a place. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 30–33:

Then God Most High said: ﴿And extended shade﴾. On this there are several interpretations:

The first: it is extended in time, meaning it has no end and is perpetual, as God Most High said: ﴿its fruit is perpetual and so is its shade﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: likewise.

The second: it is extended in place, meaning it falls upon a large thing and covers it from the land of the Garden.

The third: the meaning of "extended" (mamdud) is spread out (munbasit), as God Most High said: ﴿And the earth—We have spread it out﴾ [al-Hijr: 19]. If it is asked: how can the second interpretation be? We say: the shade may be elevated. When the sun is beneath the earth, its shadow falls into the atmosphere, so the shadow accumulates and the face of the earth turns dark. When the sun is on one of its sides, close to the horizon, its shadow spreads over the face of the earth, so the atmosphere is illuminated and the face of the earth does not become hot, and it is then in the utmost pleasantness. Thus His saying ﴿and extended shade﴾ means: when it stands upright over the earth like a shadow at night. On this view, the shade is not the shade of trees but a shade that God Most High creates.

As for His saying Most High: ﴿and flowing water﴾, there are also several interpretations on it:

The first: it is poured down from above (maskub min fawq). This is because the Arabs most commonly had wells and cisterns, so there was no pouring of water among them, unlike places where there are springs gushing from mountains that rule over the land and pour over it.

The second: flowing in no trench (ukhdud), because poured water flows in the air and there is no river there; likewise is the water in the Garden.

The third: abundant. Among the Arabs, water is precious and is not poured out but is conserved and drunk. So when they mention blessings, they count the abundance of water and express its abundance by spilling and pouring it out. The first is more correct.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And fruit in abundance﴾, ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. When He mentioned the trees whose leaves are sought, He mentioned after them the trees whose fruit is intended. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: what is the wisdom in mentioning the leafy trees before the trees that are not leafy? We say: it is evident. He mentioned foliage before the tree in the manner of ascending from one blessing to a mention of a blessing above it, and fruits are a more complete blessing.

The second issue: what is the wisdom in mentioning the leafy trees by themselves, and the fruit trees by their fruit? We say: this too is evident. The beauty of leaves lies in their being on the tree, whereas fruits are desired in themselves whether they are on the tree or cut off. For this reason, fruits have names by which their trees are known, so one says: the fig tree and its leaves.

The third issue: what is the wisdom in describing fruit with abundance rather than with goodness and pleasure? We say: we have explained in the surah al-Rahman that fruit is an active noun, like "pleasing" in His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning possessing fruit (fakih). By its nature, it is only goodness and pleasure. As for abundance, we explained that when God Most High mentioned fruit, He mentioned what indicates abundance, because fruit is not for relieving need, so that it would be only in the measure of need; rather it is for enjoyment, so He described it with abundance and variety.

The fourth issue: ﴿neither cut off﴾ means: unlike the fruits of this world, which are cut off at most times and seasons and in many places and locations. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾ means: not withheld from people in order to seek compensation and price. Being withheld from people in order to seek compensation and price is evident to the senses, since fruit in this world is withheld from some, so it is forbidden; in the Hereafter it is not forbidden. As for being cut off, it is said of this world that it has been cut off, so it is cut off (munqati'ah), not "maqtu'ah" (having been severed). So His saying Most High ﴿neither cut off﴾ is most beautiful, because it contains an indication of the cause of non-severance, just as in ﴿nor forbidden﴾ there is an indication of the absence of prohibition. Its explanation is that fruit in this world is withheld only for seeking exchange and the owner's need for its price to meet a need; in the Hereafter its owner is God Most High, and He has no need. It follows that fruit is not withheld from anyone, like one who has abundant fruit and neither eats nor sells it and has no need of it in any way; there is no doubt that he distributes it and does not withhold it from anyone. As for cutting off, we say: what is said in this world is "the fruit has been cut off," and when it is present one does not say "it has refused" (imtana'at), but rather "it has been withheld" (muni'at). This is because a person speaks only in what both the young and the old understand. Yet whenever anyone looks at fruit at the time of its existence, he sees someone possessing it and guarding it, and does not see the fruit itself refusing, so he says it is forbidden. But when it is cut off and absent, he does not see anyone who has severed it physically and caused its non-existence, so he assumes it has been cut off by itself, because he does not perceive a severer, while he does perceive a withholder. So God Most High said: if you looked in this world with the truest looking, you would know that every time, considered as night and day, is one in which fruit is possible, so it is not itself cut off; it is only not found with the one who verifies (al-muhaqqiq) because God has cut it off and singled it out for one time over another, and with the one who does not verify because of the coldness and heat of the time and its need for growth, flowering and blossoming. For this reason customs follow certain seasons, so time cuts them off in the view of one who does not verify. So when the Garden's shade is extended, with no sun there and no zamharir (intense cold), the seasons become equal, and God Most High severs it, so it is not cut off by any real or apparent cause. The cut-off thing is one whose cutting a person can reflect on, knowing it is severed, not cut off without a severer. In the Garden there is no severer, so it does not become severed.

The fifth issue: He placed the negation of its being severed before the negation of its being forbidden, because cutting applies to what exists, and prohibition after existence; for if it did not exist, it would not be forbidden or guarded. So He said: it is not cut off so that it would exist forever. Then that existing thing is not withheld from anyone. This is evident, but we want to leave nothing out of what comes to mind that is correct.
