Its explanation is that fruit in this world is withheld only for seeking exchange and the owner's need for its price to meet a need; in the Hereafter its owner is God Most High, and He has no need. It follows that fruit is not withheld from anyone, like one who has abundant fruit and neither eats nor sells it and has no need of it in any way; there is no doubt that he distributes it and does not withhold it from anyone. As for cutting off, we say: what is said in this world is "the fruit has been cut off," and when it is present one does not say "it has refused" (imtana'at), but rather "it has been withheld" (muni'at). This is because a person speaks only in what both the young and the old understand. Yet whenever anyone looks at fruit at the time of its existence, he sees someone possessing it and guarding it, and does not see the fruit itself refusing, so he says it is forbidden. But when it is cut off and absent, he does not see anyone who has severed it physically and caused its non-existence, so he assumes it has been cut off by itself, because he does not perceive a severer, while he does perceive a withholder. So God Most High said: if you looked in this world with the truest looking, you would know that every time, considered as night and day, is one in which fruit is possible, so it is not itself cut off; it is only not found with the one who verifies (al-muhaqqiq) because God has cut it off and singled it out for one time over another, and with the one who does not verify because of the coldness and heat of the time and its need for growth, flowering and blossoming. For this reason customs follow certain seasons, so time cuts them off in the view of one who does not verify. So when the Garden's shade is extended, with no sun there and no zamharir (intense cold), the seasons become equal, and God Most High severs it, so it is not cut off by any real or apparent cause. The cut-off thing is one whose cutting a person can reflect on, knowing it is severed, not cut off without a severer. In the Garden there is no severer, so it does not become severed.

The fifth issue: He placed the negation of its being severed before the negation of its being forbidden, because cutting applies to what exists, and prohibition after existence; for if it did not exist, it would not be forbidden or guarded. So He said: it is not cut off so that it would exist forever. Then that existing thing is not withheld from anyone. This is evident, but we want to leave nothing out of what comes to mind that is correct.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 30–33:

Then God Most High said: ﴿And extended shade﴾. On this there are several interpretations:

The first: it is extended in time, meaning it has no end and is perpetual, as God Most High said: ﴿its fruit is perpetual and so is its shade﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: likewise.

The second: it is extended in place, meaning it falls upon a large thing and covers it from the land of the Garden.

The third: the meaning of "extended" (mamdud) is spread out (munbasit), as God Most High said: ﴿And the earth—We have spread it out﴾ [al-Hijr: 19]. If it is asked: how can the second interpretation be? We say: the shade may be elevated. When the sun is beneath the earth, its shadow falls into the atmosphere, so the shadow accumulates and the face of the earth turns dark. When the sun is on one of its sides, close to the horizon, its shadow spreads over the face of the earth, so the atmosphere is illuminated and the face of the earth does not become hot, and it is then in the utmost pleasantness. Thus His saying ﴿and extended shade﴾ means: when it stands upright over the earth like a shadow at night. On this view, the shade is not the shade of trees but a shade that God Most High creates.

As for His saying Most High: ﴿and flowing water﴾, there are also several interpretations on it:

The first: it is poured down from above (maskub min fawq). This is because the Arabs most commonly had wells and cisterns, so there was no pouring of water among them, unlike places where there are springs gushing from mountains that rule over the land and pour over it.

The second: flowing in no trench (ukhdud), because poured water flows in the air and there is no river there; likewise is the water in the Garden.

The third: abundant. Among the Arabs, water is precious and is not poured out but is conserved and drunk. So when they mention blessings, they count the abundance of water and express its abundance by spilling and pouring it out. The first is more correct.

* * *

For this reason, fruits have names by which their trees are known, so one says: the fig tree and its leaves.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And raised couches﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of "furush" (couches), and we will mention another aspect of it, God willing. As for "marfu'ah" (raised), there are three aspects to it:

The first: raised in rank, as one says of a garment that it is "rafi'" (fine), meaning precious, elevated in status and price. This is indicated by God's saying: ﴿On couches whose linings are of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

The second: raised, some of them above others.

The third: raised above the couch.

* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾ ﴿and made them virgins﴾ ﴿loving, equal in age﴾ ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾. Regarding the "production" (inshaʾ) there are several issues:

The first issue: To whom does the pronoun in ﴿We have produced them﴾ refer? There are three aspects:

The first: to "ḥūrun ʿīn" (wide-eyed maidens). This is distant, because of their distance and their occurring in a different narrative.

The second: that what is meant by the "furush" (couches) is women, and the pronoun refers to them, based on God's saying: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. It is said of a slave-girl that she has become a "firash" (a bed-partner), and when she has become a firash her rank is raised in comparison with a slave-girl who has not become a firash. This is closer than the first, but it is apparently distant, because describing them as "marfu'ah" (raised) indicates otherwise.

The third: that it refers to a known referent indicated by "furush", because it is known in this world and in several places in the mention of the Hereafter that among the couches are "ḥaẓāyā" (secluded companions). The implied sense is: "And on raised couches are ḥaẓāyā produced [for them]." This is like what is mentioned in God's saying: ﴿with restrained gaze﴾ [al-Saffat: 48] and ﴿restrained [in pavilions]﴾ [al-Rahman: 72]. Thus God has placed the attribute in the position of the qualified noun, and has not mentioned the women of the Hereafter by any literal term at all, but has identified them by their attributes and their clothing, indicating their protection and seclusion. God's saying ﴿Indeed, We have produced them﴾ may mean the ḥūr, in which case "production" (inshāʾ) means origination (ibtidāʾ). It may also mean the daughters of Adam, in which case "production" means the bringing back to life of the resurrection. God's saying ﴿virgins﴾ indicates the second, because if "production" meant origination, it would be known from their being virgins without need for explanation. Since what is meant is the revival of the daughters of Adam, He said ﴿virgins﴾, that is, We make them virgins even if they died as non-virgins. If it is said: what is the benefit on the first aspect? We answer, the answer is in two parts:

The first: the description after it does not come from something else, if they are their spouses; its benefit is clear, because a virgin in this world is not acquainted with the pleasure of a husband, so she would not agree to marry a man she does not know, and prefers to marry among her peers and acquaintances. But the people of Paradise, if they are not of the kind of the sons of Adam, and one of them is a virgin who has not seen a husband, then marries one not of her kind, it may be suspected of her bad companionship. So He said ﴿virgins﴾, and there is not found in them what is found in the virgins of this world.

The second: what is meant by "virgins" is a virginity different from the virginity of this world, for virginity does not return except after a distance. God's saying ﴿loving, equal in age﴾ may bear several aspects:

The first: equal in age, so none of them surpasses the other in youth or old age; all of them were created at one time, and no decrepitude, infirmity, or change of color afflicts them. On this view, if they are of the daughters of Adam, the word is literal regarding them; and if they are of other than them, its meaning is "those who have grown old", and they were so named because each of them is touched at the time the other is touched, but the origin was forgotten, and it became an expression for that, like "pleasure" for two equal rational beings. So it was applied to the ḥūr of Paradise as "equal in age".

The second: "equal in age" (atrāban), alike in their appearance, like peers who are all equal, whether they exist at one time or in several times. The apparent meaning is that it is in several times, because when a believer does a righteous deed, there is created for him from them whatever God wills.

The third: "atrāban" for the companions of the right hand, that is, of their age; and in it is an indication of agreement, because when one of the spouses is older than the other, the young one reproaches him.

The second issue: If it is said, what is the benefit of God's saying: ﴿So We made them﴾? We say: its benefit is apparent, and becomes clear when we consider the lām in ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾. We say: if the lām is connected to "atrāban", the meaning would be: ﴿We have produced them﴾, and this is not permitted. If it is connected to "We have produced them", the meaning is: We have produced them for the companions of the right hand, and the production is while they are virgins and equal in age. The production is not connected to virginity in such a way that their being virgins is by the production, because an act does not affect the state with obligatory influence. So we say: its being directed to production does not indicate that the production was by an act; so the bestowal upon them is by the mere production of them for the companions of the right hand: ﴿So We made them virgins﴾, so that the ordering of the effect follows from the cause, and that required their being virgins. As for if the production was first, without the husbands being involved, that would not require making them virgins, and the fā' (so) is for the ordering of the consequence upon the requirement.

The second: raised, some of them above others.

The third: raised above the couch.

The first: the description after it does not come from something else, if they are their spouses; its benefit is clear, because a virgin in this world is not acquainted with the pleasure of a husband, so she would not agree to marry a man she does not know, and prefers to marry among her peers and acquaintances. But the people of Paradise, if they are not of the kind of the sons of Adam, and one of them is a virgin who has not seen a husband, then marries one not of her kind, it may be suspected of her bad companionship. So He said ﴿virgins﴾, and there is not found in them what is found in the virgins of this world.

The second: what is meant by "virgins" is a virginity different from the virginity of this world, for virginity does not return except after a distance. God's saying ﴿loving, equal in age﴾ may bear several aspects:

The first: equal in age, so none of them surpasses the other in youth or old age; all of them were created at one time, and no decrepitude, infirmity, or change of color afflicts them. On this view, if they are of the daughters of Adam, the word is literal regarding them; and if they are of other than them, its meaning is "those who have grown old", and they were so named because each of them is touched at the time the other is touched, but the origin was forgotten, and it became an expression for that, like "pleasure" for two equal rational beings. So it was applied to the ḥūr of Paradise as "equal in age".

The second: "equal in age" (atrāban), alike in their appearance, like peers who are all equal, whether they exist at one time or in several times. The apparent meaning is that it is in several times, because when a believer does a righteous deed, there is created for him from them whatever God wills.

The third: "atrāban" for the companions of the right hand, that is, of their age; and in it is an indication of agreement, because when one of the spouses is older than the other, the young one reproaches him.

The second issue: If it is said, what is the benefit of God's saying: ﴿So We made them﴾? We say: its benefit is apparent, and becomes clear when we consider the lām in ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾. We say: if the lām is connected to "atrāban", the meaning would be: ﴿We have produced them﴾, and this is not permitted. If it is connected to "We have produced them", the meaning is: We have produced them for the companions of the right hand, and the production is while they are virgins and equal in age. The production is not connected to virginity in such a way that their being virgins is by the production, because an act does not affect the state with obligatory influence. So we say: its being directed to production does not indicate that the production was by an act; so the bestowal upon them is by the mere production of them for the companions of the right hand: ﴿So We made them virgins﴾, so that the ordering of the effect follows from the cause, and that required their being virgins. As for if the production was first, without the husbands being involved, that would not require making them virgins, and the fā' (so) is for the ordering of the consequence upon the requirement.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And raised couches﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of "furush" (couches), and we will mention another aspect of it, God willing. As for "marfu'ah" (raised), there are three aspects to it:

The first: raised in rank, as one says of a garment that it is "rafi'" (fine), meaning precious, elevated in status and price. This is indicated by God's saying: ﴿On couches whose linings are of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

The second: raised, some of them above others.

The third: raised above the couch.

* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾ ﴿and made them virgins﴾ ﴿loving, equal in age﴾ ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾. Regarding the "production" (inshaʾ) there are several issues:

The first issue: To whom does the pronoun in ﴿We have produced them﴾ refer? There are three aspects:

The first: to "ḥūrun ʿīn" (wide-eyed maidens). This is distant, because of their distance and their occurring in a different narrative.

The second: that what is meant by the "furush" (couches) is women, and the pronoun refers to them, based on God's saying: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. It is said of a slave-girl that she has become a "firash" (a bed-partner), and when she has become a firash her rank is raised in comparison with a slave-girl who has not become a firash. This is closer than the first, but it is apparently distant, because describing them as "marfu'ah" (raised) indicates otherwise.

The third: that it refers to a known referent indicated by "furush", because it is known in this world and in several places in the mention of the Hereafter that among the couches are "ḥaẓāyā" (secluded companions). The implied sense is: "And on raised couches are ḥaẓāyā produced [for them]." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿A multitude from the earliest generations﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later generations﴾.

We have already mentioned what is in this, but here there is a subtle point: that He, exalted is He, said of the foremost (al-sabiqun): ﴿A multitude from the earliest generations﴾ before mentioning the couches, the fruits, and the maidens (al-hur), and He mentioned of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin): ﴿A multitude from the earliest generations﴾ after mentioning these blessings. We say: the foremost do not turn their attention to the maidens of spacious eyes (al-hur al-‘in), or to the food and drink, and the blessings of Paradise are ennobled by them, whereas the companions of the right turn their attention to these things, so He placed their mention before them. Then He said: "This is for you." As for the foremost, He mentioned them first and then mentioned their place, as if He said to the people of Paradise: "These are coming to you as guests."

What completes this subtle point is that He only placed the multitude of the foremost first because they are drawn near in a sensory sense. So He said: ﴿The ones brought near﴾ ﴿in gardens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 12], then He said: ﴿A multitude﴾, then He mentioned the blessings, because they are above the world, except for affection toward the near ones of Allah, for that is above everything. To this He pointed with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except affection toward the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. As for His saying: ﴿in gardens of bliss﴾ [al-Saffat: 43], we have mentioned that it is to distinguish the near ones among the believers from the near ones among the angels, for they are near in Paradise, and they are near in their places for carrying out the affairs that are for people and others by the power of Allah. It has become clear from this that what is meant by the companions of the right are the saved ones who committed sins and transgressed, and Allah pardoned them because of a least good deed, not those whose good deeds outweighed and grew numerous. We will mention the proof for this in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾.

Among the issues here:

The first issue: What is the wisdom in mentioning the scorching wind (al-samum) and the boiling water (al-hamim) while omitting mention of the Fire and its terrors? We say: in this there is an indication from the lower to the higher. He said: their air, which blows upon them, is scorching wind, and their water, which they seek for relief, is boiling water. Yet air and water are the coolest of things, and these two, namely the scorching wind and the boiling water, are among the most harmful of things, unlike air and water in the world, which are among the most beneficial of things. So what do you suppose of their Fire, which is also, for us, hotter? Had He said, "They are in fire," we would have supposed their fire to be like our fire, because we have not seen anything hotter than what we have seen, nor hotter than the scorching wind, nor colder than fresh water. So He said: the coolest of things for them is the hottest of them. How then will their state be with the hottest of them?

If it is said: What is al-samum? We say: The well-known view is that it is a hot wind that blows and mostly causes illness or death. The better view is to say: it is a putrid air that moves from one side to another; when a person inhales it, his heart is corrupted by the putrefaction and the person is killed. Its root is from the word summ (poison), like the poison of the snake and the scorpion and others. It is possible that this poison is from the word samm, meaning the eye of a needle, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40]; because the poison of the viper penetrates the pores and corrupts them. It was also said: al-samum is specific to what blows at night, and on this basis His saying ﴿samum﴾ indicates the darkness of their condition. However, this is very far-fetched, because al-samum may be seen by day due to its density.

The second issue: al-hamim is hot water. It is a fa'il form in the sense of fa'il, from hamima al-ma' (with kasra on the mim), or in the sense of maf'ul, from hamma al-ma' when he heated it. We have mentioned this many times. However, here there is a linguistic subtlety: the form fa'ul (as in samum) is used when a thing recurs from it; and since the wind blows often, coming one after another, al-samum was specified with the fa'ul form. Hot water, since repetition is not understood from it one after another, was not described with hamum. 

If it is said: What is al-yahmum? We say: there are several views:

First: it is one of the names of Jahannam.

Second: it is the smoke.

Third: it is the darkness. Its root is from al-humum, which is charcoal; as if, because of its blackness, it is charcoal, so they named it with a name derived from it. The addition of a letter in it is for the addition of that meaning in it. Perhaps the addition was for two meanings: the addition in its blackness and the addition in its heat. In these three matters there is an indication of their lowly state in punishment, always; for if they expose themselves to the path of the wind, the wind that is al-samum strikes them; and if they take shelter, as one does who protects himself from the samum by sheltering in a covered place, they will be in a shade of yahmum; and if they wish to ward off the samum from themselves by sheltering in a place of hamim, then there is no escape for them from the punishment of hamim. It may also be said that there is an order in this: the samum strikes him, so he becomes thirsty and the fire of the samum blazes in his insides; he drinks water, which cuts his intestines; and he seeks shade in a shadow, and that shadow is the shadow of yahmum.

If it is asked: What is the way of using "min" in His saying ﴿min yahmum﴾? We say: if we say it is a name of Jahannam, then it is for the beginning of the end, as you say: "A breeze came to me from Paradise." If we say it is smoke, then it is as in our saying: "a ring of silver." If we say it is darkness, then it is likewise. If it is said: How is it valid to interpret it as Jahannam, when it is a diptote, indefinite, so how was it given to a defined place, and if it were its name? We say: its use with the definite article is like al-Jahim, or it is not declined like the names of Jahannam; it would be like it in three places, all of which are yahmum.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Neither cool nor generous﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The generosity of shade is that it benefits the one who is distressed by heat and repels the harm of heat from him. If that were all, then "cool" and "generous" would have the same meaning. The better view is that the benefit of shade is twofold. The first is repelling the heat. The second is that the person sitting in it is honoured. This is because in cold weather a person seeks the sun's direct rays to warm himself when he is lightly clothed. But if he is among the honoured, he will always be in a place that protects him from heat and cold alike, in the shade. As for heat, this is obvious. As for cold, he repels it by warming the place, by lighting what warms it. So shade in hot weather is sought for its coolness, and in cold weather it is sought for its honour, not for a coolness that exists in the shade. Thus Allah's words ﴿neither cool﴾ mean that it is not sought for its coolness, ﴿nor generous﴾ meaning it is not a place of honour prepared for sitting. This is because the places that fall under shade, like those beneath trees or in front of a wall, are made into seats, and these seats are kept free of filth, while the other places become rubbish heaps. Then, when the sun falls on these seats at certain times, they are sought for their cleanliness and for being prepared for sitting, so at such times they are desired for their honour, not for their coolness. So Allah's words ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ allow for this. They also allow the reading that shade is sought either for a matter that pertains to the senses or for a matter that pertains to the intellect. What pertains to the senses is its coolness. What pertains to the intellect is that resorting to it is an honour. This shade has neither coolness nor honour. This is what al-Wahidi reported from al-Farra': that the Arabs follow every negation with "generous" when the negated thing is the more honourable, so one says: "This house is not spacious nor generous." The verification of the matter is what we have mentioned: the attribute of perfection is either sensory or intellectual. The sensory is expressed by its own word. The intellectual, because it is hidden from the senses, is indicated by a comprehensive word, since "honour" (al-karamah, and karamah) is among the most famous attributes of praise among the Arabs, and negating them is negating an intellectual attribute of perfection. So Allah's words ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ mean: there is no praise in it at all, neither sensory nor intellectual.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent﴾ ﴿and they used to persist in the great violation﴾ ﴿and they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we truly be resurrected? Or our forefathers of old?"﴾. There are subtleties in these verses, which we mention in questions.

The first question: What is the wisdom in stating the cause of their being in punishment, when He did not mention the cause of the companions of the right being in bliss? Why did He not say: "They were before that thankful and submissive"? We say: We have mentioned many times that when Allah conveys reward, He does not mention the good deeds of the servants, and when He conveys punishment, He mentions the deeds of the evildoers. This is because reward is bounty and punishment is justice. Bounty, whether its cause is mentioned or not, does not give rise to any suspicion of deficiency or injustice in the one who is granted it. But justice, if its cause is not known, may lead one to suspect injustice. So He said: "They are in it because of their affluence." What supports this subtlety is that Allah said regarding the foremost: ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24], and He did not say this regarding the companions of the right. That is because we pointed out that the companions of the right are those saved by great bounty, and we will explain this in His words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91]. Since this is so, the bounty regarding them is pure, so He said: "These blessings are for you," and He did not say "as a reward." This is because the word "reward" in such a context, which is the context of pardoning them, does not bestow joy, unlike the one whose good deeds are many, to whom it is said: "Well done, take this as your reward."

The second question: The cause given is their being affluent, yet not every one of the people of the left is affluent, for among them are poor people. We say: Allah's words ﴿they were before that affluent﴾ are not a blame. The affluent person is the one who has been made to have affluence, that is, blessing. Its apparent meaning does not necessarily imply blame. But it clarifies the ugliness of what is mentioned about them afterwards, which is His words ﴿and they used to persist﴾. This is because the occurrence of ingratitude from one who has been given the utmost favour is among the worst of ugly acts. So He said: "They were affluent, yet they did not thank Allah's blessings, but persisted in sin." On this basis we say: The blessings that require gratitude to Allah and His worship are numerous for every person. Creation, provision, and what one needs and on which his welfare depends are available to all. The most that can be said is that people's states in affluence are close to one another, so it is said of some in comparison with others that they are in distress. Yet if one restrains himself to contentment, he would be the richest of the rich. How could it not be so, when a person who looks at his own condition finds himself in need of a dwelling to shelter him, clothing against heat and cold, and what satisfies his hunger of food and drink, and other surplus things to which the soul's avarice drives him? Moreover, no one is so incapable of obtaining a dwelling, by buying or renting. If he cannot, he is no less capable than insects, which never lack a crevice or a cave. As for clothing, if he were content with what removes necessity, one garment would suffice him for his life; whenever a part of it tears, he patches it with whatever is available. What remains is the matter of food and drink. Yet when the observer looks, he finds that everyone, in all circumstances, is not deprived of a morsel of bread and a sip of water. But the pursuit of wealth brings poverty: a person wants an ornate house, good food, and other kinds of mounts and clothing, so he becomes needy and must bear hardships. The pursuit of wealth produces his poverty, and seeking high rank lowers his standing. In sum, the desire of his belly and his private parts breaks his back. Moreover, we say regarding His words ﴿they were affluent before that﴾: there is no doubt that the people of the graves, when they lost the striking hands and the seeing eyes, and the realities became clear to them, realised that ﴿they were before that affluent﴾ in comparison with that state.
* * *
The third question: What is the persistence in the great violation? We say: It is polytheism, as He said: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. There is a subtlety in it: in the three verses He alludes to the three foundations. His words ﴿they were before that affluent﴾, by usage, indicate their blame for denying the messengers, since the affluent person is arrogant because of wealth, so he denies the message. The affluent said: ﴿Shall we follow a single human being from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 24]. His words ﴿they persisted in the great violation﴾ refer to polytheism and opposition to monotheism. His words ﴿and they used to say: "When we die and become dust"﴾ refer to denying the gathering and the raising. His words ﴿and they used to persist in the great violation﴾ contain exaggerations in several respects:
The first: His words ﴿and they used to persist﴾, which is more emphatic than saying: "They persisted before that." This is because the combination of the past and the present forms indicates continuity, since saying "So-and-so used to be kind to people" indicates that this was his habit.

The second: The word "persistence" (al-iṣrār), since persistence is the continuation of disobedience and obstinacy, and one does not say "he persisted in good."

The third: al-ḥinth. It is above sin, for in the language the word ḥinth hardly applies to a minor offence, whereas sin applies to it. As for ḥinth in oaths, they used it because lying itself is ugly in the view of sensible people. The welfare of the world depends on truthfulness; otherwise, no one would trust anyone's word, and no benefits would be built upon their speech, nor would harms be avoided. Then, since lying was found among many people for corrupt purposes, they wished to confirm a matter by adding something to it that removes its doubt, so they added oaths, and there is nothing greater than them. If the oath is broken, nothing remains that gives confidence, and corruption follows that is greater than the corruption of fornication and drinking. However, when an oath concerns a future matter and the swearer sees something else, the Law permits breaking it, but does not permit it in a major sin such as fornication or killing, because oaths occur frequently and killing rarely. What shows that ḥinth is a major sin is the saying about one who has reached maturity: "He has reached the ḥinth," meaning he has reached a level at which he commits major sins. Before that, he was not described as committing minor ones, because the guardian is commanded to punish him for bad manners and for abandoning prayer.

The fourth question: His words ﴿the great﴾ indicate that what is meant is polytheism, since these matters are not combined in anything other than it.

The fifth question: Why is ﴿mitnā﴾ famous with a kasra on the mīm, although the Qur'an's usage in the future is yamūtu? Allah said regarding Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them: ﴿and the day I die﴾ [Maryam: 33], and it was not read as amāta on the pattern of akhāfu. And He said: ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 119], and He did not say: "and do not die," as He said: ﴿Do not fear﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. We say: In this there are two aspects:
The first: This word differed from others, so it was said in it: amūtu, and transmission takes precedence over analogy.

The second: māta yamātu is a dialect of māta yamūtu. So the form with a kasra was used, because the kasra in the past tense occurs more frequently in two respects:
The first: the frequency of yafʿulu on the pattern of yafʿalu.
The second: its being on the pattern faʿala yafʿalu, like khāfa yakhāfu. In its future form, the ḍamma occurs for two reasons:
The first: the verb being on the pattern faʿala yafʿulu, like ṭāla yaṭūlu. For describing it as long (ṭawīl) rather than as ṭāʾil indicates that it is of the pattern qaṣara yaqṣuru.
The second: the verb being on the pattern faʿila yafʿulu. You say: faʿiltu in the past with a kasra and in the future with a ḍamma.

The sixth question: How did He use the emphatic lām in His words ﴿truly resurrected (la-mabʿūthūna)﴾, when the intended meaning is negation, and when negating, the lām is not mentioned in the predicate of inna? One says: "Indeed Zayd will come" (inna Zaydan la-yajī'u) and "Indeed Zayd will not come" (inna Zaydan lā yajī'u), so the lām is not mentioned. And what do they intend by the interrogative except denial, meaning "we will not be resurrected"? We say: The answer to this has two aspects:
The first: when the intention is to express negation explicitly, the explicit negation and its form are used.
The second: they intended to refute the one who reports about the resurrection, so they mentioned that the one reporting it exaggerates his report, while we consider his exaggeration and emphasis excessive. So they quoted their speech in the manner of a question meaning denial. Then in their denial they pointed to matters they believed to be established as proof of the validity of their denial. They first said: ﴿When we die?﴾ but they did not limit themselves to it; rather they said after it: ﴿and we have become dust and bones﴾, meaning that our time has become long after we were dead, until the flesh became dust and the bones crumbled. Then they added: "Despite this, we are told: 'You will truly be resurrected,' with emphasis in three respects:
The first: the use of the word inna.
The second: the affirmation of the lām in its predicate.
The third: the abandonment of the form of the future, and the use of the past participle, as if it had already happened." So they said to us: "You will truly be resurrected." Then they added: ﴿or our forefathers of old?﴾, meaning: this is even more remote, for if we become dust after our death, and our fathers' condition is beyond the condition of crumbled bones, how is resurrection possible? We have explained all this in Surat al-Saffat, and we said that His words ﴿or our forefathers of old?﴾ mean: "or will they say: our forefathers of old?", indicating that they are in even greater difficulty. Then Allah answered them and refuted them, responding to each exaggeration with another exaggeration, saying:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Neither cool nor generous﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The generosity of shade is that it benefits the one who is distressed by heat and repels the harm of heat from him. If that were all, then "cool" and "generous" would have the same meaning. The better view is that the benefit of shade is twofold. The first is repelling the heat. The second is that the person sitting in it is honoured. This is because in cold weather a person seeks the sun's direct rays to warm himself when he is lightly clothed. But if he is among the honoured, he will always be in a place that protects him from heat and cold alike, in the shade. As for heat, this is obvious. As for cold, he repels it by warming the place, by lighting what warms it. So shade in hot weather is sought for its coolness, and in cold weather it is sought for its honour, not for a coolness that exists in the shade. Thus Allah's words ﴿neither cool﴾ mean that it is not sought for its coolness, ﴿nor generous﴾ meaning it is not a place of honour prepared for sitting. This is because the places that fall under shade, like those beneath trees or in front of a wall, are made into seats, and these seats are kept free of filth, while the other places become rubbish heaps. Then, when the sun falls on these seats at certain times, they are sought for their cleanliness and for being prepared for sitting, so at such times they are desired for their honour, not for their coolness. So Allah's words ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ allow for this. They also allow the reading that shade is sought either for a matter that pertains to the senses or for a matter that pertains to the intellect. What pertains to the senses is its coolness. What pertains to the intellect is that resorting to it is an honour. This shade has neither coolness nor honour. This is what al-Wahidi reported from al-Farra': that the Arabs follow every negation with "generous" when the negated thing is the more honourable, so one says: "This house is not spacious nor generous." The verification of the matter is what we have mentioned: the attribute of perfection is either sensory or intellectual. The sensory is expressed by its own word. The intellectual, because it is hidden from the senses, is indicated by a comprehensive word, since "honour" (al-karamah, and karamah) is among the most famous attributes of praise among the Arabs, and negating them is negating an intellectual attribute of perfection. So Allah's words ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ mean: there is no praise in it at all, neither sensory nor intellectual.

The first: His words ﴿and they used to persist﴾, which is more emphatic than saying: "They persisted before that." This is because the combination of the past and the present forms indicates continuity, since saying "So-and-so used to be kind to people" indicates that this was his habit.

The second: The word "persistence" (al-iṣrār), since persistence is the continuation of disobedience and obstinacy, and one does not say "he persisted in good."

Then Allah answered them and refuted them, responding to each exaggeration with another exaggeration, saying:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Neither cool nor generous﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The generosity of shade is that it benefits the one who is distressed by heat and repels the harm of heat from him. If that were all, then "cool" and "generous" would have the same meaning. The better view is that the benefit of shade is twofold. The first is repelling the heat. The second is that the person sitting in it is honoured. This is because in cold weather a person seeks the sun's direct rays to warm himself when he is lightly clothed. But if he is among the honoured, he will always be in a place that protects him from heat and cold alike, in the shade. As for heat, this is obvious. As for cold, he repels it by warming the place, by lighting what warms it. So shade in hot weather is sought for its coolness, and in cold weather it is sought for its honour, not for a coolness that exists in the shade. Thus Allah's words ﴿neither cool﴾ mean that it is not sought for its coolness, ﴿nor generous﴾ meaning it is not a place of honour prepared for sitting. This is because the places that fall under shade, like those beneath trees or in front of a wall, are made into seats, and these seats are kept free of filth, while the other places become rubbish heaps. Then, when the sun falls on these seats at certain times, they are sought for their cleanliness and for being prepared for sitting, so at such times they are desired for their honour, not for their coolness. So Allah's words ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ allow for this. They also allow the reading that shade is sought either for a matter that pertains to the senses or for a matter that pertains to the intellect. What pertains to the senses is its coolness. What pertains to the intellect is that resorting to it is an honour. This shade has neither coolness nor honour. This is because the word "reward" in such a context, which is the context of pardoning them, does not bestow joy, unlike the one whose good deeds are many, to whom it is said: "Well done, take this as your reward."

The second question: The cause given is their being affluent, yet not every one of the people of the left is affluent, for among them are poor people. This is because the occurrence of ingratitude from one who has been given the utmost favour is among the worst of ugly acts. On this basis we say: The blessings that require gratitude to Allah and His worship are numerous for every person. Creation, provision, and what one needs and on which his welfare depends are available to all. The most that can be said is that people's states in affluence are close to one another, so it is said of some in comparison with others that they are in distress. Yet if one restrains himself to contentment, he would be the richest of the rich. How could it not be so, when a person who looks at his own condition finds himself in need of a dwelling to shelter him, clothing against heat and cold, and what satisfies his hunger of food and drink, and other surplus things to which the soul's avarice drives him? Moreover, no one is so incapable of obtaining a dwelling, by buying or renting. If he cannot, he is no less capable than insects, which never lack a crevice or a cave. As for clothing, if he were content with what removes necessity, one garment would suffice him for his life; whenever a part of it tears, he patches it with whatever is available. What remains is the matter of food and drink. Yet when the observer looks, he finds that everyone, in all circumstances, is not deprived of a morsel of bread and a sip of water. But the pursuit of wealth brings poverty: a person wants an ornate house, good food, and other kinds of mounts and clothing, so he becomes needy and must bear hardships. The pursuit of wealth produces his poverty, and seeking high rank lowers his standing. In sum, the desire of his belly and his private parts breaks his back. Moreover, we say regarding His words ﴿they were affluent before that﴾: there is no doubt that the people of the graves, when they lost the striking hands and the seeing eyes, and the realities became clear to them, realised that ﴿they were before that affluent﴾ in comparison with that state.

They first said: ﴿When we die?﴾ but they did not limit themselves to it; rather they said after it: ﴿and we have become dust and bones﴾, meaning that our time has become long after we were dead, until the flesh became dust and the bones crumbled. Then they added: "Despite this, we are told: 'You will truly be resurrected,' with emphasis in three respects:
The first: the use of the word inna.
The second: the affirmation of the lām in its predicate.
The third: the abandonment of the form of the future, and the use of the past participle, as if it had already happened." So they said to us: "You will truly be resurrected." Then they added: ﴿or our forefathers of old?﴾, meaning: this is even more remote, for if we become dust after our death, and our fathers' condition is beyond the condition of crumbled bones, how is resurrection possible? We have explained all this in Surat al-Saffat, and we said that His words ﴿or our forefathers of old?﴾ mean: "or will they say: our forefathers of old?", indicating that they are in even greater difficulty. Then Allah answered them and refuted them, responding to each exaggeration with another exaggeration, saying:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 49–50:**

﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day.﴾ His saying: ﴿Say﴾ is an indication that the matter is in the utmost clarity. This is because the Message contains secrets that are not spoken except to the righteous (al-abrar), and among them is the specifying of the time of the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). For if the common people (al-awwam) knew it, they would rely on it (and neglect their deeds). The Prophets may have been aware of its signs more than they explained, and may have explained some signs to the senior Companions (al-akabir min al-sahabah), as we shall explain. So in this there are several aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿Say﴾ means that this is one of the matters that have reached such a level of clarity that both the common people and the elect (al-khawass) share in knowing it. So He said: "Say" a general statement, and so it is in every place. He said: "Say, the matter was apparent," as God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], and He said: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. That is, this is the apparent matter, whereas the matter of the Spirit and other things is hidden.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49], by placing "the former" before "the latter," is in answer to their saying: ﴿And our forefathers, the former ones?﴾ For they delayed mentioning the forefathers because the disbelief in them is greater. So He said: Indeed, the former ones, whose resurrection you consider far-fetched and whom you delay, God will raise them in a matter that comes before the latter ones. From this it becomes clear the state of those whom you delayed, [Page 151] considering them far-fetched, as an indication that the matter is easy.

The third: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿will surely be gathered﴾. They denied His saying: ﴿will surely be resurrected﴾, so He said: it occurs together with an additional matter, namely that they will be assembled and gathered in the place of reckoning. This is beyond mere resurrection, for whoever has remained under the dust for a long period and then is brought forth may not have the ability to move. How much more so if he had been alive, confined in his grave for a period, then movement would be impossible for him. Then, by His power, God, may He be exalted, will set him in motion with the swiftest movement and gather him with the strongest drive. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿will surely be gathered﴾ is stronger than the speaker's saying: "gathered," just as we said: the saying of the speaker "he will die" conveys emphasis which "he is dead" does not.

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to the appointed time of a known day﴾, for it indicates that God, may He be exalted, will gather them on one known day. The gathering of a number of the dead, whose number none knows except God the Exalted, at a single time, is more wondrous than the resurrection itself. This is like His saying, may He be exalted, in the surah al-Saffat: ﴿It will be only a single shout﴾ [al-Saffat: 19]. That is, you consider the resurrection itself far-fetched, but more wondrous than this is that He will raise them with a single cry, that is, one single blast: ﴿and behold, they are looking﴾, that is, they are resurrected together with an added matter, namely the opening of their eyes and their looking. This is unlike one who dozes off, for when he wakes he remains for a while and then looks at things. Thus the matter of bringing to life is, with God the Exalted, easier than waking a sleeper.

The fifth: The particle ﴿إلى﴾ (ila, "to") is more indicative of resurrection than the particle اللام (lam, "for"). Let us mention this in answer to a question, namely that God the Exalted said: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾ [al-Taghabun: 9], and here He said: ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾, and did not say: "for Our appointed time." And He said: ﴿And when Moses came to Our appointed time﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. We say: since mention of the gathering was an answer to the deniers, He mentioned the word "ila" (to), which indicates movement and transfer, so that it would be more indicative of an act other than resurrection, and it does not gather there. He said: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day﴾, and resurrection is not understood from the particle itself, although it is understood from the speech as a whole. For this reason He said here: ﴿will surely be gathered﴾ with the wording of emphasis, and said there: ﴿He gathers you﴾, and said here: ﴿to the appointed time﴾, which is the arrival of the time at it. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Moses came to Our appointed time﴾, we say: the place there was not what Moses, peace be upon him, sought; rather, what he sought was attendance. For whoever is assigned a time and designated a place, his movement is in reality for a matter, by way of following, toward another matter. But there the greater matter is standing in its place, not its time. So He spoke with a word whose indication of place and location is more apparent.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Then indeed you, O you who are astray, the deniers,﴾ ﴿shall surely eat from a tree of zaqqum,﴾ ﴿and fill your bellies with it,﴾ ﴿and drink on top of it from the boiling water,﴾ ﴿and drink as the thirsty camels drink.﴾

On the interpretation of the verses, there are several issues:

The first issue: To whom is the address? We say: some of the exegetes said it is addressed to the people of Makkah. The apparent meaning, however, is that it is general, addressing every astray denier, and something similar has passed in several places. It is the continuation of the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), as if God the Exalted had said to His Prophet: Say, "Indeed the first and the last will surely be gathered, then indeed you will be punished with these kinds of punishment."

The second issue: Here He said: ﴿the astray, the deniers﴾, placing "the astray" first, while at the end of the surah He said: ﴿But if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92], placing "the deniers" first. Is there a difference between them? I say: Yes. The meaning of "the astray" here is those who persisted in the great violation, so they went astray from the way of God and did not reach Him, and did not affirm His oneness, and that is a great error. Then they denied His messengers and said: ﴿When we have died...?﴾, so they denied the resurrection. So He said: ﴿O you who are astray﴾, who associated partners, ﴿the deniers﴾, who rejected the resurrection, you shall surely eat what you hate. As for there, He said to them: O deniers who denied the resurrection, ﴿the astray﴾ on the path of deliverance, who are not guided to bliss. There is another aspect to this, which is that the address here is with the disbelievers, so He said: O you who went astray first and denied second. The address at the end of the surah is with Muhammad (ﷺ), clarifying to him the state of the three groups. He said: The foremost ones, in rest and sweet basil and a Garden of bliss; and the companions of the right, in peace. As for the deniers who denied, they have gone astray, so He placed their denial first, as an indication of the honour of Muhammad (ﷺ), since He explained that the strongest cause of their punishment is their denial. What shows that the speech there is with Muhammad (ﷺ) is His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91].

The third issue: What is the zaqqum? We say: We have explained it in another place. People's opinions differed about it, and the outcome of the opinions is that it is bitter in taste, hot to touch, foul in smell, and black in appearance, such that its eater can hardly swallow it, so he is forced to gulp it down. The linguistic investigation of it is that zaqqum is an Arabic word whose structure indicates its ugliness, because the letters "z q" are never combined except in an unused root or in something disliked, such as "mazaqa," and from it "zamaqa his hair" when he plucked it, and from it "al-qazm" for baseness. More powerful than this is that the letter "q" with each of the other two letters indicates something disliked in most cases: "q" with "m" gives "qumamah" and "qumqumah," and the reverse gives "muqamiq," the thick-voiced one, and "al-qumqumah" is the wall. As for "q" with "z," "al-zaqq" is the bird's throwing of its droppings, "al-zaqzaqah" is lightness, and the reverse is "al-qaznub." So the nature recoils from the composition of a word whose letters combined indicate disgust and ugliness. Then it is joined with eating, which shows that it is a food with a lodging-in-the-throat quality. As for what is said, that the Arabs say "zaqamtani" meaning "they fed me butter, honey and milk," that is for joking, like their saying "arshaqani with a fine garment" and "arjamani with a bag of gold."

His saying ﴿from a tree﴾ indicates the starting point of the eating, i.e., your partaking of it. His saying ﴿and fill your bellies with it﴾ is an added clarification of the punishment, meaning that you will not be satisfied with a mere taste as one who eats something to fulfil an oath, but you will be obliged to fill your bellies with it. The pronoun "it" refers to the tree. As for "bellies," it may be that the intended meaning is the matching of plural with plural, i.e., each one of you fills his own belly; and it may be that the intended meaning is that each one of you fills the bellies, and the bellies then are the bellies of the intestines, since the image of the intestine within the human being suggests it, as one eats in seven intestines, so they fill the bellies of the intestines and others. The first is more apparent, and the second is more inclusive regarding punishment and threat.

His saying ﴿and drink on top of it﴾ means, after eating, its bitterness and heat draw them to drinking water, so they drink on top of that food and on top of that zaqqum from hot water. The explanation of "hamim" has already passed.

His saying ﴿and drink as the thirsty camels drink﴾ is also a clarification for the increase of punishment, meaning that your condition will not be that of one who drinks hot foul water and then refrains from it; rather, you will be obliged to drink from it as the thirsty camels drink, which are the camels afflicted by thirst, so they drink and are never quenched. This clarification concerning drinking is for the increase of punishment, just as His saying ﴿fill your bellies with it﴾ concerns eating.

If it is said: The thirsty camel, when it drinks much water, is harmed by it, yet at the moment it finds pleasure in it. Is there then for the people of Hell any pleasure in drinking boiling hot water in the Fire? We say: No; rather that is to clarify the increase of punishment. Its meaning can be stated thus: they are obliged to drink the boiling water, and they are not satisfied with that drinking, but they are obliged to drink as the camel drinks that is afflicted with "al-hiyam," or they, when they drink, the heat of the zaqqum increases in their insides, so they think that it is from the zaqqum and not from the boiling water, and so they drink from it a great deal, based on the illusion of quenching. As for "al-hiym," the discussion of it is like the discussion of "al-bid," its origin being "hawm," and this derives from "hama yahim," as if it were wandering from thirst. "Al-hiyam" is that disease which makes one like a wanderer from thirst.

(56:58–59), as proof of their lying and of the truthfulness of the messengers regarding the Resurrection. Since He is able to create at first, He is able to create a second time. There is no room for consideration of His essence and attributes, Exalted and Sanctified is He, even if they do not acknowledge Him. Rather, they doubt and say: the first creation is from semen according to nature. We say: semen is among the possible things, and the possible has no existence in itself but through another, as is known. His saying, "Af'alta," is a question about its reality, and its meaning is that in its kind it is not possible. The saying, "Lima fa'alta wa anta ta'lamu ma fihi" (why did you do it while you know what is in it), differs from "Af'alta wa anta ta'lamu ma fihi" (did you do it while you know what is in it), because in the first he treats him as one who was right in his action for a hidden cause that is to be sought from him, and in the second he treats him as one who was wrong from the outset. When the difference between "lima fa'alta" and "af'alta" is known, the difference between "lima taf'alu" and "halla taf'alu" is known.

As for "fa-lawla," we say: it is originally a conditional word, and the conditional clause is not governed by it, just as the interrogative clause is not governed by its particle. But "lawla" indicates coercion and adds the negation of reflection and negligence. So He says, "lawla tusaddiqun" (why do you not believe), in place of "lima la" and "halla," because it is more indicative of the negation of what it governs, which is the absence of belief. There is a subtle point in it: "lawla" enters upon a past verb and upon a future one. The Exalted said: "Fa-lawla nafara min kulli firqatin minhum ta'ifah" (Qur'an 9:122). What is the reason for singling out the future here, and why did He not say: "Fa-lawla saddaqtum" (why did you not believe in the past)? We say: this is speech addressed to them in this world, and Islam in it is accepted and erases what came before it. So He said: "Why do you not believe at this moment, when the proofs are clear and continuous and the benefit is attained?" As for His saying, "Fa-lawla nafara," the benefit would not be attained except after a period, so He said: "If you had set out, the benefit would have been attained immediately, and that has passed. If you do not set out now, the benefit will also be lost in the future."

Then the Exalted said: "Have you considered what you emit?" (56:58), as a confirmation of His saying, "We created you" (56:57). For when He said, "We created you," the naturalists said: "We exist from drops of creation, with hidden essences, and before each one of us there is a single drop." No one doubts this from the very beginning, when God created the drop, fashioned it, gave it life, and illuminated it. So why do you not believe that He is One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge, Capable over all things, for He will restore you as He originated you at the beginning? The interrogation conveys an increase of affirmation, and you already know this many times over.

ThenThe Exalted said: "This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgment" (Qur'an 56:56).

That is, this is not all of the punishment; rather, this is only the first thing they will encounter, and it is a part of it, and it cuts their intestines to pieces.

We say: semen is among the possible things, and the possible has no existence in itself but through another, as is known. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verse 60–62 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ ﴿in replacing your likenesses and producing you in what you do not know﴾ ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ In it are several issues:

The first issue: regarding its order (tartib), there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a confirmation (taqrir) of what preceded, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. He said: ﴿We created you﴾, then He said: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾. Whoever has power over giving life and causing death, which are opposites, is established as a chooser (mukhtar), so it is possible for Him to bring them back to life after death. This is unlike the case where the giving of life came from Him while He had no power over causing death, in which case one would suppose that He is a necessitating agent (mujib) and not a chooser, and a necessitating agent does not have power over every possible thing. So He said: We created you and We decreed death among you; so reflect upon it, and know that We are able to produce you.

The second: that it is a reply to the saying of a falsifier (mubtil) who says: If life and death are not natural matters in bodies, consisting of heats and moistures, which when they are abundant the body remains alive, and when they diminish and are exhausted it dies, then death would not occur. And how is it fitting for the Wise to create a thing whose creation He perfects and whose form He beautifies, then corrupt it and annihilate it, then restore it and bring it into being again? So He, exalted is He, said: We have decreed death. And there is no objection in your saying: Why did He annihilate, why did He originate, why did He demolish? Because perfection of power requires that. What is ugly is only for the goldsmith and the builder to shape something, build it and then break it and bring it into being again, because that requires devoting time to it and bearing hardship. Its likeness is only that of a person who looks at something, then averts his gaze from it for the blink of an eye, then returns to it, and it is not said to him: Why did you avert your gaze, and why did you look at it? ﴿And to God belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Nahl: 60] is of this kind; for here movement and time are necessary, and if the likenesses of a person were repeated upon him he would tire; but in a single instance fatigue does not arise. God, exalted is He, is far above fatigue, and His act requires neither time nor movement by a body. There is another aspect subtler than these, which is that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] means: have you considered that as dead, without life in it, which is semen? If you reflect upon it, you will know that before that it was living, connected to a living thing, and was parts perceiving, suffering and enjoying. Then, when you emit it, you do not doubt that it is dead like inanimate things. Then God, exalted is He, creates it as a human being and makes it a upright human. So the drop was living before separation, then became dead, then God, exalted is He, gave it life again. So know that when We created you first, then decreed death among you second, then produce you a third time, do not deem that unlikely, as in the case of the drops.

Page 155

The second issue: what is the difference between this passage and the beginning of Surat Tabarak, where He said there: ﴿He who created death and life﴾, with the mention of death placed first? We say: the discourse here is according to the original order, as God, exalted is He, said in several places, among them His saying: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], then He said after that: ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15]. As for in Surat al-Mulk, we shall mention its benefit, if God wills, and its return to what we have mentioned: that He said: He created death in the drops after they had been living at the time of connection, then He created life in them after death, and this is the proof of resurrection. It was also said: the death meant here is the death that follows life, and the death meant there is that which precedes life.

The third issue: He said here: ﴿We have decreed﴾, and in Surat al-Mulk He said: ﴿He created death and life﴾, so He mentioned death and life with the verb of creation. Here He said: ﴿We created you﴾ and said: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾. We say: the intent there was to explain that death and life are created in an absolute sense, not specifically among people. Here, when He said ﴿We created you﴾, He specified them with mention, so it became as if He said: We created your life. Then if He had said: We have decreed your death, it would have been expected that their death would occur immediately, and it was not so; therefore He said: ﴿We have decreed among you﴾. As for there, death and life were created in two places, and that was not in relation to a particular group.

The fourth issue: is there any benefit in His saying ﴿among you﴾ instead of other expressions? We say: yes, there is a magnificent benefit, which becomes clear when considering the expressions that could stand in its place. We could say: We have decreed death for you, or We have decreed death in you. His saying "We have decreed in you" conveys the meaning of creation, because the decreeing of a thing in a thing requires that the latter be a container for it, either a container of occurrence within it or a container of inherence in it, as one says: whiteness in the body and kohl in the eye. So if He had said: We have decreed death in you, it would have been created within us, and that is not so. And if we say: We have decreed death for you, that would indicate its delay relative to people, for when one says: this is prepared for you, it means that today it belongs to another and tomorrow to you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those days We alternate among people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140].

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿and We are not to be outdone﴾. The well-known view is that its meaning is: and We are not overcome, unable to create your likenesses and restore you after your limbs have scattered. It is said: "fatahu al-shay'" when he overpowered him and was not able to reach him; and similarly "sabaqahu." Based on this we return to the order we have mentioned and say: since His saying ﴿We have decreed among you﴾ is to show that He created life and decreed death, and these are opposites, and the Creator of opposites is capable and a chooser, He said: ﴿and We are not outdone﴾, i.e., unable regarding anything, unlike the necessitating agent who cannot bring about each of the two opposites, so it precedes him and escapes him, for fire cannot cool, since its nature necessitates heating. As for if we say that He mentioned it as a refutation of them when they said: If death were not from the decay of the original moistures and the extinguishing of the innate heat, but were by the creation of a wise chooser, its occurrence would not be permissible, since how can the Wise build and demolish, bring into being and annihilate? So He said: ﴿and We are not outdone﴾, i.e., unable in any of the ways they consider improbable from the builder and the goldsmith, for he requires time, place, enabling of the product, and possibility, and he suffers fatigue from moving and settling, whereas God creates by "Be" and it is. So He is above what we mentioned as the likeness of averting and returning the gaze in the swiftest moment, since it is not valid for one to say: Why did you avert your gaze at that subtle instant that is not perceived or sensed? Rather, perhaps the claimant of complete power over a thing in a brief time, by swift movement, produces a thing and then nullifies it, then produces its like and then nullifies it. The deeds of sleight-of-hand performers show you this, for they give the illusion that they do something and then undo it, then do the like of it, desiring to show their power.

Page 156

So we say: His saying in Surat Tabarak: ﴿He created death and life that He might test you﴾ [al-Mulk: 2] means: He caused to die and gave life, so that you know that He is a chooser who acts, so that you worship Him and believe in reward and punishment, and your deed is thereby good. Had you believed Him to be a necessitating agent, you would not have done anything. This is according to the well-known interpretation. And the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and We are not outdone﴾ is its literal sense, namely that We are not preceded. It admits of two things: one, that its meaning is that He is the First, there was nothing before Him. Second: in the creation of people and the decreeing of death among them, nothing preceded Him; and this follows another manner of prevention. It has two benefits. As for if we say ﴿and We are not outdone﴾ means nothing preceded Us, it is an indication that wherever you take the path of reflection, you end at God and stop at Him and do not go beyond Him. For if you say: before the drop there is a father, and before the father a drop, then reason judges that the drops and fathers end at an uncreated Creator, and that is Me; for I am not outdone, and there is no creator or precursor other than Me. This is by way of gradual descent from one station to another. The intelligent person whom God guides with strong guidance knows first, and the one below him knows a rank later, and the obstinate one, if he returns to his reason after the stages, must know, and says: there must be a god for all, and He is not outdone in what He has done; so its meaning is that He did what He did, and there was no model for His product. As for if we say: He is not outdone, what need is there for His restoring it with a likeness that is easier? This would be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Its support is His saying: ﴿upon Our replacing your likenesses and producing you in what you do not know﴾. If it is said: this is not valid, because such a thing occurred in the question of a questioner, and the meaning is what we have mentioned, as if He said: Indeed We are able to replace your likenesses, and We are not outdone, i.e., We are not unable or overcome; so this is our proof. This is because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We are able﴾ conveys the benefit of the negation of incapacity from Him, so there must be an evident benefit in His saying ﴿and We are not outdone﴾. Then He, exalted is He, said ﴿upon Our replacing your likenesses﴾ in the well-known view: His saying ﴿upon Our replacing﴾ relates to His saying ﴿and We are not outdone﴾, i.e., upon the replacement, and its meaning is: and We are not unable regarding the replacement.

The verification in this view is that one to whom a thing has been "sabaqahu" is as if it overpowered him and he was unable to reach it. The word "ʿalā" in this view is derived from the usage of the term "competition" (musabaqah), for it takes "ʿalā" with a thing, since whoever outstrips another in a matter is the victor. In the other view it relates to His saying ﴿We have decreed﴾, and its sense is: We have decreed among you upon the manner of replacement, not upon the manner of cutting off the offspring from the outset, just as one says: So-and-so went out on condition that he return quickly, meaning: in this manner he went out. The relation of the word "ʿalā" in this manner is more evident. If it is said: according to what the exegetes have held, there is no difficulty regarding the replacement of your likenesses, i.e., your forms and attributes; and "al-amthal" is the plural of "mithl," and the meaning would be: and We are not unable to transform you, making you into apes and swine, and this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ [Ya Sin: 67]. And according to what I said in the interpretation of "al-masbuqin," and I made the complement of His saying ﴿upon Our replacing your likenesses﴾ to be His saying ﴿We have decreed﴾, then His saying ﴿replacing your likenesses﴾ means: upon Our replacing their likenesses, not upon their deeds. We say: this is an objection that falls upon all the exegetes when they interpret "al-amthal" as the plural of "mithl," which is the apparent sense, as in His saying: ﴿then they would not be your likenesses﴾ and His saying: ﴿And if We will, We replace their likenesses with a replacement﴾ [al-Insan: 28], for His saying "idha" indicates occurrence, and the change of their attributes by transformation is not a matter that occurs. The answer is to say: "al-amthal" is either the plural of "mithl" or the plural of "mathal." If it is the plural of "mithl," we say its meaning is: We have decreed death among you in this manner, namely that We change your attributes so that you become children, then youths, then middle-aged, then elders, then the term reaches you. And We have not decreed death among you so that We destroy you all at once, except when the time for that comes, and you are destroyed by a single blast. If we say it is the plural of "mathal," we say the meaning of ﴿We replace your likenesses﴾ is: We make your likenesses substitutes, and "baddala" means "ja'alahu badalan" (made it a substitute), and it would not be good to say:

Page 157

We have substituted you with this arrangement, because it implies that We have made replacements, and so it does not indicate that annihilation has befallen them. The sole point in this matter is that the saying of one who says, "I have made such-and-such a replacement," is not complete in its meaning unless he says, "I have made it a replacement for such-and-such." However, since He, exalted is He, said, ﴿We shall replace your likenesses﴾, the likeness indicates the likeness, so it is as if He said: "We have made your likenesses a replacement for you." Its meaning, as we have mentioned, is that We did not decree death so as to annihilate creation all at once; rather, We decreed that their likeness should be a replacement for them for a long period, then We would destroy them all, then We would bring them into being again.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in what you do not know﴾, according to the well-known interpretation in tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), it means in the attributes and characters that you do not know. The apparent meaning, however, is that the intended sense of ﴿in what you do not know﴾ concerns the attributes and the time, for no one knows when he will die or when he will be brought into being. Or it is as if they had said: "And when is the Hour and the bringing into being?" So He said: "You have no knowledge of these two." This applies if we say that what is intended is what has been mentioned, according to the well-known interpretation.

There is also a subtle point in this: His saying, ﴿in what you do not know﴾, is a confirmation of His saying, ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creators?﴾ For how could the creator of a thing be ignorant of it? This is like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. In accordance with what we have mentioned, there is also a benefit, which is the encouragement to righteous action, because the substitution and the bringing into being, which is death and resurrection, when it occurs at a time that no one knows, then a person should not rely on the length of the term, nor neglect preparing provision.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation﴾, as a confirmation of the possibility of the second creation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verse 60–62 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ ﴿in replacing your likenesses and producing you in what you do not know﴾ ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ In it are several issues:

The first issue: regarding its order (tartib), there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a confirmation (taqrir) of what preceded, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. He said: ﴿We created you﴾, then He said: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾. Whoever has power over giving life and causing death, which are opposites, is established as a chooser (mukhtar), so it is possible for Him to bring them back to life after death. This is unlike the case where the giving of life came from Him while He had no power over causing death, in which case one would suppose that He is a necessitating agent (mujib) and not a chooser, and a necessitating agent does not have power over every possible thing. So He said: We created you and We decreed death among you; so reflect upon it, and know that We are able to produce you.

The second: that it is a reply to the saying of a falsifier (mubtil) who says: If life and death are not natural matters in bodies, consisting of heats and moistures, which when they are abundant the body remains alive, and when they diminish and are exhausted it dies, then death would not occur. God, exalted is He, is far above fatigue, and His act requires neither time nor movement by a body.
