Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ ﴿Is it you who make it grow, or are We the ones who make it grow?﴾

After the proof of creation, he mentioned the proof of provision (rizq). His saying ﴿Have you considered what you emit (tumnun)?﴾ is a pointer to the proof of creation, and by it is the beginning (al-ibtida'), while His saying ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ is a pointer to the proof of provision, and by it is the continuance (al-baqa'). He mentioned three matters: the food eaten, the drink consumed, and that by which the food is made fit (al-muslihat). He arranged them in order, mentioning the food first, because it is the nourishment (al-ghidha'); then the drink, because by it is digestion (al-istimra'); then the fire, by which there is preparation (al-islah). From each category he mentioned what is the foundation: from the food he mentioned the grain (al-habb), for it is the foundation; from the drink, water, for it is the foundation; and from the things that make food fit he mentioned fire, because by it is the preparation of most and the most general of foods. Each one includes what is beneath it. This is the arrangement.

As for the explanation: we say, the difference between harth (sowing/tilling) and zar' (cultivation) is that harth is the initial stages of cultivation and its preliminaries, from plowing the land, casting the seed, and watering the sown seed; and zar' is the final stage of harth, from the emergence of the plant, its thickening, and its standing evenly upon the stalk. So His saying ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ means: what you begin of the works, do you bring it to its intended end, or is it Allah? No one doubts that the existence of the grain in the ear is not by the action of people, and it is not by their action if it is other than casting the seed and watering. If it is said: this indicates that Allah is the one who cultivates, so how did He say ﴿it amazes the cultivators (zurra')﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "The crop belongs to the cultivator (al-zari')"? We say: it has been established from the explanation that harth is connected to zar', so harth is the beginnings of zar', and zar' is the ends of harth, so it is permissible to apply either of them to the other. But His saying ﴿it amazes the cultivators﴾ instead of "it amazes the plowmen (al-hurath)" indicates that the one who plows is the one who begins, so he may be amazed by what results from his action of the emergence of the plant, while the cultivator, since he is the one who finishes, is not amazed except by something great. So He said ﴿it amazes the cultivators﴾, who are accustomed to taking up plowing; so what then do you think of its amazing the plowmen?

As for his ﷺ saying "The crop belongs to the cultivator," there is a benefit in it: for if he had said "to the plowman (al-harith)," then whoever began the work of cultivation and brought the plowing of the land and its leveling would become a plowman, and that is before casting the seed; so the crop would belong to whoever performs the later act, which is casting the seed. That is, whoever possesses the seed, according to the school of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. And this is more evident, because by mere casting into the earth the crop is made to belong to the one who casts it, whether he is an owner or a usurper.

From each category he mentioned what is the foundation: from the food he mentioned the grain (al-habb), for it is the foundation; from the drink, water, for it is the foundation; and from the things that make food fit he mentioned fire, because by it is the preparation of most and the most general of foods. Each one includes what is beneath it. This is the arrangement.

As for the explanation: we say, the difference between harth (sowing/tilling) and zar' (cultivation) is that harth is the initial stages of cultivation and its preliminaries, from plowing the land, casting the seed, and watering the sown seed; and zar' is the final stage of harth, from the emergence of the plant, its thickening, and its standing evenly upon the stalk. So His saying ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ means: what you begin of the works, do you bring it to its intended end, or is it Allah? No one doubts that the existence of the grain in the ear is not by the action of people, and it is not by their action if it is other than casting the seed and watering. If it is said: this indicates that Allah is the one who cultivates, so how did He say ﴿it amazes the cultivators (zurra')﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "The crop belongs to the cultivator (al-zari')"? We say: it has been established from the explanation that harth is connected to zar', so harth is the beginnings of zar', and zar' is the ends of harth, so it is permissible to apply either of them to the other. But His saying ﴿it amazes the cultivators﴾ instead of "it amazes the plowmen (al-hurath)" indicates that the one who plows is the one who begins, so he may be amazed by what results from his action of the emergence of the plant, while the cultivator, since he is the one who finishes, is not amazed except by something great. So He said ﴿it amazes the cultivators﴾, who are accustomed to taking up plowing; so what then do you think of its amazing the plowmen?

As for his ﷺ saying "The crop belongs to the cultivator," there is a benefit in it: for if he had said "to the plowman (al-harith)," then whoever began the work of cultivation and brought the plowing of the land and its leveling would become a plowman, and that is before casting the seed; so the crop would belong to whoever performs the later act, which is casting the seed. That is, whoever possesses the seed, according to the school of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. And this is more evident, because by mere casting into the earth the crop is made to belong to the one who casts it, whether he is an owner or a usurper.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If We willed, We would make it debris, and you would remain astonished﴾ ﴿Indeed, we are laden with debt﴾ ﴿Nay, we are deprived﴾. This is a gradual progression in the affirmation. Its explanation is that when He said: ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the growers?﴾, it would not be far-fetched for a stubborn opponent to say: "We plough, and it becomes crop by itself, neither by our action nor by the action of anyone else." So God, exalted is He, said: "Suppose this falsehood of yours were sound; what then do you say about its safety from the blights that strike it, so that it spoils before the grain hardens and before it forms, or before the grain hardens and before the grain appears in it? Do you preserve it from these, or do you repel them from it? Or does this crop itself repel those blights from itself, as you say that it grows by itself?" No one doubts that the repelling of blights is by the permission of God, exalted is He, and its preservation from them is by the bounty of God. On this basis He repeated it in order to mention matters arranged one after another: the first matter is for the guided; the second is for the wrongdoers; the third is for the stubborn misguided. Thus He mentions the matter about which there is no doubt at the end, as an establishing of the proof against the misguided stubborn one.

There is a question here: He, exalted is He, said here ﴿We would make it﴾ with the lam of the answer (lam al-jawab), and said regarding water ﴿We made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70] without a lam. So what is the difference between them? We say: al-Zamakhshari mentioned two answers from him. One of them: God's words ﴿If We willed, We would make it debris﴾ were mentioned earlier, so the lam in it sufficed and it was not necessary to mention it again. This is weak, because God's words ﴿If We willed, We would obliterate their eyes﴾ [Ya-Sin: 66] together with His words ﴿If We willed, We would transform them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 67] are closer than His words ﴿We would make it debris﴾ and ﴿We made it salty﴾. Unless we say: one of them is close to the other in mention but not in meaning, since obliteration does not necessitate transformation, nor the reverse; and what is eaten with it is what is drunk over time. So the two matters are close in wording and meaning. The second answer: the lam gives a kind of emphasis, so He mentioned the lam with what is eaten, to make known that the matter of food is more important than the matter of drink and its blessing is greater. What we mentioned also applies to this, because the matter of obliteration is less than the matter of transformation, and He included the lam in both. Here there is another answer, which becomes clear by first presenting an inquiry into the function of the lam in the answer of "law" (lau). We say: when the particle of condition enters a sentence, it takes it out of being a sentence in meaning, so they needed a sign indicating the meaning. So they used the jazm (apocope) in the future, because the condition requires a consequent, and this is lengthy. The jazm, which is quiescence, is more fitting to the position, and there is also a correspondence between it and the meaning. But the word "law" is specifically restricted to entering upon the past in meaning, for when it enters upon the future it makes it past. The verification in this is that the conditional sentence does not leave its divisions, for when it is mentioned the condition must be known to occur: if the condition is known to occur, then the consequence is necessarily occurring. So making the utterance a conditional sentence is a shift from a declarative sentence to a conditional one, and this is lengthy without benefit. So the saying of one who says "I will come to you if the sun rises" is lengthy, and the better is to say "I will come to you, definitely, without a condition." Knowing this, the condition's state is either that its non-occurrence is known or that it is doubtful. The condition, when it is divided into two kinds, must have two words for them, and they are "in" and "law." "In" is specific to the doubtful, and "law" to the known, for a reason we explained elsewhere. But whatever's non-occurrence is known, the other is affirmed from it, so it is past or in its ruling, because knowledge of things comes after their occurrence. What is doubted is future or in its meaning, because we doubt future matters whether they will occur or not, while the past has left uncertainty.

Page 159

Having established this, we say: when "law" entered upon the past, and the other does not differ by the governing element, the i'rab (case inflection) did not appear in it. But when "in" entered upon the future, the i'rab appeared in it. Then the consequent follows the condition, and the consequent in the case of "law" is past, so the state was not shown by a vowel or a quiescence. Therefore a particle is added indicating its exit from being a sentence and its entry into being a part of a sentence. Having established this, we say: when the consequent is apparent, it dispenses with the diverting particle. But the fact that the water mentioned in the verse, which is the drinkable water sent down from the clouds, is salty is not an occurring matter that one might suppose to be an independent report. It is strengthened by His saying ﴿We made it salty﴾ in the manner of reporting. And the tilling and the crop have very often come to be debris, so if He had said "We made it debris," it would be suspected to be a report; so He said there: ﴿If We willed, We would make it﴾, to take it out of what is suitable for it in reality, which is being debris. And He said: the sent-down water, drinkable, from the clouds, We made it salty, because that is not suspected, so He dispensed with the lam. There is in this another subtle grammatical point: that in the Qur'an the lam is dropped from the consequent of "law" when "law" is followed by a future verb in wording. But when what follows "law" is past, and the consequent is affirmative, it is not dropped, as in His saying ﴿And if We willed, We would have given﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13] and ﴿Had God guided me, I would have guided you﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. That is because when "law" enters upon a future verb, as in His saying ﴿If We willed﴾, it has been taken out of its sphere in wording, since "law" is for the past; so when the condition has left its sphere, it is permissible for the consequent to leave its sphere in wording and the lam to be dropped from it. For "in" has the future as its sphere and enters upon the future; so when what "in" enters upon is made past, as in your saying "in ji'tani" (if you came to me), it is permissible for the predicate to leave its sphere and to abandon the jazm. So you say "ukrimuka" with the raf' and "ukrimka" with the jazm, as you say in "If We willed, We would make it" and in "If We willed, made it." What we mentioned as the answer to His saying ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if God willed, He would feed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47], if you look at it, you find it sound. And since he did not say "law sha'a Allahu atamahu" (if God had willed, He would have fed him), it is known that the other is a consequent and no doubt remains in it; for it is either with the speaker, and that is not permissible, since the speaker knows the reality of his speech, or it is with them, and that is not permissible here, since their saying "if God willed, He would feed him" is a rejection of the believers in their claim, meaning: you say that if God willed an act, we would not feed. From "if God willed, He would feed him," according to your claim. So when "He would feed him" was a consequent known to both hearer and speaker, it dispensed with the lam.

The hutam (debris) is like fuataat (crumbs) and judhadh (shavings), and it is from al-hatm, just as fuataat and judhadh are from al-fatt and al-jadd. The pattern fu'al, in most cases, indicates something disliked or reprehensible. In meanings, as in subat (coma), fuwaq (hiccup), zukam (cold), duwar (dizziness), and suda (headache), for diseases and calamities in people and plants. In concrete things, as in judhadh, hutam and fuataat; and likewise when the ha' attaches, as in buradah (filings) and suhalah (scrapings). There is in this an added clarification: that the ḍamma of the fa' in the word indicates what we mentioned regarding verbs. For we say: fu'ila for what has no named agent, and the reason is that the initial letters of words, since there is no absolute lightening in them, which is sukun, the absolute heaviness, which is ḍamma, is not established. When it is established, it is due to an accident; if it is known, as we mentioned, there is no discussion; and if it is not known, as in burd and qufl, the matter is obscure and its discussion is long, and the form indicates it in the triliteral.

For we say: fu'ila for what has no named agent, and the reason is that the initial letters of words, since there is no absolute lightening in them, which is sukun, the absolute heaviness, which is ḍamma, is not established. When it is established, it is due to an accident; if it is known, as we mentioned, there is no discussion; and if it is not known, as in burd and qufl, the matter is obscure and its discussion is long, and the form indicates it in the triliteral.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we are laden with debt﴾ ﴿Nay, we are deprived﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66–67]. In it there are two aspects:
As for the first aspect: it is as if it is a speech supposed from them, as if He says: at that point it is right that you say: "Indeed, we are punished, perpetually in the torment."

As for the second aspect: they say: "Indeed, we are punished and deprived of re-growing the crop a second time." They say: "Indeed, we are punished by hunger, by the ruin of the crop, and deprived of repelling it by other than crop, because water has perished." The second aspect concerning ghurm: "Indeed, we are compelled by the burden," from "ghurima al-rajul" (the man incurred a loss), and the origin of ghurm and gharam is the necessity of what is disliked.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink?﴾ ﴿Is it you who send it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the sender?﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty and bitter; so why do you not give thanks?﴾

He singled it out for mention because it is finer and cleaner; or [it is mentioned] as a reminder to them of the favour bestowed upon them. Al-muzn (الْمُزْنُ) is the cloud heavy with water, and not with other kinds of punishment. The heaviness of it is indicated by the inversion of the word (قَلْبُ اللَّفْظِ, qalb al-lafz, metathesis), and by the notion of pushing back (مُدافَعَةُ الأمْرِ), and it is the nazm (النَّزْمُ) in some dialects, meaning the cloud that has touched the earth. The meaning of ajaj (الأُجاجُ) has already been explained: it is water that is bitter from extreme saltiness. The apparent meaning is that it is also hot, from the blazing of fire (أجِيجِ النّارِ), like al-hutam (الحُطامُ) from al-hatim (الحَطِيمِ). We have mentioned this in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is sweet and palatable, and this is salty and bitter﴾ [al-Furqan: 53]. He mentioned two attributes of the sweet water: one returns to its taste, and the other returns to the manner of its feel on the skin, which is coolness and lightness. And of the other water too there are two attributes: one returns to its taste, and the other returns to the manner of its feel, which is heat.

Then He said: ﴿so why do you not give thanks?﴾ He did not say "give thanks" when mentioning the food, and that is for two reasons:

The first: He did not mention their eating in relation to what is eaten. Since He did not say "you eat," He did not say "you give thanks" [in that case]. And for the water He said ﴿you drink﴾, so He said ﴿you give thanks﴾.

The second: regarding food He said ﴿you till﴾, thereby attributing effort to them, so He did not say "you give thanks." Regarding water He said ﴿you sent it down from the rain-cloud﴾, with no action of theirs in it at all; it is pure favour, so He said ﴿so why do you not give thanks?﴾

There is also a third reason, and it is the best: it may be said that the blessing is not complete except at eating and drinking. Do you not see that in the deserts where water is not found, a person does not eat anything for fear of thirst? So when He mentioned the food first and completed it by mentioning the drink second, He said ﴿so why do you not give thanks?﴾ for this complete blessing.

The first: it is the tree from which fire is struck with the firestick and the tinder, such as the markh (a tree used for making fire).

The second: it is the tree that is suitable for kindling fire, like firewood, for if it did not exist, kindling fire would not be easy, since fire does not take hold of everything in the way it takes hold of firewood.

The third: it is the roots of its blaze and the fuel of its tree; and were it not that it has a blaze, it would not be fit for cooking things. The rest is clear.

God Most High said: ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the wayfarers﴾ (al-muqwin). Regarding His words ﴿a reminder﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: a reminder of the fire of the Resurrection, so that a rational person must fear God and His punishment when he sees the kindled fire.

The second: a reminder of the soundness of the Resurrection, because whoever is able to place fire in green wood is not unable to place innate heat in the body of the dead. We have mentioned this in the commentary on God's words: ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]. The muqwi is the one who kindles it and then strengthens it and increases it. There is also a subtle point in it: God placed its being a reminder before its being a provision, so that it is known that the otherworldly benefit is more complete and more important to mention.
* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, and in it there are several issues:

First issue: regarding how it connects to what precedes it. We say: when God mentioned the state of those who deny the Resurrection and the Oneness (of God), He mentioned the proof for both through creation and provision, and faith did not benefit them. He said to His Prophet ﷺ: your duty is to perfect yourself, which is your knowledge of your Lord and your action for your Lord: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord﴾. We have mentioned this in His words: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130] in another place.

Second issue: tasbih (glorification) is declaring God free of what is not fitting for Him. So what is the benefit of mentioning "the name," and why did He not say: "glorify your Lord, the Mighty"? We answer this in two ways:

The first, which is the well-known one, is that "the name" is an insertion (muqhamm). On this answer, we say: there is in it the benefit of increasing glorification, because whoever magnifies a great one and exaggerates in magnifying him does not mention his name except with magnification, and does not mention it in a lowly place or casually, however it happens. That is because one who honors a person in his presence may not honor him in his absence, and so he mentions him by his name as a designation. If he is in his presence, he does not say that; but when he is great in his estimation, he does not mention him, whether present or absent, except with attributes of greatness. If it is said: then on this basis what is the function of the bi (in bi-ism), and how did it come about, when He did not say "fasabbih ism rabbika al-azim" or "al-Rabba al-azim"? We say: it has been stated many times that when a verb's connection to its object is extremely evident, it does not reach it by a preposition, so one does not say "darabtu bi-Zaydin" meaning "darabtu Zaydan" (I struck Zayd); and when it is in extreme obscurity, it reaches it only by a preposition, so one does not say "dhahabtu Zaydan" meaning "dhahabtu bi-Zaydin" (I went with Zayd); and when it is between the two, both forms are permissible, so we say: "sabbahtuhu" and "sabbahtu bihi," and "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." Given this, we say: when He attached glorification to "the name," and the name is an insertion, glorification in reality is connected to something else, namely the Lord, and the connection is somewhat hidden, so inserting the bi is permissible. If it is said: since both omission and inclusion are permissible, what is the difference between this place and His words: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾? We say: here the evidence for greatness is placed first, so that it is said: the bi in His words "bi-ism" is not superfluous, and its explanation is in two ways:

The first: that when He mentioned the matters and said: "Is it We or you?", everyone acknowledged that the matters are from God. When they were challenged regarding Oneness, they said: "We do not associate in meaning; we only take idols as gods in name and call them gods. The One who created them and created the heavens is God, so in reality we declare Him free (of partners)." So He said: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord﴾. Just as you, O rational one, have acknowledged that the two do not share in reality, acknowledge that they do not share in name, and do not say to anyone other than Him "god," for the name follows the meaning and the reality. On this (reading), the address is not with the Prophet ﷺ; rather it is like a preacher saying: "O poor one, you have spent your life and not corrected your deeds," not meaning any particular person, and its implied sense is "O you poor listener."

The second: that the intended meaning of "mention of your Lord" is: when you say "and they turned away," then glorify your Lord by mentioning His name among your people, and occupy yourself with conveying the message. The meaning is: mention Him with the tongue and the heart, and explain His attributes to them; and even if they do not accept, you are engaged in your task, which is conveying. Had He said "fasabbih rabbaka," it would not have conveyed mention to them, and it would have indicated glorification by the heart alone. Since He said "fasabbih bi-ism rabbika," and the name is what is pronounced verbally, this shows that he is commanded to remember with the tongue, and he is not permitted to limit himself to remembrance of the heart alone. It may also be said: "fasabbih" beginning with the name of your mighty Lord, so the bi is not superfluous.

Third issue: how is our Lord glorified? We say: either in meaning, by believing that He is One, free of partners, and capable, free of incapacity, so He is not unable to resurrect; or in words, by saying: "Subhan Allah," "Subhan Allah al-Azim," and "Subhanahu 'amma yushrikun," or what takes their place of speech that indicates His transcendence above partner and incapacity. For when you glorify Him and believe that He is One, free of everything that is impermissible in His essence, it follows that He is not a body, for a body has many components, whereas He is a true unity with no plurality in His essence; nor is He an accident, nor in a place. Everything impermissible for Him is negated by monotheism, and He is not upon anything, nor in anything, nor from anything. And when you say "He is capable," knowledge, will, life, and other attributes are established for Him. We will mention that in the commentary on Surat al-Ikhlas, God willing.

Fourth issue: what is the difference between "al-Azim" (the Mighty) and "al-A'la" (the Most High), and is there any benefit in mentioning "al-Azim" here instead of "al-A'la," and in mentioning "al-A'la" in His words "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" instead of "al-Azim"? We say: as for the difference between al-Azim and al-A'la, al-Azim indicates nearness, and al-A'la indicates remoteness. Its explanation: whatever is great among perceptible things is near to everything possible, for if it were distant from it, its place would be empty of it; and if it had other parts, it would be greater than it is. So the Great, in relation to all, is the one that is near to all. As for the small, when it is near from one direction, it is distant from another. As for the Exalted, it is the one most distant from everything, for whatever is near something from the direction of "above" is more distant from it and higher. So the absolutely Exalted, in relation to everything, is the one at the utmost remoteness from everything. Knowing this, perceptible things glorify God, and when we know of God a negative meaning, it is correct to say: He is too exalted for our perception to encompass Him. When we know of Him an affirmative attribute of knowledge and power that increases His magnification beyond what our knowledge reaches, we say: He is greater and higher than our knowledge can encompass. Our saying "greater" (a'zam) means "great, with no one great like Him," so it contains a negative understanding and an affirmative understanding. And His saying "a'la" means "He is Exalted, and there is no exalted one like Him," and "al-Ali" points to a negative understanding, while "al-A'la" is similar to it by another cause. So "al-A'la" is used in its true sense both in wording and meaning, while "al-A'zam" is used in its true sense in wording, and it contains a negative meaning. It seems that the original sense of "al-Azim" is an affirmative understanding with no negation in it, so "al-A'la" is a better usage than "al-A'zam." This is the difference.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 75–79 (part 1 of 2):

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the order (of the verses) and its reason. It is that when God the Exalted sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, He gave him everything that befits him and purified him from everything that does not befit him. He gave him wisdom (al-hikmah), which is the decisive proofs and the proper use of them in their right ways; good admonition (al-maw'izah al-hasanah), which is beneficial matters that soften the hearts and illuminate the breasts; and argumentation (al-mujadalah) that is in the best of methods. He brought all of this, and everyone was unable to oppose him with anything, yet they did not believe. The one to whom all of this is recited and who does not believe has nothing left to say except that this demonstration is not for the manifestation of the claim, but for the strength of the mind of the one who makes the claim and his power in constructing proofs. He knows that he prevails by the strength of his argument, not by the clarity of his statement. Sometimes one of the two debaters says to the other when he is at a loss: "You know that the truth is in my hand, but you belittle me and do not deal justly with me." At that point the opponent has no answer except to swear by oaths from which there is no escape, that he is not obstinate and that he is fair. That is because if he brought another proof, the other could say: "This proof too you overcame me in with your strength and power." Likewise, when God, Mighty and Majestic, gave the Prophet (ﷺ) what befits him, they said: "He wants to prefer himself over us, and he argues with us about what he knows to be otherwise." So nothing remained for him except to swear. God then revealed to him various kinds of oaths after the proofs. This is why oaths are numerous at the beginning of the revelation and especially in the final seventh (al-sub' al-akhir, the last seventh of the Qur'an by its division into seven parts).

The second issue: concerning the attachment of the preposition (the bā'). We say: when He made clear that He is the Creator of creation and the Provider, and that He has greatness, by decisive proof, and they did not believe, He said: "Nothing remains except the oath. So I swear by God that I am truthful."

It is that when God the Exalted sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, He gave him everything that befits him and purified him from everything that does not befit him. He gave him wisdom (al-hikmah), which is the decisive proofs and the proper use of them in their right ways; good admonition (al-maw'izah al-hasanah), which is beneficial matters that soften the hearts and illuminate the breasts; and argumentation (al-mujadalah) that is in the best of methods. He brought all of this, and everyone was unable to oppose him with anything, yet they did not believe. The one to whom all of this is recited and who does not believe has nothing left to say except that this demonstration is not for the manifestation of the claim, but for the strength of the mind of the one who makes the claim and his power in constructing proofs. He knows that he prevails by the strength of his argument, not by the clarity of his statement. Sometimes one of the two debaters says to the other when he is at a loss: "You know that the truth is in my hand, but you belittle me and do not deal justly with me." At that point the opponent has no answer except to swear by oaths from which there is no escape, that he is not obstinate and that he is fair. That is because if he brought another proof, the other could say: "This proof too you overcame me in with your strength and power." Likewise, when God, Mighty and Majestic, gave the Prophet (ﷺ) what befits him, they said: "He wants to prefer himself over us, and he argues with us about what he knows to be otherwise." So nothing remained for him except to swear. God then revealed to him various kinds of oaths after the proofs. This is why oaths are numerous at the beginning of the revelation and especially in the final seventh (al-sub' al-akhir, the last seventh of the Qur'an by its division into seven parts).

The second issue: concerning the attachment of the preposition (the bā'). We say: when He made clear that He is the Creator of creation and the Provider, and that He has greatness, by decisive proof, and they did not believe, He said: "Nothing remains except the oath. So I swear by God that I am truthful."

The third issue: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿So I swear﴾ (fa-la uqsimu), when you say that it is an oath? We say: there are reported and rational explanations, not contrary to transmission. As for the reported ones:

The first is that (la) is superfluous, like its usage in His saying: ﴿so that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], meaning "so that he may know."

The second: its origin is la uqsimu with the emphatic lam (lam al-ta'kid), whose vowel was lengthened so it became la, as in pausing (al-waqf).

The third: la is a negation, and its origin according to their statement, with the oath following it, is as if he said: "No, by God, there is no validity to the claim of the unbelievers (that) I swear to it." As for the rational explanation, it is that the word la is a negation with its own meaning, but in the speech there is a compositional metaphor (majaz tarkibi). Its sense is that we say: la in negation here is like its use in the saying of one who says: "Do not ask me about what befell me," indicating that what befell him is greater than being explained, so one should not ask him. His purpose in forbidding the question is not to be met with a request for information, and his purpose in that prohibition is only to show the greatness of the event, and it becomes as if he said: "A great matter befell me." This is supported by the fact that the listener says to him: "What befell you?" Had he understood from the literal meaning of his speech a prohibition against asking, he would not have said "What befell you?" So it is valid for him to say: "I was wrong in forbidding you from asking, and then you asked me." And how not, when that speaker often says it when his companion is silent about asking, or says "Do not ask me," and no one says "What befell you?" and the listener does not say: "You forbade me from asking." All of this is established in their understanding: the intended meaning is to magnify the event, not to forbid. Once this is known, we say that in the oath something similar exists in one of two ways:

Either because the event is extremely evident, so he says: "I do not swear that it is so, because it is clearer than needing to be made known and too well known to be denied." So he says "I swear not," and he does not mean by it the oath and its negation, but he intends only to inform that the event is manifest.

Or because the one sworn by is greater than what one swears by, and the speaker has come to affirm himself, so he says: "I do not swear one oath, but a thousand oaths," and "I do not swear by the head of the emir, but by the head of the sultan," and he says: "I do not swear by such-and-such," intending by this that he is absolutely certain.

The second: it is indicated by the fact that this formula does not occur in the Qur'an, and the one sworn by is God the Exalted or one of His attributes, whereas what came are created things. The first answer poses no problem if we say that the one sworn by in all cases is the Lord of things, as in His saying: ﴿By those who line up in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1], meaning the Lord of those who line up in ranks, the Lord of the Resurrection, the Lord of the sun, and so on. So His saying ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ means: the matter is clearer than to be sworn to, or that doubt could reach it.

The fourth issue: what are the positions of the stars? We say: there are several views:

The first: they are the risings and settings, or the settings alone, for at them the stars fall.

The second: they are their places in the sky, in their constellations and stations.

The third: their positions in pursuing the devils at the time of their jostling.

The fourth: their positions on the Day of Resurrection, when the stars are scattered. As for the positions of the stars of the Qur'an, they are the hearts of His servants, His angels, His messengers, and the righteous believers, or their meanings and the rulings that came in them.

The fifth issue: is there any benefit in specifying the positions of the stars for the oath? We say: yes, a great benefit. Its explanation is that we have already mentioned that swearing by their positions is an oath as they are, and likewise they are among the proofs. This has been explained in al-Dhariyat, in al-Tur, in al-Najm, and elsewhere. We say here too it is similarly so, because when God the Exalted mentioned the creation of the human from semen and his death, He showed through the allusion to the creation of the two opposites in the souls His power and His choice. Then when He mentioned one of the proofs from the souls, He also mentioned from the proofs of the horizons His power and His choice, saying: ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63], ﴿Have you considered the water?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68], and so on. He mentioned His power over its growth and His making it debris, and His creating the water sweet and fresh, and His making it salty, as an indication that the one capable of two opposites is one who chooses. He had not mentioned any of the heavenly proofs, so He mentioned the heavenly proof within the context of the oath, saying: "the positions of the stars." For these too are a proof of choice, because each one being in one place in the sky rather than another, while the places are equal in reality, is the proof of a free and choosing agent. So He said ﴿by the positions of the stars﴾, not as a reference to the proofs of the souls and the horizons, as He said: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. This is like His saying: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain. And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20–22], where He mentioned the three kinds; so here too.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾. The pronoun refers to the oath implied in His saying ﴿So I swear﴾, for it contains the mention of the verbal noun (al-masdar, the infinitive or verbal noun). That is why verbal nouns that do not appear after the verb are described, so one says: "I struck him strongly." Regarding this there are grammatical and semantic issues. As for the grammatical:

The first issue: it is to be asked: what is the answer (jawab) of ﴿if you only knew﴾? Some who lack knowledge say that its answer is what came before, but this is invalid in all cases, because the answer of a conditional does not precede it. That is because the operation of particles on what they govern does not occur before their existence. So one does not say: "Zaydan in qama," nor any other particle. The reason is that the operation of particles is analogous to the operation of meanings; it distinguishes subject from object and others. When the operating element is a meaning with no place in the senses, its precedence and posteriority are known, and so it is permissible to say: "Standing, I struck Zayd," or "A strong striking, I struck him." But particles have precedence and posteriority perceptible to the senses, so after we know their posteriority, it is impossible to assume their existence as prior, unlike meanings. Once this is established, we say: the operation of the conditional particle in meaning is to remove each of the two clauses from being an independent sentence. So when you say "man" and "in" (conditional particles), it is impossible to remove the first clause from being a clause after the other clauses have occurred, so that it is known that its particle is weaker than the operation of meaning, because it depends on the operation of meaning. Yet meaning can be assumed as preceding and following. The operation of verbs is a semantic operation, and the operation of particles is an operation analogous to meaning. This is false for what we have mentioned, and here it is even more evidently false, because what precedes cannot serve as the response of what follows. Whoever says "if you only knew that Zayd is standing" has not spoken Arabic. Once this is clarified, the statement admits two possibilities:

One: that it is said that the answer is entirely omitted, and no answer is intended by it. Rather, what is intended is the negation of what "if" (law) has entered upon, and it is as if he said: "And indeed it is a mighty oath, which you do not know." Its realization is that law is mentioned to indicate the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another, so the first must be negated. So the entry of law upon "you know" informs us that their knowledge is negated, whether or not we know the answer. This is like their saying of a transitive verb: "So-and-so gives and withholds," where no object is intended, but only the affirmation of power. If it is said: "What is the benefit of departing from the literal meaning, and leaving out His saying: 'and indeed it is an oath, and you do not know'?" We say: its benefit is to emphasize the negation, because one who says "if you knew" makes a claim, and when he is challenged and asked, "Why did you say we do not know?", he says, "If you knew, you would have done such and such." But if he said at the outset, "You do not know," he would be intending negation, as if he said: "I say that you do not know, without any connection to proof or cause."

Two: that it has an answer, whose implied form is: "If you knew, you would have magnified it, but you have not magnified it, so it is known that you do not know, for if you knew, it would be great in your eyes, and there is no magnification, so you do not know."

The second issue: if it is asked, does the saying ﴿if you only knew﴾ have an object (maf'ul) or not? We say: in the first view, it has no object, as in their saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," and as if he said: "You have no knowledge." It may also be said: "You have no knowledge of the greatness of the oath," in which case it has an object. This is like His saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18], and His saying: ﴿They are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]. In the second view, too, there are two possibilities:

One: if you had knowledge of the oath, you would have magnified it.

Two: if you had knowledge of its greatness, you would have magnified it.

**Third issue: how does the statement ﴿if you knew﴾ connect with what comes before and after it?**

We say: it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*, an interjected sentence) within the discourse. Its implied sense is: "And indeed it is a great oath; if you knew, you would confirm it."

If it is asked, "What is the benefit of the parenthetical clause?" we say: it serves to cut off the objection of an objector. When He said ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾, He wished to describe it with greatness, by saying "great." The unbelievers were ignorant of this and claimed knowledge of the matters of the stars. They would say: "If it were so, why do we not attain any knowledge or even conjecture?" So He said: "If you knew, certainty would have come to you." According to what we have mentioned, the matter is clearer than this. This is because we have said that His statement ﴿So I swear not﴾ means that the matter is too evident to be confirmed by an oath. The unbelievers would say: "Where is the evidence, when we are certain of its absence?" So He said: "If you knew anything, it would not be so." What is clearer still is that we have explained that everything God has made an oath is in itself a proof of the thing sought, and He presented it in the form of an oath. Thus His statement ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ means, on careful examination: "Indeed it is a proof and a strong argument. If you knew its aspect, you would acknowledge what it signifies, which is the oneness of God (*tawhid*) and the power to resurrect (*hashr*, the gathering of creatures on the Day of Resurrection)." This is because the indication of the stars' specific placement in their positions is most evident, and the philosophers (*al-falasifa*) have no clearer proof than it.

As for the semantic (*ma'nawiyya*) points:

**First issue: What is the thing sworn to?** We say: there are two views.

The first: the Qur'an. The unbelievers would call it at one time poetry, at another time sorcery, and other things besides.

The second: it is the oneness of God and the resurrection, and this is the clearer view. His statement ﴿indeed it is a Qur'an﴾ is the beginning of a new statement, and we will explain this.

**Second issue: What is the benefit of describing it as "great" in His statement ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾?** We say: when He said ﴿So I swear not﴾, and its meaning was "I do not swear by this, because the thing sworn by is evident," He then said, in effect: "I am not leaving off swearing by this, because it is not an oath, or it is not a great oath. Rather, it is a great oath, and I do not swear by it; rather, I swear by something greater than it, because I am certain of the matter and I know its reality."

**Third issue: An oath is, for the most part, described as emphatic and great.** It is said of the one who swears: "So-and-so swore by the great oaths," and then one says of his oath that it is an emphatic oath (*yamin mughallaza*), because its sins are grave. As for God, the Mighty and Majestic, He is described as "the Great," and this is fitting, because its meaning is that He is the One whose speech draws near to every heart and fills the breast with awe, since we have explained that the meaning of "great" in Him includes this. Just as a great body is one that is adjacent to great things and fills many places with greatness, so too the great being that is not a body is one that draws near to many matters and fills many breasts.

The first: the Qur'an. The unbelievers would call it at one time poetry, at another time sorcery, and other things besides.

The second: it is the oneness of God and the resurrection, and this is the clearer view. His statement ﴿indeed it is a Qur'an﴾ is the beginning of a new statement, and we will explain this.

**Second issue: What is the benefit of describing it as "great" in His statement ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾?** We say: when He said ﴿So I swear not﴾, and its meaning was "I do not swear by this, because the thing sworn by is evident," He then said, in effect: "I am not leaving off swearing by this, because it is not an oath, or it is not a great oath. Rather, it is a great oath, and I do not swear by it; rather, I swear by something greater than it, because I am certain of the matter and I know its reality."

**Third issue: An oath is, for the most part, described as emphatic and great.** It is said of the one who swears: "So-and-so swore by the great oaths," and then one says of his oath that it is an emphatic oath (*yamin mughallaza*), because its sins are grave. As for God, the Mighty and Majestic, He is described as "the Great," and this is fitting, because its meaning is that He is the One whose speech draws near to every heart and fills the breast with awe, since we have explained that the meaning of "great" in Him includes this. Just as a great body is one that is adjacent to great things and fills many places with greatness, so too the great being that is not a body is one that draws near to many matters and fills many breasts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 75–79 (part 1 of 2):

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the order (of the verses) and its reason. It is that when God the Exalted sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, He gave him everything that befits him and purified him from everything that does not befit him. He gave him wisdom (al-hikmah), which is the decisive proofs and the proper use of them in their right ways; good admonition (al-maw'izah al-hasanah), which is beneficial matters that soften the hearts and illuminate the breasts; and argumentation (al-mujadalah) that is in the best of methods. He brought all of this, and everyone was unable to oppose him with anything, yet they did not believe. The one to whom all of this is recited and who does not believe has nothing left to say except that this demonstration is not for the manifestation of the claim, but for the strength of the mind of the one who makes the claim and his power in constructing proofs. He knows that he prevails by the strength of his argument, not by the clarity of his statement. Sometimes one of the two debaters says to the other when he is at a loss: "You know that the truth is in my hand, but you belittle me and do not deal justly with me." At that point the opponent has no answer except to swear by oaths from which there is no escape, that he is not obstinate and that he is fair. That is because if he brought another proof, the other could say: "This proof too you overcame me in with your strength and power." Likewise, when God, Mighty and Majestic, gave the Prophet (ﷺ) what befits him, they said: "He wants to prefer himself over us, and he argues with us about what he knows to be otherwise." So nothing remained for him except to swear. God then revealed to him various kinds of oaths after the proofs. This is why oaths are numerous at the beginning of the revelation and especially in the final seventh (al-sub' al-akhir, the last seventh of the Qur'an by its division into seven parts).

The second issue: concerning the attachment of the preposition (the bā'). We say: when He made clear that He is the Creator of creation and the Provider, and that He has greatness, by decisive proof, and they did not believe, He said: "Nothing remains except the oath. So I swear by God that I am truthful."

The third issue: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿So I swear﴾ (fa-la uqsimu), when you say that it is an oath? We say: there are reported and rational explanations, not contrary to transmission. As for the reported ones:

The first is that (la) is superfluous, like its usage in His saying: ﴿so that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], meaning "so that he may know."

The second: its origin is la uqsimu with the emphatic lam (lam al-ta'kid), whose vowel was lengthened so it became la, as in pausing (al-waqf).

The third: la is a negation, and its origin according to their statement, with the oath following it, is as if he said: "No, by God, there is no validity to the claim of the unbelievers (that) I swear to it." As for the rational explanation, it is that the word la is a negation with its own meaning, but in the speech there is a compositional metaphor (majaz tarkibi). Its sense is that we say: la in negation here is like its use in the saying of one who says: "Do not ask me about what befell me," indicating that what befell him is greater than being explained, so one should not ask him. His purpose in forbidding the question is not to be met with a request for information, and his purpose in that prohibition is only to show the greatness of the event, and it becomes as if he said: "A great matter befell me." This is supported by the fact that the listener says to him: "What befell you?" Had he understood from the literal meaning of his speech a prohibition against asking, he would not have said "What befell you?" So it is valid for him to say: "I was wrong in forbidding you from asking, and then you asked me." And how not, when that speaker often says it when his companion is silent about asking, or says "Do not ask me," and no one says "What befell you?" and the listener does not say: "You forbade me from asking." All of this is established in their understanding: the intended meaning is to magnify the event, not to forbid. Once this is known, we say that in the oath something similar exists in one of two ways:

Either because the event is extremely evident, so he says: "I do not swear that it is so, because it is clearer than needing to be made known and too well known to be denied." So he says "I swear not," and he does not mean by it the oath and its negation, but he intends only to inform that the event is manifest.

Or because the one sworn by is greater than what one swears by, and the speaker has come to affirm himself, so he says: "I do not swear one oath, but a thousand oaths," and "I do not swear by the head of the emir, but by the head of the sultan," and he says: "I do not swear by such-and-such," intending by this that he is absolutely certain.

The second: it is indicated by the fact that this formula does not occur in the Qur'an, and the one sworn by is God the Exalted or one of His attributes, whereas what came are created things. The first answer poses no problem if we say that the one sworn by in all cases is the Lord of things, as in His saying: ﴿By those who line up in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1], meaning the Lord of those who line up in ranks, the Lord of the Resurrection, the Lord of the sun, and so on. So His saying ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ means: the matter is clearer than to be sworn to, or that doubt could reach it.

The fourth issue: what are the positions of the stars? We say: there are several views:

The first: they are the risings and settings, or the settings alone, for at them the stars fall.

The second: they are their places in the sky, in their constellations and stations.

The third: their positions in pursuing the devils at the time of their jostling.

The fourth: their positions on the Day of Resurrection, when the stars are scattered. As for the positions of the stars of the Qur'an, they are the hearts of His servants, His angels, His messengers, and the righteous believers, or their meanings and the rulings that came in them.

The fifth issue: is there any benefit in specifying the positions of the stars for the oath? We say: yes, a great benefit. Its explanation is that we have already mentioned that swearing by their positions is an oath as they are, and likewise they are among the proofs. This has been explained in al-Dhariyat, in al-Tur, in al-Najm, and elsewhere. We say here too it is similarly so, because when God the Exalted mentioned the creation of the human from semen and his death, He showed through the allusion to the creation of the two opposites in the souls His power and His choice. Then when He mentioned one of the proofs from the souls, He also mentioned from the proofs of the horizons His power and His choice, saying: ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63], ﴿Have you considered the water?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68], and so on. He mentioned His power over its growth and His making it debris, and His creating the water sweet and fresh, and His making it salty, as an indication that the one capable of two opposites is one who chooses. He had not mentioned any of the heavenly proofs, so He mentioned the heavenly proof within the context of the oath, saying: "the positions of the stars." For these too are a proof of choice, because each one being in one place in the sky rather than another, while the places are equal in reality, is the proof of a free and choosing agent. So He said ﴿by the positions of the stars﴾, not as a reference to the proofs of the souls and the horizons, as He said: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. This is like His saying: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain. And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20–22], where He mentioned the three kinds; so here too.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾. The pronoun refers to the oath implied in His saying ﴿So I swear﴾, for it contains the mention of the verbal noun (al-masdar, the infinitive or verbal noun). That is why verbal nouns that do not appear after the verb are described, so one says: "I struck him strongly." Regarding this there are grammatical and semantic issues. As for the grammatical:

The first issue: it is to be asked: what is the answer (jawab) of ﴿if you only knew﴾? Some who lack knowledge say that its answer is what came before, but this is invalid in all cases, because the answer of a conditional does not precede it. That is because the operation of particles on what they govern does not occur before their existence. So one does not say: "Zaydan in qama," nor any other particle. The reason is that the operation of particles is analogous to the operation of meanings; it distinguishes subject from object and others. When the operating element is a meaning with no place in the senses, its precedence and posteriority are known, and so it is permissible to say: "Standing, I struck Zayd," or "A strong striking, I struck him." But particles have precedence and posteriority perceptible to the senses, so after we know their posteriority, it is impossible to assume their existence as prior, unlike meanings. Once this is established, we say: the operation of the conditional particle in meaning is to remove each of the two clauses from being an independent sentence. So when you say "man" and "in" (conditional particles), it is impossible to remove the first clause from being a clause after the other clauses have occurred, so that it is known that its particle is weaker than the operation of meaning, because it depends on the operation of meaning. Yet meaning can be assumed as preceding and following. The operation of verbs is a semantic operation, and the operation of particles is an operation analogous to meaning. Once this is established, we say regarding His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf: 24], some preachers (al-wu'az) said that it is attached to "lawla" (had it not been), so that the desire did not occur from him. This is false for what we have mentioned, and here it is even more evidently false, because what precedes cannot serve as the response of what follows. Whoever says "if you only knew that Zayd is standing" has not spoken Arabic. Once this is clarified, the statement admits two possibilities:

One: that it is said that the answer is entirely omitted, and no answer is intended by it. Rather, what is intended is the negation of what "if" (law) has entered upon, and it is as if he said: "And indeed it is a mighty oath, which you do not know." Its realization is that law is mentioned to indicate the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another, so the first must be negated. So the entry of law upon "you know" informs us that their knowledge is negated, whether or not we know the answer. This is like their saying of a transitive verb: "So-and-so gives and withholds," where no object is intended, but only the affirmation of power. If it is said: "What is the benefit of departing from the literal meaning, and leaving out His saying: 'and indeed it is an oath, and you do not know'?" We say: its benefit is to emphasize the negation, because one who says "if you knew" makes a claim, and when he is challenged and asked, "Why did you say we do not know?", he says, "If you knew, you would have done such and such." But if he said at the outset, "You do not know," he would be intending negation, as if he said: "I say that you do not know, without any connection to proof or cause."

Two: that it has an answer, whose implied form is: "If you knew, you would have magnified it, but you have not magnified it, so it is known that you do not know, for if you knew, it would be great in your eyes, and there is no magnification, so you do not know."

The second issue: if it is asked, does the saying ﴿if you only knew﴾ have an object (maf'ul) or not? We say: in the first view, it has no object, as in their saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," and as if he said: "You have no knowledge." It may also be said: "You have no knowledge of the greatness of the oath," in which case it has an object. The first is more eloquent and more fitting in beauty, because they know nothing at all; for if they had knowledge, the most deserving things to be known would be these manifest matters established by decisive proofs. This is like His saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18], and His saying: ﴿They are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]. In the second view, too, there are two possibilities:

One: if you had knowledge of the oath, you would have magnified it.

Two: if you had knowledge of its greatness, you would have magnified it.

**Third issue: how does the statement ﴿if you knew﴾ connect with what comes before and after it?**

We say: it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*, an interjected sentence) within the discourse. Its implied sense is: "And indeed it is a great oath; if you knew, you would confirm it."

If it is asked, "What is the benefit of the parenthetical clause?" we say: it serves to cut off the objection of an objector. When He said ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾, He wished to describe it with greatness, by saying "great." The unbelievers were ignorant of this and claimed knowledge of the matters of the stars. They would say: "If it were so, why do we not attain any knowledge or even conjecture?" So He said: "If you knew, certainty would have come to you." According to what we have mentioned, the matter is clearer than this. This is because we have said that His statement ﴿So I swear not﴾ means that the matter is too evident to be confirmed by an oath. The unbelievers would say: "Where is the evidence, when we are certain of its absence?" So He said: "If you knew anything, it would not be so." What is clearer still is that we have explained that everything God has made an oath is in itself a proof of the thing sought, and He presented it in the form of an oath. Thus His statement ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ means, on careful examination: "Indeed it is a proof and a strong argument. If you knew its aspect, you would acknowledge what it signifies, which is the oneness of God (*tawhid*) and the power to resurrect (*hashr*, the gathering of creatures on the Day of Resurrection)." This is because the indication of the stars' specific placement in their positions is most evident, and the philosophers (*al-falasifa*) have no clearer proof than it.

As for the semantic (*ma'nawiyya*) points:

**First issue: What is the thing sworn to?** We say: there are two views.

The first: the Qur'an. The unbelievers would call it at one time poetry, at another time sorcery, and other things besides.

The second: it is the oneness of God and the resurrection, and this is the clearer view. His statement ﴿indeed it is a Qur'an﴾ is the beginning of a new statement, and we will explain this.

Rather, it is a great oath, and I do not swear by it; rather, I swear by something greater than it, because I am certain of the matter and I know its reality."
