As for God, the Mighty and Majestic, He is described as "the Great," and this is fitting, because its meaning is that He is the One whose speech draws near to every heart and fills the breast with awe, since we have explained that the meaning of "great" in Him includes this. Just as a great body is one that is adjacent to great things and fills many places with greatness, so too the great being that is not a body is one that draws near to many matters and fills many breasts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verse 80 (part 1 of 3):

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. And in this are several issues:

[page 166]

The first issue: To what does the pronoun in His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, it﴾ refer? We say: there are two views on this.

The first: it refers to something known, namely the speech that was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), which was well known to all, and the disbelievers used to say: "It is poetry," and "It is magic." So the Exalted said, refuting them: ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾. Alternatively, it refers to something mentioned, namely all that preceded in Surat al-Waqi'ah of tawhid (the oneness of God), resurrection (al-hashr), the proofs mentioned for both, and the oath in which He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a mighty oath﴾. This is because they had said: "All of this is the speech of Muhammad and his own invention." So He said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾.

The second issue: Is "Qur'an" a verbal noun (masdar) or a noun other than a verbal noun? We say: there are two views on this.

The first: it is a masdar used in the sense of the passive object, namely "that which is recited" (al-maqru'). Its like is in His words, the Exalted: ﴿And if a Qur'an had by it the mountains been set in motion﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. This is like what is said of a great body: "Look at the power of God, the Exalted," meaning His created thing (maqdur). It is as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿This is the creation of God, so show me﴾ [Luqman: 11]. On this basis, we will explain the corruption of the view of one who rejected the jurists' statement in the chapter on zakat: "He gives something better than what is obligatory and takes the jubran (compensation), or gives something less than it and also gives the jubran," when he said: "Jubran is a masdar; it is not taken or given." It is said to him: it is like "Qur'an" in the sense of "that which is recited." It is also permissible to say of what is taken: jabir (compensator) or majbur (compensated), or it is said: it is a noun for what is compensated with, like qurban (sacrifice).

The third issue: If this speech is a refutation of the polytheists, then they did not deny that it was recited, so what is the benefit of His words, ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾? We say: there are two views on this.

The first: it is an informing about the whole, namely His words, ﴿a noble Qur'an﴾. They denied that it was a noble Qur'an, and they did not acknowledge it as such.

The second, and it is better than the first: they said, "It is an invention from himself," and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say, "It is heard; I heard it and recited it to you." Yet the Qur'an was not "recited" in their view, and they did not say that the Prophet (ﷺ) recites the Qur'an. There is a difference between recitation and composition. So when He said, ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾, He affirmed that it was recited upon the Prophet (ﷺ) so that it would be read and recited. Thus He said, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾; He named it "Qur'an" because of how much it is recited, and it will be recited forever, part of it in this world and part of it in the Hereafter.

The fourth issue: His words ﴿noble﴾ contain a subtle point, namely that speech, when it is recited much, becomes cheap in the eyes and ears. For this reason you see that whoever says something in the assembly of kings does not repeat it a second time, and if it were said, one would say to its speaker, "Why do you repeat this?" Then when the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾, meaning "recited," and it is recited and will be recited, He said, ﴿noble﴾, meaning it is not cheapened by much recitation, and it remains forever like fresh speech and a new discourse. From here arises the description of the Qur'an as "discourse" (hadith), although it is eternal (qadim); it draws strength from this, so it is eternal, heard by listeners as if it were speech of the present hour, striking the hearing of the community. This is because the angels who knew it before the Prophet by thousands of years, when they hear it from one of us, take pleasure in it as a listener takes pleasure in a new speech never mentioned to him before.

"Noble" (karim) is a comprehensive name for the attributes of praise. It was said: the karim is one whose origin is pure and whose virtue is manifest, so that one whose origin is not pure is not called karim absolutely, but is called "karim in himself." And one whose origin is pure but whose soul is not pure is not called karim except with qualification; it is said: "He is noble of origin but base in himself." Then, the pure generous person is one who gives abundantly to people, or whose giving is easy, and he is called karim even if he has no other virtue in the true sense; but that is for a reason: people love whoever gives to them and rejoice in one who gives more than they rejoice in others. So when they see an ascetic or a scholar, they do not call him karim. This is confirmed by the fact that when they see someone who does not ask them for anything, they call him "noble of soul" merely for his abstaining from begging, because taking from them is difficult for them. All of this is in customary, base usage. But in its original sense, it is said: the karim is the one in whom what is fitting is gathered: purity of origin and manifestness of virtue. This is shown by the fact that the generous person in his dealings should not have anything from him for which he would be called base. So the Qur'an too is karim in the sense of pure origin and manifest virtue: its wording is eloquent and its meaning is sound. But the Qur'an is also karim according to the understanding of the common people: whoever asks it for something, it gives him. The jurist derives proof from it and takes from it; the sage draws support from it and argues by it; the man of letters benefits from it and is strengthened by it. And the Exalted described the Qur'an as karim, and as 'aziz (mighty), and as hakim (wise). Because it is karim, everyone who turns to it attains what he seeks, for many people do not understand any of the sciences, yet when they occupy themselves with the Qur'an, its memorization becomes easy for them. And rarely is one seen who memorizes a book he reads without changing a word for another word, or a letter for another letter, while all the readers recite the Qur'an without hesitation or substitution. And because it is 'aziz: whoever turns away from it, nothing of it remains with him, unlike other books. For whoever reads a book, memorizes it, and then abandons it, its meaning still clings to his heart until he transmits it correctly. But as for the Qur'an, whoever abandons it, nothing of it remains with him, because of its might; and it does not stay with one who is not obliged to memorize it. And because it is hakim, whoever occupies himself with it and turns to it with his heart, it makes him independent of all other sciences.

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿in a Book﴾, He made it a thing enclosed within a book. So what is that? We say: there are two views on this.

The first: the enclosed thing is the Qur'an; that is, it is a Qur'an in a Book, just as one says: "So-and-so is a noble man in his house." The hearer does not doubt that the speaker means that he is seated in the house, and he does not mean that he is noble only when he is in the house and ignoble when he is outside. Nor does he doubt that the speaker does not mean that he is noble in his house, but rather that he is a noble man and he is in the house. Likewise here: the Qur'an is noble while it is in a Book. Or the enclosed thing is noble in the sense that it is noble in a Book, just as one says: "So-and-so is a noble man in himself," so everyone understands that the speaker did not make him an enclosed man, for the speaker did not mean that he is a man in himself sitting or sleeping, but meant that he is noble, his nobility being in himself. Likewise, "a noble Qur'an": the Qur'an is noble in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), even if it is not noble in the eyes of the disbelievers.

The second: the enclosed thing is the whole of His words, ﴿indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾; that is, it is thus in a Book, just as one says: ﴿And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 19] in the Book of God, the Exalted. The meaning then is that in the Preserved Tablet, its description is written: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾. All of this is correct, but the first is more eloquent in magnifying the heavenly recited text.

The fifth issue: What is meant by "the Book"? We say: there are several views:

The first, which is the most correct, is that it is the Preserved Tablet, and His words, the Exalted, support it: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21-22].

The second: the Book is the codex (mushaf).

The third: a Book among the revealed books, so it is a Qur'an in the Torah, the Gospel, and others. If it is said: how is the Book called "Book," when "kitab" is on the pattern fi'al, and it, if it is for the singular, is either a masdar like hisab and qiyam and others, or a noun for what is written, like libas and litham and others? In whatever way it is, the Qur'an would not be "in a Book" in the sense of a masdar, nor would it be in a written thing; rather it is written on a tablet or a sheet, and what is written is not in the Book; it is in the parchment. We say: what you mention of these patterns indicates that the Book is not the written thing, nor is it that in which the written is, nor that upon which the written is. For al-litham is what one veils with, and al-siwan is what the garment is kept in. But since the tablet is only that in which writing is done, it is correct to call it a Book.

The sixth issue: The written is the hidden, as God the Exalted said: ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23], and He said: ﴿like eggs, well-guarded﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. If the intended meaning of the Book is the tablet, then it is not hidden; rather the thing in it is spread out. And if the intended meaning is the codex, then its being written and hidden is absent. So what is the answer to this? We say: what is well-guarded, if it is not precious, is preserved by being kept in view, and it is apparent to people. But if it is noble and precious, it is not satisfied with preservation and safeguarding by sight; rather it is concealed from eyes. Then the more its nobility increases, the more its concealment increases, so sometimes it is stored, then it is made buried. Concealment has become like a necessary part of perfect preservation. So He said, ﴿well-guarded﴾, meaning preserved to the utmost degree of preservation. He mentioned the necessary (al-lazim) and meant what it entails (al-malzum), and this is a type of eloquent speech. You say, for example: "So-and-so is red sulfur," meaning he is rare in existence.

The second answer: the Preserved Tablet is hidden from the eye; none has access to it except specially appointed angels, and none looks at it except purified folk. As for the Qur'an, it is written and hidden forever from the eyes of those who alter it, and preserved from the hands of distorters. If it is said: what is the benefit of its being "in a Book," when every recited thing is in a book? We say: it is to reinforce the refutation of the disbelievers, because they used to say, "It is an invention from himself, fabricated." So when He said it is recited upon him, their claim was dispelled. Then they said: "If it is recited upon him, then it is the speech of jinn." So He said, ﴿in a Book﴾, meaning that the angel did not bring it down upon him except after he took it from a Book, so it is not the speech of angels, let alone the speech of jinn. As for if we say: if it is noble, then it is in a Book, its benefit is clear. As for the benefit of its being ﴿in a well-guarded Book﴾, it is a refutation of those who say: "It is the fables of the ancients" in visible books, meaning: why do the disbelievers not consult it, and why do they not have access to it? Nay, it is ﴿in a well-guarded Book﴾ ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾. So from what we have mentioned, it becomes clear that describing it as a Qur'an became a refutation of those who said: "He mentions it from himself." And His words, ﴿in a Book﴾, are a refutation of those who said: "The jinn recite it to him," since they acknowledged it as recited but disputed something else. And His words, ﴿well-guarded﴾, are a refutation of those who said: "It is recited in a Book, but it is among the fables of the ancients."

The seventh issue: The pronoun in ﴿which none touches﴾ refers, according to the correct view, to the Book. It is possible to say that it refers to what the pronoun in His words ﴿Indeed, it﴾ referred to, and its meaning is: none touches the Qur'an except the purified. The form is an informing, but there is disagreement over whether it is in the sense of a prohibition, just as His words, the Exalted, ﴿and divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] is an informing in the sense of a command. Whoever says the intended Book is the Preserved Tablet, which is the more correct view as we have explained, holds that it is an informing in meaning as it is an informing in wording, if we say the pronoun in ﴿touches﴾ refers to the Book. And whoever says the intended one is the codex, the view differs about it. There is a weak view, transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah, that it is a prohibition both in wording and meaning, and the vowel of the ha' was brought to it not for grammatical inflection; and it has no basis.

[Page 169]

**The Eighth Issue:** If the more correct view is that the Book refers to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), then the correct reading is that the pronoun in ﴿which none touches﴾ refers to the Book. How then can the statement of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, be valid: "It is not permissible for one in a state of minor impurity (muhdith) to touch the mushaf (the bound codex of the Qur'an)"? We say: The apparent meaning is that he derived it from the explicit wording of the verse. Perhaps he derived it from the Sunnah, for the Prophet ﷺ wrote to 'Amr ibn Hazm: "None touches the Qur'an except one who is in a state of purity." Or he derived it from the verse by way of inference (istinbat), and said: Touching in a state of purity is one of the qualities that indicate honour, while touching without purity is a kind of disrespect in meaning. This is because opposites should be matched with opposites. Touching in purity is set against touching without purity, and abstaining from touching is a departure from both of them. Likewise, honour is set against disrespect, but there is a state in which there is neither honour nor disrespect. So we say: One who does not touch the mushaf is neither honoured nor disrespected, and by abstaining from touching he has departed from both opposites. Thus, touching in a state of purity is honour, and touching in a state of minor impurity is disrespect, so it is not permissible. This is a subtle meaning worthy of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and whoever is close to him in rank.

Then there is a subtle juristic point that occurred to this weak servant while reflecting on the interpretation of this verse. He wished to specify it here, for it is one of God's bounties, and it is incumbent upon me to honour it by specifying it with the Book. It is this: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, forbade the one in a state of minor impurity (muhdith) and the one in a state of major impurity (junub, one who is in janabah) from touching the mushaf, and he regarded both as not purified. Then he forbade the one in janabah from reciting the Qur'an, but he did not forbid the muhdith from reciting, and this is an inference from him

[Page 170]

from the words of God Almighty. That is because God forbade the junub from the mosque by His explicit words: ﴿nor one in major impurity, except when passing through [the mosque]﴾ (4:43). This shows that he is not fit for remembrance (dhikr), for if he were fit for remembrance, He would not have prevented him from entering the mosque. This is because God permitted those who remember Him to enter by His words: ﴿in houses which God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned﴾ (24:36), and the one permitted to remember in the mosque is necessarily permitted to enter the mosque. So if the junub were fit for remembrance, he would not be forbidden from entering the mosque and from remaining in it. Yet he is forbidden from both, or from one of them. As for the muhdith, it is known that he is not forbidden from entering the mosque, for some of the Companions used to enter the mosque, and the Prophet ﷺ permitted the people to sleep in the mosque. Sleep is not a ḥadath (minor impurity), since deep sleep necessitates a ruling of ḥadath according to the disagreement among the scholars. Whoever is not forbidden from entering the mosque, it is not established that he is unfit for remembrance, so it is permissible for him to recite.

If it is said: It should not be permissible for the junub to glorify God (tasbih) and seek forgiveness (istighfar), since these are remembrance (dhikr). We say: The Qur'an is the absolute remembrance. God Almighty said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (43:44), and God Almighty said: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ (38:1). His words ﴿in which His name is mentioned﴾ (24:36), together with the fact that we know that the mosque is called a mosque, and the mosque of a people is the place of prostration, and what is meant by it is the prayer, and the remembrance obligatory in prayer is the Qur'an, so the Qur'an is understood from His words ﴿in which His name is mentioned﴾. From the rational standpoint, other than the Qur'an may be mentioned while intending its meaning, so it is speech that is not remembrance. For whoever says, "I seek forgiveness from God," informs about his own state, and whoever says, "There is no power and no strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty," likewise informs about an existing matter. This is unlike one who says: ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ (112:1). He is not speaking it as his own words, but rather he is reciting it, not commanding others to say it. So the Qur'an is the remembrance that is only with the intention of remembrance, not with the intention of mere speech. It is the absolute, and other than it may or may not be remembrance.

If it is said: When he says ﴿Enter it in peace﴾ (15:46) and intends mere information, it should not be Qur'an and remembrance. We say: It is in itself Qur'an, but whoever mentions it with the intention of informing, and intends a command or permission to enter, he is no longer reciting the Qur'an, though it does not cease to be Qur'an. For this reason we say, in our view, that his prayer is invalidated. If he were reciting, it would not be invalidated. This is an answer with subtlety that the reader of this book should notice, because I have distinguished between saying: The utterance of the speaker, "Enter it in peace," with the intention of permission, is not Qur'an, and saying: The speaker of "Enter it in peace" without intention is not a reciter of the Qur'an. As for the rational answer, it is that worship is in opposition to desire, and desire is either the desire of the belly or the desire of the private parts, in most cases, for no one is free of these two, even if he does not desire anything else of food, drink, or marriage. But the desire of the belly may cease to be desire and become a need when hungry, and a necessity when in fear. For this reason God Almighty said: ﴿and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ (56:21), meaning, not for need nor necessity, but merely for desire. We have explained this in this surah. As for the desire of the private parts, it does not cease to be desire, though it may be in the place of need, not necessity. So it is known that the desire of the private parts is not pure desire. Worship is combined with that desire, so the desire of the private parts has never ceased to be a bodily worship. Rather, the Sharia has ruled that the Hajj is invalidated by it, and the fast and prayer are invalidated. As for satisfying the desire of the belly, since it is not pure desire, the prayer and fast are invalidated by it, but not the Hajj, and perhaps the prayer is not invalidated by it either. Having established this, we say: The emergence of what emerges is evidence of satisfying the desire of the belly, and the emission of semen is evidence of satisfying the desire of the private parts. Purification of the soul is obligatory by both of them, but the outward and inward are parallel. So God Almighty commanded the purification of the outward at the occurrence of minor impurity and emission, to match the inward. A person who has insight, and reflects on purifying his inward when performing ghusl for janabah, finds lightness and eagerness for prayer and remembrance.

Here is a completion of this subtle point: If someone says: If your statement were correct, it would necessitate that ablution be obligatory by eating, just as it is obligatory by minor impurity, since eating is satisfying desire. [Page 171]

This is just as ghusl was made obligatory by emission, because it is evidence of satisfying desire, and likewise by penetration, because it is satisfying by penetration. So likewise, minor impurity and eating. We say: Here is a hidden secret, which is what we have explained: that eating may be for need and necessity. So we say: Eating cannot be known to be for desire except by a sign. When one has a minor impurity, it is known that he has eaten, but it is not known whether it was for desire. As for penetration, it is not for need, nor for necessity, so it is desire in any case. The Lawgiver therefore attached the obligation of purification to two indicators. One is his ﷺ saying: "Water is only from water," for emission is like minor impurity. Just as minor impurity, which is what emerges, is the root in making ablution obligatory, so likewise emission, which is emergence, should be the root in making ghusl obligatory, for by it the satisfying of need and desire becomes clear, since after emission a person does not, outwardly, desire intercourse. The second is what has been narrated from him ﷺ: "Ablution is due from eating what fire has touched." That is evidence of satisfying desire, just as the emergence of minor impurity is its evidence. This is because one under compulsion does not wait until food is fully cooked by fire, but eats however it is. So eating a thing after cooking is evidence that it is eaten to satisfy desire, not to remove necessity.

Let us return to the answer to the question and say: When this has become clear, al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, judged that the desire of the private parts is pure desire, so worship does not combine with major impurity. Therefore the junub should not recite the Qur'an, while the muhdith is permitted to recite, because minor impurity does not arise from pure desire.

**The Ninth Issue:** His words ﴿except the purified﴾ refer to the angels. God purified them at the beginning of their existence and kept them so throughout their lives. If the meaning were the negation of minor impurity, He would have said: "None touches it except those who are in a state of purity (mutatahhirun)," or "those who are purified (muṭṭahharun)" with the doubling of the ṭā' and the hā'. The well-known and sound reading is ﴿the purified (muṭahharun)﴾, from taṭhir (purification), not from ilhar (causing to be pure). On this basis, another reason is supported for what we have mentioned. Some used to say that it came from the sky, brought down by the jinn, who cast it upon him, just as they used to say about soothsayers (kahin). For they used to say: The Prophet ﷺ is a soothsayer. So He said: ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾, those who have been purified from impurity and are not a place of corruption and bloodshed, so they do not corrupt and do not shed blood. Others are not purified in this sense. Thus this is a rebuttal to those who said he was a fabricator, and to those who said he was a poet, and to those who said he was possessed by a jinn, and to those who said he was a soothsayer. All of these were their claims, and all were refuted by what God Almighty mentioned here of the attributes of the Book of God, the Mighty.

**The Tenth Issue:** His words ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar). The Qur'an that is in a book is not a revelation (tanzil) but rather something revealed (munazzal), as God Almighty said: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ (26:193). We say: Using the verbal noun to mean the object is common, as we said regarding His words: ﴿This is the creation of God﴾ (31:11). If it is asked: What is the benefit of shifting from the literal to the figurative in this place? We say: The revelation (tanzil) and the revealed (munazzal) are both objects, and both have a relation to the agent, but the relation of the agent to the verbal noun is stronger, while the relation of the object is an expression of the attribute that subsists in it. We say this about speech as well, for the speech of God is also an attribute subsisting in God in our view, and we say only that it is from the standpoint of form and wording. You may consider another example, so that the matter becomes easy for you without error or mistake in belief. We say, regarding power and what is empowered: the relation of power to the agent is more eloquent than the relation of the empowered object, for power is in the one who has power, while the empowered object is not in it. So if one says, "This is the power of God, the Most High," it has a greatness that does not exist in saying, "This is what God has empowered," because the greatness of a thing is by the greatness of God. So when you make the thing subsisting in the magnification, not separate from it, it is greater. And when you mention it with a term that is said of what does not subsist in God, namely the object, it is less than that. So He said ﴿revelation﴾ and did not say ﴿revealed﴾. Then there is another eloquence here: the object may be mentioned while meaning the verbal noun, contrary to what we have mentioned, as in His words: ﴿an entry of truthfulness﴾ (17:80).

[Al-Isra: 80] That is, "an entry of truthfulness" or "a bringing-in of truthfulness." And He, exalted, said: ﴿every torn-apart [one]﴾ [Saba: 7], that is, *tamziq* (tearing apart). So *al-mumazzaq* (الْمُمَزَّق, "the torn-apart") has the meaning of *at-tamziq* (التَّمْزِيق, "the tearing apart"), just as *al-munazzal* (الْمُنَزَّل, "the sent-down") has the meaning of *at-tanzil* (التَّنْزِيل, "the sending down"), and the reverse is equally so. This eloquence is that the verb is not seen, while the object of the verb becomes visible, and the visible is stronger in knowledge. So one says: "He tore them apart with *tamziq*," and it is an act known to everyone with a clear knowledge that reaches the degree of sight. The *tamazzuq* (التَّمَزُّق, "being torn apart") here becomes, just as *al-mumazzaq* became, fixed and visible. Speech varies according to the contexts of speech, and the one granted success extracts [meanings] by God's granting of success.

His saying: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is also for the glorification of the Qur'an, because speech is magnified by the magnificence of the speaker. For this reason it is said to the messenger of a king: "This is the speech of the king," or "your speech," or "this is the speech of the greatest king," or "the speech of the king who is below him," if the messenger is the messenger of kings. So speech is magnified according to the degree of the speaker's greatness. So when He says: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, there is shown from it a greatness for which there is no equal. We have already explained the interpretation of "the worlds" (al-'alamin) and what it contains of subtleties.

His saying: ﴿a revelation﴾ is a refutation of another group, namely those who say that it is in a book and that none touches it except the purified ones, who are the angels. But the angel takes and teaches people from it, and it is not from God, exalted. That is because a group of the Rafidah (an early Shi'i group) say: "Gabriel was sent down to Ali, so he descended to Muhammad." God, exalted, said: it is from God, not by the choice of the angel either. At this point the truth became clear, so it returned to rebuking the disbelievers.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Is it then this discourse that you are treating lightly?﴾ ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it?﴾

And in this there are issues.

The first issue: What does "this" (hadha) refer to? We say: the well-known view is that it refers to the Qur'an. The use of "hadith" (discourse) for the Qur'an in reference to the eternal speech is frequent, in the sense of it being a noun rather than an adjective. For "hadith" is a noun for what is spoken of, and an adjective describing what is renewed; so one says "amr hadith" (a newly occurring matter) and "rasm hadith" (a new mark), meaning new. And one says: "The hadith (discourse) of so-and-so and his speech pleased me." We have already explained that the Qur'an is eternal, yet it has the delight of new speech and of a discourse that has never been heard.

The second view: it refers to what they had discussed earlier, in His saying, Most High: ﴿And they used to say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers of old?"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 47–48]. This is because the speech is self-contained and coherent, for He, Most High, answered them with His saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed, the former and the latter"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49], and mentioned the proof against them in His saying: ﴿We created you﴾, and in His saying: ﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ ﴿Have you considered that which you sow?﴾ Then, after establishing the proofs, He swore an oath with His saying: ﴿So I swear﴾, and He made clear that all of that is information from God with His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾. Then He returned to their speech and said: ﴿Is it then this discourse﴾ which you speak of ﴿that you are treating lightly?﴾, [meaning] for the sake of your companions, knowing its opposite while saying it, or are you resolute in it, firm in persistence? We will make its meaning clear by explaining the one who "treats lightly" (mudhin), and in this there are two views:

One: that the "mudhin" is meant as "the one who denies." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "Is it with the Qur'an that you deny?" The verification in this is that *idhan* (treating lightly) is softening speech to win over the listener without believing the speech to be sound on the part of the speaker, just as an enemy, when unable to overcome his enemy, says to him: "I am praying for you and praising you," as flattery, while lying. So the use of "mudhin" for "denier" becomes a second usage. This holds if we say that the "hadith" is the Qur'an.

The second view: the "mudhin" is one who softens his speech and agrees verbally while persisting in opposition. So He said: ﴿you﴾. Among them are those who say that the Prophet is a liar and that resurrection is impossible; this is due to their love of leadership, and you fear that if you believe and prevent your weak followers from disbelief, what you gain through them of your earnings will be lost to you; so you make your provision that you deny the Messengers. The first view is held by most of the exegetes, but the second corresponds to the explicit wording, for "hadith" referring to their speech is more appropriate, and it is an expression of their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ The "mudhin" remains in its literal sense, for they were not "treating the Qur'an lightly." Al-Zajjaj's statement "denying" came after it explicitly. As for His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾, there are several views:

The first: "You make the thanks for blessings that you say, 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ),'" and most of the exegetes hold this.

The second: "You make your livelihood and earnings the denial of Muhammad." It is said: "So-and-so cut off the road as his livelihood." *Rizq* (provision) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) used for what is provided; it is said of what is eaten "rizq," just as of what is power "qudrah" and of what is created "khalq." On this basis, *takdhib* (denial) is a verbal noun intended to refer to that by which they obtained their aims. As for His saying: ﴿you deny﴾, on the first view the meaning is their denial of what God, Most High, said: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon God is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6], and other than that; and on the second view the meaning is all that proceeded from them of denial, and this is closer to the wording.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 83–85:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat,﴾ ﴿while you are looking on at that moment,﴾ ﴿and We are nearer to it than you, but you do not see,﴾ and in this there are issues:

The first issue: the meaning of ﴿fa-lawla﴾ (why then) is "hallā" (why not), from the four exhortative particles (al-tahḍīḍ, expressions of urging): "lawlā," "lawmā," "hallā," and "alā." It may be said that the origin of these words is "lima lā" (why not), in the form of a question, as a speaker says: "If you are truthful, why does your truthfulness not appear?" We said the origin is "lima lā" because it resembles our saying "hallā" in being a question. Further, a question is sometimes about the existence of a thing and sometimes about the cause of its existence. It is said: "Has Zayd come?" (hal jā'a Zayd) and "Why has he come?" (lima jā'a). The question with "hal" precedes the question with "lima." Further, the interrogative is sometimes used for denial, and this is frequent. Among its instances here is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Is it then at this discourse that you scoff?﴾ (56:81), and His saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and leave off the best of creators?﴾ (37:125), and His saying: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?﴾ (37:86), and their parallels are many. We have already mentioned to you the wisdom in this: the one who negates or forbids does not command that the addressee be called a liar, so he alludes to the negation, lest he need to explain the negation. Having established this, the question with "hal" is for denying the act, and the question with "lima" is for denying its cause. The explanation: whoever says "Why did you do such-and-such?" indicates that the act had no cause, and implies that the act occurred without a cause of its occurrence, which is impermissible. Whoever says "Did you do it?" denies the act itself, not the act without a cause. It is as if in the first he is saying: "If the act had a cause, its doing would have been more fitting," and in the second he is saying: "The act is improper, even if it had a cause."

The second issue: each of the two (the "hal" question and the "lima" question) occurs at the beginning of speech and requires a sentence composed of two sentences originally. As for "hal," its origin is that you use it in two clauses, so you say: "Has Zayd come, or has he not come?" But you may sometimes omit one of the two. As for "law" (if/had), you say: "If such-and-such were, such-and-such would be," and you may sometimes omit the consequent, as we mentioned in the Exalted's saying: ﴿If you knew﴾ (56:76). This is because by "law" he indicates that the thing negated has a proof. So when the speaker says: "If you were knowing," and it is said to him: "Why do they not know?" he says: "If they knew, they would have done such-and-such." Its proof is at hand, and if he is challenged for it, he states it. Since it is established that negation with "law" and negation with "hal" are more emphatic than negation with "la," and negation by his saying "lima," although there is shared meaning, wording, and ruling between them, the exhortative expressions "lawma," "lawlā," "hallā," and "alā" have become like your saying "lima lā" (why not). So the speaker's saying "Will you do it while you are independent of it?" is like his saying "Why do you do it when it is ugly?" and his saying "Hallā will you do it while you are in need of it?" and "Alā will you do it while you are in need of it?" And his saying "Lawlā, lawma" is like his saying "Why do you not do it?" and "Why did you not do it?" In "alā" there is an addition of text, because the transfer of the wording is never free of some text, just as the meaning has come to have some addition over what is in the original, as we have explained.

The Exalted's saying ﴿fa-lawlā idhā balaghat al-ḥulqūm﴾ means: why do they not say at death, which is the time when matters become manifest and the time when words agree? If what they say were a clear truth as they claim, it would have been necessary for them to affirm at the moment of the throes. This points to the fact that everyone believes at death, but the faith of one who did not believe before it is not accepted. It may be said that the origin of these words is "lima lā" (why not), in the form of a question, as a speaker says: "If you are truthful, why does your truthfulness not appear?" We said the origin is "lima lā" because it resembles our saying "hallā" in being a question. The question with "hal" precedes the question with "lima." Further, the interrogative is sometimes used for denial, and this is frequent. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 56, verses 86–87:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then why, if you are not to be held accountable,﴾ ﴿do you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: Most of the exegetes hold that ﴿fa-lawla﴾ in the second instance is a repetition, and it is the very same one that the Exalted mentioned in ﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾. It has one single answer (jawab), and its estimated form, according to what al-Zamakhshari said, is: "Then why do you not bring it back when it reaches the throat," meaning: "if you are not to be held accountable." Some others said: it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whenever there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance, no fear shall be upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38], where ﴿no fear﴾ is made the answer to two conditions. The apparent meaning, however, is contrary to what they said, and it is that one should say: the answer of lawla in His saying ﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾ is what is indicated by what precedes it, that is, "you deny during the duration of your lives, making denial your provision and livelihood." So "then why do you not deny at the time of the death-throes," while at that time you know the matters and witness them. As for the lawla in the second instance, its answer is ﴿do you not bring it back﴾.

The second issue: Regarding ﴿madinin﴾ there are several opinions. Some said: it means "owned/subjugated" (mamlukin), and some said: "recompensed" (majziyyin). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from dana-hu al-sultan, when he governed him. It may also be said that it means "not residing" (ghayra muqimin), from madana, when he resided; it is then of the pattern fa'il, and from it comes al-madinah (the city), whose plural is madai'in without showing the ya', whereas if it were of the pattern maf'alah, its plural would have been madayin, like ma'ayish with the ya' retained. The reasoning is that it may be said: some people denied the lasting punishment, and some people acknowledged punishment but denied its permanence. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. It was said: if you are as you claim, that you will not remain in the lasting punishment, then why do you not return yourselves to the world, if the Hereafter is not the abode of residence? As for the interpretation on the basis of "recompensed" (majziyyin), the explanation is similar to this, as if He said: you will affirm at the time of death-throes the messengers of God concerning the gathering; then if after that you are not recompensed, why do you not return yourselves to your worldly life? For the hindrance is only to the recompense, and were it not for recompense you would be free to choose, as you were in your worldly life, which is not the abode of recompense, choosing to be wherever you wish among places. As for our opinion, "owned" (mamlukin), from al-milk, and from it al-madinah for the queen's domain, the matter is more evident, in the sense that: when you are not under the power of anyone, then why do you not return yourselves to the world, as you were in your worldly life, which is not an abode of recompense, while that is the desire of your souls and the wish of your hearts? All of this, upon close examination, returns to one single statement. They used to take the words of the philosophers in some matters and not others, and they used to say in terms of natures (tiba'i') that rain comes from clouds, which are generated by celestial causes, and plants are likewise, and animals likewise, and there is no choice for God in anything. It is all the same to Him, the denial of the messengers and the gathering. So the Exalted said: If the matter is as they say, then what is the matter with the naturalist who claims knowledge, that he is unable to return the soul from the throat, while in nature there is, in his view, a possibility for that? For they hold that survival is through nourishment and the removal of diseases through medicine. And when this is known, if we say ﴿not subject to account﴾ means "not owned," it returns to their statement of denying choice and reversing affairs as God wills; and if we say "not residing," it is likewise, because denial of the gathering is based on the doctrine of nature; and if we say "not called to account and recompensed," it is likewise. Then, when He made clear that death is certain and the gathering after it is necessary, He made clear what will be after the gathering, so that this would be an incentive for the responsible person toward righteous deeds and a deterrent for the rebellious from disobedience and lying, and so He said:

It is all the same to Him, the denial of the messengers and the gathering. So the Exalted said: If the matter is as they say, then what is the matter with the naturalist who claims knowledge, that he is unable to return the soul from the throat, while in nature there is, in his view, a possibility for that? For they hold that survival is through nourishment and the removal of diseases through medicine. And when this is known, if we say ﴿not subject to account﴾ means "not owned," it returns to their statement of denying choice and reversing affairs as God wills; and if we say "not residing," it is likewise, because denial of the gathering is based on the doctrine of nature; and if we say "not called to account and recompensed," it is likewise. Then, when He made clear that death is certain and the gathering after it is necessary, He made clear what will be after the gathering, so that this would be an incentive for the responsible person toward righteous deeds and a deterrent for the rebellious from disobedience and lying, and so He said:

﴿And if he is of those brought near [to God],﴾ ﴿then there is rest and provision and a Garden of bliss.﴾ This is the way its connection is understood in meaning. As for its connection in wording, we say: when He said, ﴿Why, then, if you are not to be held to account,﴾ ﴿would you not bring it back?﴾ and this implied that bringing back life and soul into the body is not within their power, and that there is no return for them to the world after death, it was as if He had said: "You, after death, will remain forever in the abode of permanence and will be recompensed." So the one who is recompensed, if he is of those brought near, then for him is ﴿rest [rawḥ] and provision,﴾ and in this there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the meaning of rawḥ (rest/mercy), and in this there are several views.

The first: it is mercy. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not despair of the mercy [rawḥ] of God﴾ [Yusuf: 87], meaning, of the mercy of God.

The second: it is comfort.

The third: it is joy. The root of rawḥ is spaciousness, and from it comes the word al-rawḥ, for the spaciousness between the two legs without a wide gap. It has also been read as "fa-rūḥun" with a damma on the rāʾ, meaning mercy.

The second issue: in the sentence there is an implied element, its estimated form being: "then for him is rawḥ." The fāʾ made this explicit because it is the fāʾ of the apodosis (fāʾ al-jazāʾ), which links the clause to the condition. Thus it is known that the clause is an apodosis. The same applies when it is a command, a prohibition, or a past verb. This is because when the apodosis is in the future tense, its being an apodosis is known by the apparent jazm (jussive) in hearing and in writing. These things that were mentioned do not admit of jazm. As for other than the command and prohibition, this is clear. As for the command and prohibition, the jazm in them is not because they are apodoses, so there is no sign of the apodosis in them. Therefore they chose the fāʾ, for it indicates the ordering of one matter upon another, and the apodosis is ordered upon the condition.

The third issue: concerning al-rayḥān (provision/sweet herb). Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ ﴿and burning in Hellfire﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: He said here, ﴿of the deniers, the astray﴾, and earlier He said: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 51], and we have already explained the benefit of the advancement and postponement there.

The second issue: He mentioned the three pairs at the beginning of the surah in one expression and repeated them in another. He said: ﴿the companions of the right hand (maymanah)﴾, then He said: ﴿the companions of the right hand (yamin)﴾; and He said: ﴿the companions of the left (mashʾamah)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 9], then He said: ﴿the companions of the left (shimal)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 41], and He repeated them here. In the three places He mentioned the companions of the right hand either with one wording or with two wordings, one different from the other. He mentioned the foremost at the beginning of the surah with the wording "the foremost," and at the end of the surah with the wording "the close ones." He mentioned the companions of the Fire at the beginning with the wording "the companions of the mashʾamah," then with the wording "the companions of the shimal," then with the wording "the deniers." So what is the wisdom in this? We say: as for the foremost, he has two states: one in this world and the other in the Hereafter. So He mentioned him the first time by what belongs to him in the first state, and the second time by what belongs to him in the final state. He has no intermediate state between standing for the reckoning and the reckoning itself; rather he is transported from the world to the highest of ʿIlliyyun. Then He mentioned the companions of the right hand with two close wordings, because their state is near the state of the foremost. He mentioned the disbelievers with three wordings, as if in this world they deceived them by saying that they were the people of an inauspicious place, so they were described with the inauspicious place, for mashʾamah is a noun of place. Then He said: ﴿the companions of the left﴾, for in the Hereafter they are given their book in their left hand and stand in a place that is on the left, because they are of the people of the Fire. Then, when He mentioned their state at the first gathering by their being of the companions of the left, He mentioned what they would have of scorching winds and boiling water, and did not limit Himself to that. Then He mentioned the cause of it, saying: ﴿Indeed they were before that affluent﴾ ﴿and they used to persist﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 45–46]. So He mentioned the cause of the punishment, because, as we have explained many times, the just one mentions a cause for punishment, while the bountiful one does not mention a cause for favor and bounty. Thus He reminded them in the Hereafter of what they had done in the world, saying: ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers﴾, so that the ordering of the punishment would be upon denying the Book, and justice would become apparent. The rest is clear.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed this is the truth of certainty﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: To what does "this" (hadha) refer? We say: there are several aspects:

First: the Qur'an.

Second: what He mentioned in the surah.

Third: the recompense of the three pairs.

The second issue: How did He attribute "truth" (haqq) to "certainty" (yaqin) when both have the same meaning? We say: there are several aspects:

First: this is the construction of attribution, just as He attributed "the side" to "the western" in His words: ﴿You were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], and attributed "the abode" to "the Hereafter" in His words: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. However, the implied element here is not apparent, for the condition for that is that it be such that it is described as certainty and that truth is attributed to it, and what is described as certainty after the attribution of truth to it.

Second: it is from the construction that carries the meaning of "min" (from), as one says: "a door of teak" and "a teak door," and "a ring of silver" and "a silver ring," so it is as if He said: "it is the truth from certainty."

Third: and it is closer to these, what Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned, that this is a kind of emphasis. One says: "this is of the very truth of truth," and "the correctness of correctness," meaning its ultimate end and final limit beyond which there is no reaching. What is established in explaining this is that the human being's clearest light is what is perceived by the senses, and most of those lights are mixed with other things. So when the seeker reaches its beginning, he says: "I found such-and-such a matter," but then, although the wording applies to it correctly, it is not distinguished from other things; so the seeker goes into the middle and takes his object from its center. An example: one who seeks water, then reaches a great pool; if he takes some from its edge, he says: "It is water," and perhaps another says: "This is not water, it is mud." But the water is what he takes from the middle of the pool; what is at the edge of the pool is water relative to other bodies. Then if it is compared to pure water, it may be called something else. So if he says: "This is truly the water," he has emphasized, and he may say: "the truth of the water," meaning: this is water in truth, such that no one can say anything against it. Likewise here, as if He said: "This is certainty in truth, not the certainty which some say is not certainty." There is another possibility: the attribution is on its real meaning, and its sense is that this statement is for you, O Muhammad, and for the believers, and the truth of certainty is that you say such-and-such. Close to this is what is said: "the truth of perfection is that the believer prays." This is like what has been said regarding his words (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to fight people until they say 'there is no god but Allah'; when they say it, they have protected their blood and property from me, except by its right," that the pronoun refers to the word, meaning "except by the right of the word," and from the right of the word is the payment of zakah and prayer. Likewise, the truth of certainty is to know what Allah the Exalted said in the event concerning the three pairs. Based on this, its meaning is: certainty is not right and does not exist unless it is true in what it states, so affirmation is the truth of certainty which it deserves.

As for His words: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, its explanation has already been given, and we said that when He made the truth clear and the disbelievers refused, He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): this is the truth; if they refuse, do not abandon them nor turn away from them, glorify your Lord within yourself, and it is not incumbent upon you regarding your people whether they affirm you or deny you. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: glorify and remember your Lord by His Greatest Name. This is connected to what follows, for in the surah after this one He says: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾ [al-Hadid: 1]. So it is as if He said: whatever is in the heavens glorifies Allah; so you must agree with them and not turn to the small, misguided faction, for everything with you glorifies Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

The exegesis of the surah is complete, and Allah knows best what is correct; to Him is the return and the final place of return. May Allah send blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right hand﴾ ﴿Then, "Peace be upon you," from the companions of the right hand﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first: the companions of the right hand greet one another with it, as Allah the Exalted said earlier: ﴿They hear therein no ill speech nor sinful utterance﴾ ﴿but only the saying, "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25].

The second: ﴿Then peace for you﴾ means safety for you from a matter your heart feared, for he is at the highest of ranks. This is like what is said to one whose heart is attached to his absent son, when the son is serving with a generous person: he says to him, "Be free of concern regarding your son, for he is at ease."

The third: this sentence conveys the greatness of their state, as one says, "So-and-so, how excellent he is (inahuka bihi), and it is enough for you that he is so-and-so," indicating that he is praised beyond excellence.

We say: some of this has already become clear, so we say: it is possible that the intended addressee of the speech is the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case there is an aspect, which is what we mentioned: that this is a consolation to the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they are not in need of any intercession or other things. As for the close ones, they remain with you and do not separate from you, even though you are higher in rank than them.
